Chapter 1

The red notification sat in the corner of Mara’s vision.

Cam glitching. Report disruption.

She looked across the aisle. Cam sat completely still, his hands flat on his desk. Fingers pale against the surface. His eyes were locked on a scuff mark on the floor, pointedly avoiding the space where his classmates sat. One finger tapped the desk twice, stopped, then tapped twice again, like he was stuck on the same small piece of a thought. Around him, a few other students glanced over before looking away quickly. They had all seen the notification too.

The Guide lived in the corner of her vision and, most days, in the middle of her thoughts.

The notification pulsed in her peripheral vision. It would not go away until she answered it. Across the room, Mr. Halden stood at the front of the class, his posture relaxed, though his attention was a physical weight. He was watching them. He was watching her, specifically.

"Mara," he said.

Not a question. A prompt.

Mara knew what he meant. Everyone knew.

Lila leaned over, her voice barely a whisper. "Just report it. It is fine."

It was not fine. But she looked genuinely scared. Lila never said it like that, all the words standing separate.

The Guide pulsed the report button again. Insistent.

Mara turned back to Cam. He still had not raised his head.

If she pressed the button, Cam would be pulled from class within the minute. Someone from Wellness would come for him. There would be questions, forms, maybe a review.

Maybe recalibration.

Fixed, according to the Guide.

If she did not press it, the system would flag her too.

Her thumb moved toward the prompt. One press. That was all it would take. Cam would get help. She would stay out of trouble. Everything would smooth over. Her thumb hovered there.

Then she thought about Cam’s eyes locked on that scuff mark. About how still he was sitting. How he was trying to hold himself together by not moving at all.

“He is not a disruption,” Mara said.

Mr. Halden’s expression did not change.

“The system disagrees.”

"He is a person. Not a glitch to report."

Halden walked toward her slowly. He did not look angry. He looked disappointed in a way that felt heavier.

"Mara, you are a good student. You understand how this works. The system flagged him. Now someone needs to report it officially. That activates the response. The student closest to the disruption reports it. That's you. A flag is not a report, Mara. People report people."

"I am not reporting him."

He stopped. Behind him, the rest of the class watched and did not move, the way they had been trained to.

Halden tapped his tablet.

Warning: Insubordination logged.

Mara stared at the word.

She had to ask the Guide what it meant, which felt unfair since the Guide was the one accusing her of it.

Refusing to follow authority, the Guide supplied.

Mara frowned.

So basically: asking questions.

Mara’s stomach dropped. The notification appeared in her vision, cold and clinical.

Recommendation: Wellness Recalibration Assessment. Schedule TBD.

Not immediate. But scheduled. Pending.

"Sit down, Mara," Halden said quietly.

Cam finally looked at her. His eyes were wet.

Mara stood up.

For a second, no one moved. Then a few students looked down at their desks like that would make them less involved.

She walked to the door.

The lock clicked before she reached it.

Automatic.

The Guide logged another notice in the corner of her vision.

Exit restricted during active classroom incident.

Mr. Halden sighed and turned back to his screen. He did not look surprised. He looked like he had done this a hundred times.

“Mara,” he said, “you can sit down, or you can go to Student Wellness.”

Mara kept her hand near the door.

The room was too quiet.

Halden tapped something on his tablet.

The lock released.

Not because he had changed his mind. Because the system knew where she would go next.

Mara stepped into the hall.

Behind her, class started again like she had already been removed from it. The hallway smelled like floor wax and another chemical that she had never noticed before. She stood outside the door, her hand hovering near the door frame. Inside, she could already hear Mr. Halden’s voice starting up again. She looked down the hallway and started walking.

Halfway down the hall, a new line opened under the warning in her vision.

Student Wellness. Third floor. Now.

The Guide already knew where she was going. It just wanted her to arrive on time.

Chapter 2

The Student Wellness office was on the third floor in a room that felt designed to make you calm whether you wanted to be or not. The walls were soft gray. The lighting was warm. There were plants in corners that probably never got actual sunlight.

A woman behind the desk didn't look up whenMara walked in. She already knew she was coming.

"Mara Vale," she said, reading from her screen. Not asking. Confirming. "Insubordination incident, first period. Refusal to report a peer disruption."

"Yes."

She tapped her tablet. Information flowed directly into her overlay.

"Your emotional regulation markers show elevated stress," the woman said, studying her screen. "But I see an anomaly here. Response Latency. The system tracks the time between an external prompt and your internal choice. You're... pausing. Too often. It’s an unproductive data loop, Mara. You’re letting silence sit where an optimized decision should be. It’s inefficient."

New meditation times appeared in her vision. Adjusted lunch period. Different class routes designed to minimize hallway interaction. All of it official. All of it already decided.

"These recommendations will help stabilize you," she said. "You can return to class now."

Mara didn't argue. There was no point.

Mara walked back down to the bathroom instead of class, there was only 5 minutes left until lunch anyways. The Guide didn't stop her. It already knew where she was going.

\* \* \*

The cafeteria was loud the way it was always loud. Not messy loud. Not people talking over each other loud. Just a steady, organized kind of noise. The Guide kept conversations moving. It gave you the right comeback when somebody teased you and the right laugh when something was only kind of funny. By the time you sat down with your tray, half the day had already been smoothed flat behind you.

Mara followed Lila through the line, knowing what was being served before she saw it. Roasted grain bowls, apple chips, protein bars, and something green that everybody called salad even though it looked like it had been printed instead of grown. Mara’s Guide suggested the grain bowl with extra carrots because she had skipped breakfast. She took it because there wasn't really a reason not to.

Lila grabbed the same thing and frowned at her tray. "You copied me."

"The Guide copied you."

"Fair."

They found our usual table by the side wall. Not the best table. Not the worst. Just the one we had been sitting at since fourth year, before friend groups became official without anyone ever saying they were. Nessa, June, and Connor were already there. Nessa and June were both talking at the same time so fast Mara had to focus to catch the real conversation under the polished words. Connor was destroying his protein bar with a fork for reasons no one had asked about.

GUIDE30: 30 YEARS OF CONNECTION. JOIN THE FUTURE. A banner was projected on the cafeteria wall. It shifted colors every few seconds. Gold, blue, then white. Brighter than the rest of the room.

"My dad already bought our family passes," Nessa said. She took a bite of her apple. "He says it's going to be the biggest event of the decade."

"My mom is worried about the crowd," June added. "But she wants to be there."

Connor poked his straw into his milk carton and looked at her. "Where were you this morning?"

"Student Wellness."

"What for?"

"Insubordination."

Connor didn't react like it was a big deal. He just nodded and turned to June. "See? This is why you always report the glitches. Way less paperwork."

Lila set her drink down harder than necessary.

"That's not funny," she said.

Connor shrugged. "I'm not joking."

"Mara had a choice and she made it," Nessa said carefully.

"She made the wrong choice," Lila said. She was looking at me now. Really looking at me. "Cam's going to get recalibrated anyway. The system already flagged him. Your refusal to report it just made everything worse. For you. For nothing."

Mara kept her lips sealed, she had so much to say but knew it wouldn’t make a difference to Lila. .

"Now you're marked," she continued. "And Cam still gets recalibrated. So what was the point?"

"The point was—"

"The point was you wanted to feel like you were doing something. But you weren't. You just made it harder for yourself."

The table went quiet.

Connor looked between them like he was watching a tennis match. "So... back to the party, or..."

"It's not a party," Nessa said quietly. "It's an event."

"Same difference," Connor said. He took a sip of his milk. "Both have food that doesn't taste like the cafeteria."

Lila turned away from Mara and leaned closer to Nessa. They started talking again, but Mara barely heard them.

Guide30. Placement. Who was going with whose family.

The banner on the wall shifted from blue to gold.

GUIDE30. THE FUTURE IS WAITING. 24 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.

"...in the Lumen training cohort now," Nessa was saying. "Tobias." She said his name with a smile, the way you do when you're proud of someone.

Mara had met Nessa’s brother Tobias once, a long time ago.

She and Nessa had both been five. Tobias had been ten, and he had barely spoken in full sentences back then. His Guide had been installed at three, like everyone else’s, but it had not worked right for him.

Mara remembered him standing in the kitchen doorway, trying so hard to get one word out. Nessa had hung off his arm and answered for him, like if she talked fast enough, nobody would notice that Tobias couldn’t.

A few months later, Tobias had been recalibrated.

Mara’s mom had explained the word in the car on the way home from a birthday party. She had said it gently. “It just means they fixed his Guide so it can help him the way it’s supposed to,” Mom had said.

Now Tobias was nineteen. He gave presentations to actual scientists. He called Nessa on Sundays, and Nessa shared pieces of those calls all week, bragging on how good her brother was doing now.

The Guide had been part of all of it.

Around them, the cafeteria buzzed. Everyone was excited about the Guide30 event. Everyone was sure. Everyone except her.

Mara felt a notification slide across her vision.

Wellness suggestion: Please maintain recommended social distance. Meditation time approaching.

She dismissed it. She could tell it did not like that. But it was right. Mara was supposed to be somewhere else. Doing something else. Existing smaller.

Lila laughed at something Nessa said. She kept her eyes fixed on the display, intentionally avoiding Mara’s gaze.

The banner shifted colors again. Gold to white to blue.

Over and over. 24 Days to THE GUIDE30

Chapter 3

Lila was still annoyed that Mara had not reported Cam. She just was not saying it directly. After last period, she walked beside Mara and talked about the weekend like nothing had happened. Guide30 practice. Nessa’s family passes. Whether June’s mom would actually let her go to the city center.

Her voice was quick and bright, but her eyes kept sliding toward Mara and away again. Mara knew that look. Lila was waiting for her to admit she had been wrong.

Even though Lila was clearly still fuming, the system was actively adjusting her social output, keeping the sharp edges of her annoyance suppressed so she could communicate appropriately. That was the Guide at work. It was smoothing the friction between us in real-time, preventing the messy, honest outburst she clearly wanted to have.

"My mom wants to do something on Saturday," she said, her inflection perfectly calibrated. "I don't know what yet. Probably something boring."

It sounded like she was reading from a script, but her delivery was perfectly modulated, not too loud, not too quiet, just the right amount of casual. She was not happy, but because of the Guide’s subtle interference, she was operating as if everything was perfectly fine.

Mara shifted her bag on her shoulder, listening but not really listening. The hallway was crowded. Bodies moved past them in both directions, everyone heading somewhere the Guide had already mapped out.

"That could be fun," Mara said absently.

They pushed through the doors into the afternoon. The rain had stopped, but the sidewalks were still wet. The air smelled sharp and clean the way it always did after a storm. Students spread across the front steps in clusters while transit lanes filled steadily along the street below, the vehicles moving in smooth, synchronized patterns.

Cam was sitting on the concrete wall by the bike racks.

He had a paper book open in his lap. An actual book, with a spine and everything. The pages were thin and yellowed. He wasn't checking feeds or looking around. He was just reading, turning the pages slowly like he had all the time in the world.

A couple of kids walked past him without slowing down.

Lila stared. "What is he doing?"

"Looks like reading…"

"In public?"

Mara watched Cam for a moment. He seemed completely alone, even though they were surrounded by people. A gust of wind caught the corner of one of the pages, and he caught it with one hand before it could fold over. The movement was quick and sure. He'd been expecting it.

"He's probably waiting for someone," Mara said.

"He's reading a paper book in front of everyone. At school." Lila said it like those two facts together added up to something wrong. "That's weird."

Cam looked up. His eyes moved across the crowd until they landed on Mara. For a second he just looked at her, really looked at her, like she was actually worth noticing. Then Mara looked away too fast.

"Oh my gosh," Lila said immediately.

"What?"

"You were totally looking at him."

"I was not."

"You were. You got that look."

Mara kept walking down the steps. "He's marked, like I am. That's why I was looking."

Lila stopped walking. When Mara turned back, Lila was standing there with her arms crossed, looking at her like she didn't quite recognize her.

"He's not marked," Lila said. "You didn't report him, he hasn't been recalibrated."

"Not yet."

They stood there on the wet steps, rain dripping from the gutters above them. The afternoon was getting darker. The city felt smaller, more crowded, even though everyone was spread out.

"Since when do you care this much?” Lila’s voice dropped. “That’s not like you. And it’s going to make things worse for you.” Her voice was quieter now, and that made it worse. “Cam’s his own person, okay? He’s not your responsibility.”

"I know he's not my—"

"You're marked for recalibration. Do you understand what that means? That means the system sees you as a problem. And if you keep standing up for people like Cam, if you keep questioning things and not following protocol, they're going to push it faster. They're going to fix you faster."

The words hung there between them. Around them, other students moved past, heading toward the transit platform. Nobody else was having conversations like this. Nobody else seemed to notice that anything was wrong.

"I'm not trying to be a problem," Mara said.

"I know you're not. That's the thing. You're not trying to be anything. You're just... acting weird, it’s going to pull you away. From all of us." Lila's expression softened a little, like the frustration underneath had shifted into something closer to worry. "I'm just scared for you, okay?"

The transit platform doors slid open below them.

"Come on," Lila said, and started down the steps.

✦✦✦

The next morning Mara headed to her first period class. The hallway was still full. Students brushed past each headed in every direction, backpacks swinging. The Guide routing them around each other in smooth automatic patterns. Nobody slowed down. Nobody noticed the women with the grey badge standing in the middle of the hall, outside the library waiting.

"Mara Vale," she said. "I'm glad I caught you."

Mara's stomach did that drop thing it did now whenever an adult said her name like that.

"Hi," Mara said.

"I'm Ms. Marie Cole. I oversee the wellness programs across all the district schools." She stepped a little closer. Not threatening. Just intense. "I wanted to check in about your assessment yesterday. And your insubordination incident."

Marie Cole. A name she had heard before. Mara tried to place it.

"The system flagged some interesting patterns," Ms. Cole ontinued, glancing at her tablet. "Elevated stress markers. Social withdrawal. And then refusing to follow protocol during first period."

The hallway was emptying out. Most students were already in classes. It was just the two of them.

"It's was nothing," Mara said.

"Actually, it's something I want to understand better." Ms. Cole smiled. It didn't change her face. "Can you walk me through what happened in Mr. Halden's class?"

Mara did. She explained about Cam glitching. About being asked to report it. About saying no.

Ms. Cole listened without interrupting. When Mara finished, Ms. Cole was quiet for a moment. Then she smiled again. The same smile. Like it was programmed.

"My father, Dr. Adrian Cole, created the Guide … for me," Ms. Cole said, something in her voice changed when she said his name. Not like a daughter. Like a believer.

"When I was fifteen, I had an accident," Ms. Cole said. She was looking past Mara now, remembering another time and place.

"A car crash. I was in a coma for three weeks. When I woke up, my brain wasn't working the way it was supposed to. The doctors said I might never function normally again. I couldn't remember things. I couldn't make decisions. I couldn't even recognize my own parents sometimes."

Ms. Cole turned back to look at Mara directly.

"My father was developing the Guide then. He was working on something that could help people think clearly. Help them navigate the world without getting lost in confusion." Ms. Cole expression didn't change, but something in her voice shifted. "He wanted to use it to help me. Everyone said it was too risky. Too new. Too much."

She paused.

"But it worked. Within weeks, I could think again. I could remember. I could function. I could be myself again." Ms. Cole looked down at her tablet, but she wasn't reading it. She was remembering. "My father didn't just create the Guide for public good, Mara. He created it because he wanted his daughter back. And it worked."

Mara thought about that. About what it would feel like waking up broken. About someone rebuilding you. About being grateful for the rest of your life.

"When the system identifies a problem, like what happened with Cam, it's not trying to hurt anyone," Ms. Cole said. "It's trying to help. Reporting a peer disruption is how we support students who are struggling. It gets them the help they need."

"By recalibrating them?"

"By stabilizing them, yes. By helping them function the way they're supposed to." Ms. Cole’s smile stayed exactly the same. "I know this is confusing. Growing up with the Guide means you've never had to navigate the world without support. That can feel limiting sometimes. But that limitation is actually a protection. It's what my father gave me. It's what saved my life."

Mara thought about Ms. Cole waking up broken. About the Guide putting her back together. About how she must feel about anyone questioning the thing that made her human again.

"I also know that some students start questioning the system around your age," Ms. Cole continued. "It's normal. You're developing independent thought. You want to make your own choices. But here's what I've learned: people who start questioning protocol, who start isolating from their peers, who start deliberately ignoring guidance,those patterns tend to escalate, and it doesn't turn out good for them."

She said it firmly, like it was a medical fact. Like she was describing symptoms of a disease that needed treatment.

"And when they escalate, the system has to intervene more actively." Ms. Cole closed her tablet. Her smile remained perfectly steady. "I want to help you before that happens. I'm here if you need to talk. About anything. Whenever you need to."

She stood, smoothing one hand down the front of her jacket like the conversation was now over.

Mara did not move.

Her Guide pulsed softly behind her eyes.

Wellness check recommended.

Mara dismissed it before the full message could open.

Ms. Cole paused at the door and looked back once. "Take care of yourself, Mara."

Then she was gone.

For a few seconds, the hallway felt too quiet.

Mara pulled the library doors open. She could see books on shelves. Real paper books, old ones, the kind that nobody checked out anymore. They sat there gathering dust.

Mara thought about Ms. Cole waking up in a hospital bed, unable to remember her own name. Mara thought about what it would feel like to have a machine fix that. To have something give you back to yourself.

But she also thought about Ms. Cole’s smile. How it never wavered. How it never reached anywhere real. And she thought about what it might cost—not to be broken, but to be reassembled by something that wasn't human.

She thought about whether Ms. Cole was actually grateful, or whether the Guide had taken her gratitude and made it into something else. Something that looked like kindness from the outside. Something that felt like being crushed very, very gently from within.

Mara reached for her own mind. Tried to feel where she ended and the Guide began. Tried to understand if there was a difference.

She couldn't tell anymore.

Chapter 4

Mara’s apartment building sat between a grocery market and a boarded up repair shop that had been closed for as long as Mara could remember. Most things didn’t really break now. Systems caught problems early, ordered replacements automatically, scheduled maintenance before anybody noticed anything was wrong.

Her mom still called the repair shop “Mr. Eli’s place” though, even after ownership transfers and company mergers and whatever else had happened to it over the years.

“He fixed my dad’s heater once in the middle of winter,” she had told Mara when she was younger. “Back before homes diagnosed themselves.”

Mara had laughed when she was younger. How did you even know your heater was broken if your house didn't tell you? How did a person just... show up and fix it?

By the time she reached the third floor, the Guide had already reminded her twice about unfinished assignments and once about hydration levels. She ignored all three notifications and unlocked the apartment door.

The smell of garlic and onions hit her immediately.

Her mom stood at the stove stirring something in a pan while music played softly from the kitchen speaker. Real music, not generated mood tracks like most people used. Older songs with actual instruments and uneven voices.

"How was school?" her mother asked, like she did every day.

"Fine."

Her mother glanced at her. She had that look. The one where she wanted to say something but wasn't sure if she should.

"There's a recalibration notice on your account," her mother said finally. "Pending district reassessment. Scheduled to be determined."

Mara already knew. The notification had been there in her overlay since yesterday’s incident, quiet and persistent.

"What happened?" her mother asked.

It was such a simple question. Such a normal thing for a parent to ask. But the answer wasn't simple anymore.

"I just didn’t want to report someone," Mara said. "And now it’s like I have become a problem."

Mom looked up as Mara dropped her bag near the couch and kicked off her shoes then tried to switch the subject . “So what are you making for dinner?”

“Something you’ll complain about and then eat anyway.”

“That narrows it down.”

Her mom laughed.

Mara headed around the kitchen counter, grabbing a piece of chopped pepper from the cutting board before her mom slapped her hand away.

“Rude.”

“You’re supposed to wash your hands first.”

“I’ll survive.”

“Barely.”

Mara grinned and leaned against the counter while her mom kept cooking. The apartment windows were cracked open a little, letting cool air drift inside along with the sound of traffic from the street below.

For a minute neither of them talked.

Most families filled silence immediately. The Guide helped with that too. Suggested conversation starters. Emotional check-ins. Shared current events based on household interests.

Her mom ignored most of those prompts. She said it made conversations feel fake. At the time, Mara had rolled her eyes so hard it hurt.

Now she wasn’t so sure.

“So how was the rest of your day?” her mom asked, trying to continue the conversation.

“Fine.”

“That answer usually means not fine.”

Mara shrugged, avoiding her mother’s eyes. “Lila annoyed at me.”

The Guide pulsed softly, offering a 'calming response'—a perfectly polite, non-confrontational way to explain herself. It always wanted things clean and tidy. She dismissed it.

“Again? You two have been getting annoyed at each other since second year.”

“It’s worse this time.” Mara picked up a piece of pepper, spinning it in her fingers. “She, she was really upset at me because of the “incident” Mara said making quotes with her fingers as she said incident. “She told me I’m basically a ‘glitch magnet’ now. She said the whole group is nervous because of me.”

Her mom’s expression sharpened. “Because of the incident in class you mentioned?”

“She thinks I’m trying to cause problems on purpose. Since I didn’t report Cam, she’s been watching everything I do and is being super judgy. Today, we had a simulation in Applied Response and she thinks I slowed the team down.”

“Well did you?”

“I don’t think so. I just... I wanted to verify the data before we submitted the input. Lila panicked. She started whispering that I was acting like a collaborator again. She said ‘normal people’ don't second-guess the Guide’s output.”

Her mom stopped stirring for a second. The music in the kitchen felt a little louder in the silence. “And what did you say?”

Mara hesitated. The easiest explanation appeared in her head immediately, thanks to the Guide. Clean. Organized. Quick. She ignored it.

“I didn't say anything. I just did the simulation my way. I thought it would be more accurate. But she... she looked at me like I was a stranger. She told me I was going to get us all flagged.”

Her mom turned the stove lower and leaned back against the counter across from her. “So she’s not just annoyed. She’s scared.”

“She’s embarrassed,” Mara corrected. “She thinks I’m the weird kid now. The one that’s going to get the whole table recalibrated.”

Mara kicked her shoe against the floor tiles and continued softly “Maybe she’s right.”

“Is she?” Her mom’s voice was quiet, steady. “Is trying to think for yourself the same thing as being a disruption?”

“To Lila? To the teachers? To Ms. Cole? Yeah. It is.”

The second Mara said it out loud, her face went hot. It sounded dramatic, but it felt true. It was the core of the friction: she wasn't actually breaking anything, she was just refusing to pretend that everything was perfect.

Her mom stayed quiet for a long moment, then looked at Mara with a look that wasn't pity, it was something closer to pride, and something deeper, like a warning. “Well,” her mom said finally. “Lila isn't raising you. And she definitely doesn't know what’s going on inside your head.”

“She said normal people don’t ignore the Guide.”

Her mom’s expression changed slightly at that. “She said that?”

“She didn’t mean it mean.”

“That doesn’t make it less dumb.”

A sad, tight curve touched Mara’s lips, not quite a smile, Her mom’s features softened into a sympathetic, fleeting expression. then turned back toward the stove. “The Guide is supposed to help people. That’s all.”

"Then why do I feel like I have to listen to it, even when I don't want to?"

Her mom turned from the stove. She looked at Mara for a long moment before answering.

"Because that's how it works," she said. "Once it knows what you need, it's hard to ignore."

"Did it feel like that for you? When you first got it?"

Her mom looked back at the stove. She thought for a minute, as if trying to remember.

"Yes," she said finally. "It did. A little.”

“What was different?”

Her mom huffed softly. “Everything.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It’s the one I have.”

Mara waited.

Her mom grabbed some bowls from the cabinet before continuing. “People forgot things constantly. Directions. Birthdays. Names. Half the time nobody knew what they were doing.”

“That sounds terrible.”

“It was sometimes.” Her mom smiled faintly. “But people also learned things differently.”

“How?”

“You had to sit with questions longer.”

Mara immediately thought of the feeling from class earlier. That uncomfortable pause before an answer settled into place.

“Didn’t that drive everybody crazy?”

“Oh, absolutely.” Her mom handed her a bowl. “But I think it also made people more interesting.”

They ate quietly for a couple of minutes before the apartment lights flickered overhead.

Once. Then again.

Her mom sighed immediately. “Seriously?”

A maintenance notice slid automatically across Mara’s thoughts. Temporary district fluctuation. No action required.

The lights steadied again.

“Can you grab the emergency lantern from the hall closet?” her mom asked. “Just in case the building grid drops completely.”

“We have emergency lanterns?”

"My Guide says we do. Top shelf behind the winter stuff."

Mara wandered into the hallway while the lights flickered one more time overhead.

The closet was packed so full she could barely pull the door open. Storage bins leaned sideways against old coats and tangled cords.

“Why do we keep all this stuff?” Mara called.

“Because every time I try throwing something away, I convince myself I’ll need it later.”

“That seems inefficient.”

“That’s because you’re almost fifteen.”

A reluctant smile tugged at the corner of Mara’s mouth as she dragged the bin out.

The lantern wasn’t on top. Of course not.

She dug through blankets and old boxes while dust floated through the hallway light. One plastic container shifted sideways when she pulled another loose, sending a stack of printed photographs sliding across the floor.

Mara paused.

Printed pictures still felt weird to her. Why print something when the Guide could store every image perfectly forever?

She picked one up carefully.

Her mom looked younger in it. Wind blew her hair across her face while she laughed at whoever had taken the picture. Somebody’s thumb partly covered one corner.

For some reason Mara liked it more because of that.

Another flicker pulsed through the apartment. She heard her dad come through the front door and drop his laptop on the table.

“Hurry before I make your father come help,” her mom warned from the kitchen.

“I’m literally searching through ancient history.”

“Hey now, watch yourself.”

Mara shoved another box aside and spotted a smaller container tucked behind the blankets near the back wall.

Inside were papers. Actual papers. Folded cards. Handwritten grocery lists. Receipts. A map with circles drawn on it in dark blue ink.

People really used to write everything down.

Near the bottom sat a thick dark blue notebook wrapped in a stretched elastic band. The corners were bent and worn soft.

Mara picked it up carefully.

“What even is this?” she muttered.

Her mom appeared in the hallway carrying a glass of water. She stopped when she saw the notebook. “Oh wow,” she said quietly. “I haven’t seen that thing in years.”

“What is it?”

“My journal.”

Mara blinked. “Like… you wrote stuff in it?”

Her mom laughed. “That’s usually how journals work.”

“But why?”

The question slipped out. Her mom looked amused.

“Because people used to write things down when they didn’t want to forget them.”

“The Guide remembers everything.”

“Yeah,” her mom said softly. “That’s kind of the point.”

Mara looked back down at the notebook. The idea of handwriting your own thoughts instead of storing them digitally felt strangely personal.

"You can read it if you want," her mom said. She smiled. "I'm fine with it."

“Seriously?”

“Sure. Just don’t judge me too hard. I was dramatic in my twenties.” She turned and headed back toward the kitchen, where the onions were starting to sizzle louder.

Mara slid the elastic band free and opened the first few pages.

Dad called three times while I was driving and I missed every single one because my phone was buried under fast food wrappers and I was trying to figure out where I was and where I was going. Ugh hate being lost

Mara laughed immediately. “You got lost?”

“All the time,” her mom called from the kitchen.

"So you'd just be driving around with no idea where you were?"

“Pretty much”

Mara flipped another page. The entries were messy. Long stories. Complaints about traffic and work and church people. Nothing sounded polished. That was the weird part. People didn’t really leave unfinished thoughts anymore.

“Mara,” her mom called. “Did you find the lantern or are you reading my emotional baggage?”

Mara smirked slightly and grabbed the lantern from the back corner of the closet. But before she shut the storage bin again, she glanced down at the journal in her hands. She looked at the notebook carefully, as it seemed almost fragile. The cover was soft from being touched a lot, and slightly dusty from being stored. She closed the journal, then opened it again, then closed it. She could hear her mom still moving around the kitchen. She heard her dad walk in the door and put his keys on the table. Mara set the journal on top of the bins, grabbed the lanterns and headed to the kitchen.

✦✦✦

Chapter 5

Mara waited until her mom went to bed before taking the journal into her room. Even though her mom had said it was okay to read, carrying it down the hallway felt strangely personal, like she was opening a door into a life her mom had lived before Mara even existed.

Her room was quiet, except for the low hum of the air system and the soft, glowing projection on the wall. The Guide had already shifted the room into "Nighttime Mode." Dark blue water moved across the display, with artificial moonlight reflecting off the waves. It was supposed to be soothing. It was supposed to help her fall asleep at the optimal time.

Mara swiped at the display, silencing it.

The room instantly felt different. Smaller. More real. The artificial light vanished, leaving the space in actual, deep shadow. Her stomach did a nervous flip. She knew the Guide would flag this as a "disruption of sleep routine," and she knew it would go straight onto her Wellness record. It wasn’t like turning off a lamp; it was like closing a door on someone who was still standing in the room.

She climbed onto her bed and opened the journal near the beginning. The pages crackled softly under her fingers. Even that felt strange. Most things in her world didn’t make noise unless they were supposed to.

The first entries were long. Not organized. Not polished. Just thoughts spilling across paper.

Dad called three times while I was driving and I missed every single one because my phone was buried under fast food wrappers in the passenger seat.

I finally called him back from a gas station twenty miles in the wrong direction because apparently I still can’t follow maps correctly.

He laughed at me for five full minutes.

Mara smiled before she could stop herself. She tried picturing her mom getting lost. It honestly felt impossible.

She turned another page.

Church today felt different.

Pastor Ben talked about how faith requires trust even when we don’t know what’s coming next.

I kept thinking how much of life is basically just not knowing things and trying anyway.

Kind of exhausting honestly.

Mara frowned slightly. Not knowing things sounded exhausting.

She found herself thinking about her grandmother's church.

Three Sundays ago she had agreed to meet Grandma for the morning service. The Guide had pulled up the address automatically. Briarwood Memorial on Elm. It seemed normal. Mara had taken the transit, walked in fifteen minutes early, and texted Grandma to say she was inside.

Grandma had texted back: "Briarwood? I'm at St. Anne's."

Mara had stared at the text for a second before understanding. St. Anne's. Six blocks east. The wrong church entirely.

She had pulled up her Guide history and found the explanation immediately. Grandma had attended Briarwood for a friend's funeral eight years ago. The Guide had logged it, filed it somewhere in its routing, and when Mara asked for "Grandma's church," the Guide had pulled up the wrong association. A ghost from before. A place Grandma hadn't gone in eight years.

The Guide had made a mistake.

Mara had taken the transit over to St. Anne's and arrived twenty minutes late. Grandma had been standing in the parking lot, already dressed to leave. She had hugged Mara, but there was something stiff in it.

"I waited for you," Grandma had said. Just like that. Not a question.

Mara had tried to explain. The Guide had sent her to Briarwood. A routing error. The Guide had logged the wrong church as Grandma's church.

Grandma's expression had shifted then. Not softer exactly, but different. Like she was processing two different pieces of information at once.

"So the Guide sent you to the wrong place," Grandma had said slowly.

"Yeah. It thought you still went to Briarwood."

Grandma had been quiet for a moment. Then she had looked at Mara in a way that made it clear she was thinking about something larger than a missed church service. Something about relying on the Guide. Something about the Guide not always being right.

"Well," Grandma had said finally. "That's unsettling."

Although the Guide had been wrong. The apology had been hers.

After that she had started paying attention to how the answers arrived. The small pause before the Guide spoke. Whether what it told her made sense or just sounded smooth.

Most of the time it made sense.

But it had been wrong once, and once was enough to want to start noticing.

Another page.

Prayed in the car after work because I was overwhelmed and didn’t want to cry in the grocery store parking lot again.

Still not sure God answers prayers the way people say He does.

But sometimes talking to Him feels like breathing out after holding my breath too long.

Mara read that one twice.

Nobody talked like that anymore. Not even her mom. Especially not her mom.

The Guide quietly offered a definition for faith before she even fully thought about the word. She ignored it.

The next few entries jumped forward months at a time. Work stress. Family dinners. A vacation. Small things.

Then the writing changed slightly. Not all at once. Just enough to notice.

Everyone at work got the new assistant update today.

Scheduling is way easier now.

Honestly kind of amazing.

Another page.

Schools are starting implant trials next year.

Parents are freaking out like it’s either the end of the world or the greatest thing ever invented.

Probably somewhere in the middle.

Then:

Saw a little girl answer a math problem faster than I could even read it.

Wild.

Mara kept turning pages. The entries slowly became shorter. Not empty exactly. Just thinner somehow.

Guide integration at work went well.

Less stress overall.

Another.

Traffic has gotten so much better since city sync updates.

Another.

Forgot my password today and realized I barely remember anything myself anymore.

Funny.

Mara stared at that last word. It didn’t feel funny.

The room around her stayed completely still.

She flipped farther ahead. The handwriting itself looked different now. Cleaner. Faster. Less crossed out. Like the thoughts arrived already finished.

Busy week.

Guide update fixed most scheduling issues.

Need groceries.

Another.

Long day.

Didn’t sleep enough.

That was it. No stories. No prayers. No wondering.

Mara frowned and flipped backward a few pages, like maybe she had skipped something by accident.

But she hadn’t.

The journal just… changed. Slowly enough that you almost wouldn’t notice unless you were looking for it.

She kept reading. Something sat in the middle of her chest she didn’t have a name for. Not sadness exactly. More like missing someone she hadn’t met before.

Pages passed. Short entries. Quick thoughts. Doodles.

Then suddenly, squeezed into the corner of one page between two ordinary notes, her mom had written:

I realized today I haven’t actually prayed in weeks.

Not really prayed. Just quick thoughts before bed.

I think constant answers make it easy to forget you still need God.

Mara held her breath, the realization hanging in the air.

Outside her window, lights blinked across apartment towers stretching toward the center of the city. Thousands of windows. Thousands of people probably hearing the same quiet stream of suggestions and reminders moving through their minds every second of the day.

The Guide nudged her gently about tomorrow’s assignments. Then hydration. Then recommended sleep timing.

Mara dismissed all three.

For the first time, the constant interruptions didn’t feel helpful. They felt loud.

She looked back down at the journal.

Near the bottom of the next page was another line written smaller than the others, almost like her mom hadn’t meant to include it.

The Guide always answers quickly.

God usually doesn’t.

But somehow prayer still feels less lonely.

Mara stared at the words until the room around her seemed unusually quiet. Not empty quiet. Just still. The kind of stillness people usually filled immediately.

She realized suddenly that she hadn’t checked a feed, message, or update in almost 15 minutes. That should have felt uncomfortable. Instead it felt like standing outside after being indoors too long.

Mara closed the journal slowly and rested her hand on the cover.

Then, before she could really think through why she was doing it, she whispered softly into the quiet room.

“God?”

The word sat in the room like she dropped it there. Nothing happened. The walls didn’t change. The hum of the air system kept going. Somewhere below, traffic honked and continued on its way. She didn't know what she was expecting.

There was no answer. No sign. No feeling rushing over her.

Just silence. The room didn't feel smaller, just still. The kind of still that felt unfamiliar and comfortable at the same time.

23 days until Guide30.

✦✦✦

Chapter 6

School the next day was uneventful. Mara managed to get through the day without attracting more attention. Even with the recalibration notice hanging silently in her side view, like a warning that any minute something could change, and Lila still pretending nothing was wrong acting just a little upset, she couldn’t stop thinking about her mom’s diary.

As soon as she got home Mara dropped her bag by the door, called a quick “hi” toward the kitchen and went upstairs before her mom could ask how school was. She had homework, but knew that her mom wouldn’t believe that is why she was rushing to her room.

The journal was balanced open beside her while assignment prompts stacked themselves unfinished across the corner of her vision. Mara kept pretending to work for a few minutes, then drifting back to the journal again.

She was rereading one of the older entries about getting lost near a river outside the city when her elbow knocked the journal sideways. The notebook slipped off the bed and disappeared into the narrow gap between the mattress and the wall.

“Seriously?”

Mara groaned and leaned over the side of the bed, reaching blindly down into the gap.

Her fingers caught the back cover first. Then the page.

Rrrrip.

The sound stopped her immediately.

“Oh no.”

She pulled the journal back up carefully. One of the pages had torn near the center fold while she yanked it loose. Not badly. But enough to matter.

Her stomach dropped.

It was ridiculous. Just paper. Old paper.

Still, she smoothed the torn edge carefully with her hand like that might somehow undo it.

The Guide instantly supplied repair suggestions.

ARCHIVAL RESTORATION SERVICES NEAR YOU

A list opened automatically in her vision. Most were shipping services or automated repair centers downtown where machines scanned and restored damaged material in sealed units. Fast turnaround. Guaranteed preservation.

Mara scrolled through listings looking for the closest ones.

One listing sat near the bottom.

Merrick Repair and Restoration. Hand restoration available.

Just an address and a tiny picture of a crooked shop sign hanging over a narrow front window. The shop was closed for the day, but it opened again Saturday morning.

The Guide checked her calendar.

No scheduled events.

Recommended route: transit, sixteen minutes.

A second option sat beneath it in smaller text.

Walking route: twenty-two minutes. Not recommended due to low efficiency.

Mara stared at the listing for another second, then saved the directions. Apparently, she was going to a repair shop on Saturday.

By Saturday morning, Mara had checked the directions to Merrick Repair and Restoration four times.

The Guide still recommended transit. Sixteen minutes, including one transfer and a three-minute walk. It also suggested three automated restoration centers with higher trust ratings, faster service, and verified preservation tools.

Mara ignored those.

She packed the journal into her bag like it was something breakable, which, technically, it now was. Then she chose the walking route before she could talk herself out of it.

Twenty-two minutes. Not recommended due to low efficiency.

For some reason, that made her want to take it more.

The shop sat on an older side street near the edge of the city market district, where buildings crowded closer together and fewer screens covered the windows. Mara almost walked past it because the sign was small and partly faded.

ELI MERRICK REPAIR & RESTORATION

The front window displayed clocks. Not digital ones. Actual clocks with hands. Some were ticking. Some weren’t.

Mara hesitated outside the door longer than necessary. Then she stepped inside.

A bell rang softly overhead.

The smell hit her first. Dust. Paper. Wood polish. Something warm underneath it she couldn’t identify.

The shop felt crowded without feeling messy. Shelves lined every wall, stacked with books, tools, boxes of screws, loose clock parts, framed photographs, old radios, and things Mara couldn’t even name. Nothing matched. Nothing looked optimized. Ticking filled the room softly from a dozen different directions.

Not synchronized.

That was the strange part. The clocks were all slightly off from each other. Mara didn’t know if she liked it or was annoyed by it.

She stood there listening for a second before an older man appeared from the back room, wiping his hands on a cloth.

“Well now,” he said warmly. “Either you’re lost or I finally got a customer under seventy.”

Mara blinked. Then laughed before she meant to.

The man smiled like he hadn’t expected that to work.

“I’m Eli Merrick, You can call me Mr. Eli ” he said. “This is my shop.”

“Mara,” she said.

“Well, Mara,” he said, looking at the torn page in her hand, “what are we trying to save?”

“You repair paper?”

“Depends. You trying to save it or just make it look less guilty?”

She held out the torn journal page carefully.

The man took it gently, adjusting his glasses lower on his nose while he examined the tear. “Mm,” he said quietly. “Good news is paper’s forgiving.”

Something about the way he said it made Mara feel weirdly relieved.

He motioned toward the counter. “I can fix this. Might take a little while though.”

“That’s okay.”

“Well, that’s a rare sentence these days.”

Mara smiled awkwardly, unsure if she was supposed to answer that.

The man set the page carefully beneath a small lamp. “You can wait if you’d like.”

Mara nodded and wandered slowly while he worked.

The ticking sounded louder farther inside the shop. Not annoying. Steady.

She stopped in front of a shelf filled with books. Actual books. Some looked ancient. Others had handwritten labels taped to the spines.

One title caught her eye.

The Chronicles of Narnia.

“Good choice.”

Mara jumped slightly.

A familiar voice came from behind her.

Cam stood near the back doorway holding two mugs in one hand and a stack of books under the other arm. His expression shifted from surprise to immediate embarrassment.

“Oh,” he said. “You’re here.”

Mara stared at him. “You’re here.”

Excellent response, Mara.

Cam looked mildly horrified. “I work here sometimes.”

The older man glanced up from the counter. “You know each other?”

“We go to school together,” Mara and Cam said at the exact same time.

Mr. Eli grinned. “That explains why both of you look uncomfortable.”

Cam sighed. “Grandpa.”

Grandpa.

Mara looked from Cam to Mr. Eli. That made sense. The shop, the books, the way Cam seemed half embarrassed and half at home here.

Cam set one of the mugs beside his grandfather without looking at Mara directly. “You didn’t tell me somebody was here.”

“You didn’t ask.”

“That’s not how information works.”

His grandfather shrugged. “Seems to have worked fine for me.”

Mara laughed again before she could stop herself.

Cam looked even more embarrassed now, which honestly made it harder to stop smiling.

“You ripped a book?” he asked finally.

“A journal.”

His grandfather glanced up briefly. “Important one too, judging by the panic level.”

Mara folded her arms. “I was not panicking.”

“You walked in holding that page like it was a wounded bird.”

Cam snorted softly into his tea.

Mara narrowed her eyes. “I can still leave.”

“No you can’t,” Mr. Eli said easily. “I already started fixing it.”

The ticking filled the room again for a moment.

Cam didn’t rush to fill the silence. Neither did Mr Eli.

For once, Mara didn’t feel like she needed to either.

Chapter 7

Mara stayed at the shop longer than she meant to. At first she blamed the journal page, Mr. Eli had laid it beneath a bright lamp near the counter and was carefully smoothing the torn edges together with tiny tools Mara had never seen before, working like the paper was something that mattered. But honestly, she could have left twenty minutes ago. She just didn't want to.

Cam had disappeared into the back room after the awkward introduction, which somehow made things easier. Mara wandered slowly through the shelves while Mr. Eli worked, running her fingers lightly across old book spines and faded labels. Some of them looked ancient, not museum-preserved ancient, but genuinely old. Used over years. The kind of books people had actually read and loved enough to keep.

"You read?" Mr. Eli asked without looking up from his work.

Mara glanced over at the books in her hands. "Not really."

"Mm."

"That sounded judgmental."

"That's because it was." Mr. Eli’s

Mr. Eli allowed himself a brief, private amusement, while adjusting something on the torn page. His hands moved slowly but confidently, like he wasn’t worried about time running out.

Nobody moved like that anymore. Most people’s attention jumped constantly even when they were standing still. The Guide always kept a dozen things moving in the background at once. Messages. Reminders. Suggestions. Schedules.

Here, the silence stayed where it was.

Mara found herself listening to the clocks again.

“They’re all different,” she said.

“Good observation.”

“No, I mean… shouldn’t they match?”

Mr. Eli finally looked up at her over his glasses. “Why?”

Mara opened her mouth automatically, ready to answer. Then stopped. Because she honestly didn’t know.

Mr. Eli went back to working before rescuing her from it. “People get nervous when things don’t match up exactly anymore,” he said casually. “Used to be normal.”

The Guide quietly offered historical context about pre-sync mechanical variation. Mara ignored it.

“Doesn’t it bother you?” she asked. She stayed by the shelf for a moment listening. The ticking wasn’t random, each clock was keeping it’s own time, it’s own place, its own idea of what ‘right now’ meant.

“Does what bother me?”

“The noise.”

Mr. Eli chuckled softly. “This isn’t noise.”

He pointed upward with the tiny repair tool still in his hand. “Noise is what everybody carries around in their heads all day.”

Mara looked down at the floor before she could stop herself. Noticing the continued notifications from the guide were still sliding through her view.

The bell over the shop door jingled suddenly as someone walked in carrying an old tabletop radio. Mr. Eli greeted him by name immediately. Not through recognition software. Just memory.

Mara watched the entire conversation while pretending not to. The man talked about his granddaughter, Mr. Eli asked questions, and the conversation wandered completely off topic twice. Nobody seemed in a hurry to fix it. Mara realized she'd never seen conversations like this before.

When Cam finally came back out carrying another stack of books, he stopped short when he saw her still there. "You're still here," he said flatly.

"You said that already."

"Yeah, well, usually people leave faster." Cam started reorganizing books on a nearby shelf, moving deliberately, like her presence required him to do something productive. Mara watched him for a second before it occurred to her.

"You are disconnected right now, aren't you?"

Cam froze just slightly. Mr. Eli suddenly became very interested in the journal page in front of him.

"You are," Mara said quietly. It wasn't really a question anymore.

Cam set a book down carefully. "Ya, I do... Sometimes." He didn't look at her while he said it.

"You can actually do that?"

"Technically everybody can. Most people just hate the quiet." Cam slid another book onto the shelf. "My grandpa used to unplug me when I was little. Took me fishing outside the city zones where the signal was weaker. At first I hated it because there was nothing to do."

Mr. Eli smiled faintly at that but didn't interrupt.

"Your parents let him?" Mara asked.

"Not at first. They thought he was making me fall behind socially." Cam glanced at her briefly before looking back at the books. "After a while though, I started liking it. You ever notice how loud your head feels all the time? Like there's always something pulling at you?"

Mara didn't answer immediately. She was still thinking about her room last night, the stillness when she'd muted the display. The way the quiet had felt real in a way nothing else had in months.

Cam leaned against the shelf slightly. “When you unplug, it’s weird at first. Your brain keeps waiting for the next thing to show up. The next answer. The next reminder.” He shrugged again. “Then eventually everything kind of settles down.”

The room felt very still after that.

Mr. Eli finally set down his tools and lifted the repaired journal page carefully beneath the light. “There we are,” he said softly.

Mara walked toward the counter. The tear was barely visible now.

“How did you do that?”

“Very slowly,” Mr. Eli replied, humor reaching his eyes.

Mr. Eli slid the page carefully into a protective sleeve before handing it back to her. Mara held it gently this time.

“Thanks,” she said.

“You’re welcome.”

She reached for her payment band automatically, but Grandpa waved it away.

“Oh no,” Mara said immediately. “My mom will absolutely make me come back and pay you.”

“Then I guess I’ll see you again.”

Cam looked mildly alarmed by that possibility. Mr. Eli looked delighted by it.

Mara laughed before she could help it. And for the first time in weeks, the sound didn’t feel forced at all.

Chapter 8

Verbal Synchronization was the last class before lunch, and the room already felt too warm from everybody packed inside waiting for their turn. The front wall shifted through conversation prompts while Mr. Halden paced slowly near the center of the room holding his tablet against one arm.

The class wasn't really about learning information. The Guide handled information already. The point was learning how to respond correctly and quickly without making people uncomfortable.

"Your teammate takes credit for your work," the system prompted.

Nessa answered immediately. "I would address the misunderstanding privately first so it doesn't create unnecessary conflict."

"Good," Mr. Halden said. "Efficient response."

The next student stepped forward. Mara tried paying attention, but her head already felt crowded. The Guide kept sliding little reminders and suggestions through her thoughts every few seconds. Lila replied to your lunch message. Recommended study adjustment tonight: 7:10 p.m. Usually she barely noticed the interruptions. Today they felt nonstop.

Then Cam stepped into the response circle. Mara looked up automatically, knowing she would be next..

Mara instinctively looked for the answer, and for a second, she didn’t just think, she prayed. God, give me the right words.

*Warning: Response latency detected,* the Guide pulsed in her vision, sharp and red. *Suggesting optimized response: "I cannot fulfill this request due to current capacity limitations."*

The back of her neck went cold. It seemed that the Guide didn't just want to help; it wanted to fill the silence before she could. Before God could. It wanted to fill the silence so she never had to be alone with her own thoughts again.

"Your parent forgets an important promise," the system said.

Cam stood there quietly for a second. Not even long. Just long enough that people noticed.

"I'd probably be upset," he said finally. The system waited for him to continue. Cam shrugged one shoulder. "I don't know. Maybe I'd ask what happened first."

The answer sounded unfinished compared to everybody else's. Mr. Halden marked something down on his tablet. "Expand your emotional clarification next time." Cam nodded and stepped away.

The class moved on, but Mara barely heard any of it after that. She kept thinking about the shop instead. The clocks ticking softly everywhere. The smell of old paper and wood polish. The way the quiet had felt when she was standing there while Mr. Eli fixed the journal page. Noise is what everybody carries around in their heads all day. That's what Cam had said, and it kept replaying in her head all afternoon.

By the time she got home, the headache was starting. A low pressure behind her eyes that made everything feel slightly out of focus. She told her mom she was fine, just tired, and went to her room early. She lay in bed thinking about the shop, about Cam standing in the response circle not knowing what to say, about her grandfather's careful hands smoothing paper back together.

She fell asleep without checking her Guide.

Chapter 9

Mara woke up with the headache even worse. Not terrible, but enough pressure behind her eyes to make the whole room feel slightly off. The Guide noticed immediately, of course. Notifications slid quietly through her thoughts before she had even fully opened her eyes.

Good morning, Mara.

Wellness check available.

She blinked at the message. She hadn't requested a wellness check.

She dismissed it and lay there for a moment, watching the ceiling. The headache felt different than usual headaches. It felt like the pressure of too many things trying to happen at once. Like her own thoughts were crowded, and the Guide was standing in the middle of them, handing out suggestions.

Another message slid into place.

Stress indicators elevated overnight. Voluntary recalibration support available through your school wellness office.

Mara muted it.

A second notification slid into place underneath the first one.

Notification frequency increased based on recent activity.

She read it three times. The Guide had never told her it was doing something before, it just did it. It adjusted and smoothed and suggested and she just absorbed it all without being asked. This was something different. The Guide was telling her it was going to be increasing the frequency notifications.

She sat up slowly. Her room was still dim, but the wall display had already shifted into morning mode. Soft light. Gentle colors. A calm ocean scene that moved in slow perfect waves.

It was supposed to help.

Today it made her want to throw something.

Her eyes moved to the journal sitting on her desk.

The blue cover looked ordinary in the morning light. Worn corners. Stretched elastic band. A little tear on the edge where the page had been repaired.

Downstairs, her mom was already making breakfast while older music played softly from the kitchen speaker. Real music again. Guitars. Actual voices. Songs that sounded slightly uneven instead of perfectly balanced and corrected.

"You look tired," her mom said when Mara walked into the kitchen.

"Thanks."

"Did you sleep ok?"

Mara stopped halfway to the fridge. "Yeah, just still have a headache."

Her mom looked over while flipping something in the pan. "Unplugging can do that sometimes. Give you headaches when you're not used to it." Mara didn't answer immediately. She poured juice into a glass and sat down.

“I didn’t really unplug,” Mara said.

Her mom raised one eyebrow.

“Not for long.”

“How long is not long?”

“I don’t know. A little while.”

Her mom turned the stove down and set two plates on the table. “Your brain has had the Guide running in the background since you were three. Even a little while can feel like stepping outside in the cold with no coat.”

Mara sat down slowly.

“You’ve done it before?” she asked.

“Unplugged?”

Mara nodded.

Her mom brought the pan to the table. “A few times.”

“When?”

Her mom paused like she was deciding how much to say. Her eyes flicked toward the kitchen speaker, then back to the eggs.

“Mostly when I needed quiet.”

“But why didn’t you tell me that was a thing?”

“Because most parents don’t sit their kids down and say, ‘Hey, here’s how to disconnect from the national system that monitors your stability.’”

Mara stared at her.

Her mom gave a tiny smile. “Too much?”

“A little.”

They ate in silence for a minute. Mara kept waiting for the Guide to correct the conversation. To warn her. To flag something. But nothing came except another hydration reminder, which she dismissed so quickly it barely finished forming.

Outside the window, traffic moved through the morning lanes in smooth lines. Nobody honked. Nobody swerved. Nobody looked lost.

Everything worked.

That was the problem. Everything worked so well it was hard to explain why it felt wrong.

Before Mara could ask anything else, her mom changed the subject.

“We’re going to your grandfather’s next week for his birthday.”

Mara looked up. “Really?”

“Yes. He’s turning sixty-seven. And before you ask, no, he does not want anything useful.”

“What does that mean?”

“It means if we bring him something that makes life more efficient, he’ll pretend to be thankful and then hide it in a drawer.”

Mara smiled despite herself.

Her grandfather was not around much. Not in a dramatic family secret kind of way. He just lived outside the city center and hated group chats, transit scheduling, and anything that beeped at him.

At least that was what her mom always said.

“He doesn’t use the Guide much, right?” Mara asked.

Her mom glanced at her. “Technically he uses it minimally. But yeah, he chose not to integrate fully." Her mom said it matter-of-factly, like this wasn't strange at all. "He's been doing fine without it."

Mara sat with that for a second. She'd never thought about the Guide as something people could refuse. It had always been presented as normal. Necessary. Like electricity or clean water. Nobody talked about it like something people once debated.

“What does that mean?”

“He uses limited support. Health monitoring. Emergency systems. Basic routing if he absolutely has to.” Her mom took her plate to the sink. “Older generations could choose that before national integration became standard.”

Mara stared at her.

“So he just chose not to?”

“Pretty much.”

“And people let him?”

Her mom laughed once. “People used to let people do a lot of things.”

Mara sat with that for a second.

She had never really thought about the Guide as something anyone could refuse. It had always been there. Like electricity. Like clean water. Like gravity.

Necessary.

Normal.

The idea that someone could look at it and say no made her feel strange.

Kind of scared.

Kind of jealous.

By the time Mara left for school, the Guide had suggested a wellness check three more times.

She ignored all three.

By third period, her head felt worse.

The Guide had not gotten louder exactly. It had just become harder to ignore. Every notification arrived with a little more pressure behind it. Every suggestion felt less like help and more like someone tapping her shoulder over and over.

Hydration recommended.

Focus pattern unstable.

Breathing exercise available.

Social tone adjustment suggested.

Mara dismissed the last one harder than necessary, which did nothing because thoughts did not have buttons you could slam. It recommended a wellness office check-in by lunch. She wondered if anybody else's Guide acted like that, or if it was just hers now.

* * *

Mara got called for her wellness evaluation in the middle of Systems History.

The notification slid quietly into her thoughts while Mr. Halden talked near the front of the room about early integration laws and how society had “stabilized rapidly” after national Guide adoption. Mara had stopped really listening ten minutes earlier, somewhere around the third chart explaining reduced conflict percentages.

Student Evaluation Room 4B. Report immediately.

Three other students stood up at almost the same time she did. Nobody complained about leaving class early, but nobody looked excited either. Wellness evaluations always made people weirdly tense even though everyone pretended they didn’t care.

As Mara grabbed her bag, Lila looked over from across the room.

“You’ll be fine,” she whispered.

Mara nodded like she believed that.

The evaluation rooms were upstairs near the health offices where everything smelled faintly like disinfectant and recycled air. The walls were bright white and too clean. The lighting was soft in that fake calming way that somehow made Mara feel more nervous instead.

A woman stood outside the evaluation room with a gray district badge clipped neatly to her jacket.

Mara’s stomach tightened before she even read the name.

Marie Cole.

Of course.

Ms. Cole smiled when she saw her, the same calm, careful smile from the hallway outside the library. The one that looked kind without ever quite feeling warm.

“Good morning, everyone,” Ms. Cole said. “This should only take a few minutes.”

Her eyes moved across the group, then paused on Mara for half a second longer than the others.

Not long enough for anyone else to notice. Long enough for Mara to know she had.

Inside, the room was divided into separate stations with curved privacy screens between them. Mara sat down and immediately felt the system connect to her Guide.

Connection confirmed. Emotional calibration beginning.

The words settled into her thoughts before the screen in front of her even lit up.

Questions appeared one at a time.

How often do you experience delayed response hesitation?

Mara stared at it.

The Guide suggested an answer before she had even fully thought about it.

No unusual delay.

She selected it.

The next question appeared.

Have you intentionally muted Guide prompts within the last thirty days?

Suggested response:

No.

Mara’s finger hovered over the answer.

The room felt too quiet. She could hear someone breathing behind the privacy screen to her left. A chair shifted. Ms. Cole walked slowly between the stations with her hands folded in front of her.

“These evaluations are designed to support healthy synchronization,” Ms. Cole said gently. “There are no wrong answers.”

Mara immediately trusted the whole thing less.

She selected:

Rarely.

The screen paused.

Not long.

Just long enough for Mara to notice.

Across the room, Ms. Cole noticed too.

Her eyes flicked toward Mara’s station, and for one awful second Mara remembered what Ms. Cole had said in the hallway.

People who start questioning protocol… those patterns tend to escalate.

Then Ms. Cole looked away like nothing had happened.

The next question appeared.

Do social interactions feel increasingly overwhelming or distracting?

Suggested response:

No.

Mara thought of Lila watching her too closely. Of Nessa choosing careful words at lunch. Of Connor joking because jokes were easier than paying attention.

She selected:

Sometimes.

Another pause.

Her headache pulsed behind her eyes.

Question after question followed. Sleep patterns. Emotional regulation. Focus consistency. Response timing. Peer alignment. Trust in Guide recommendations.

Every time Mara hesitated, the Guide supplied something smoother.

Something safer.

Something that sounded like the right version of herself.

By the end, Mara felt tired in a way that had nothing to do with sleep.

As students began standing, Ms. Cole smiled at all of them.

“A small number of students may receive temporary recalibration recommendations this week. This is completely normal.”

Nobody asked what that meant.

That made it worse.

Out in the hallway, Mara stopped near the water fountain and adjusted her backpack strap while other students moved past her toward class.

“You paused too long,” Cam said.

Mara turned so fast she almost dropped her bag. “What?”

He stood beside the water fountain, crushing a paper cup slowly between his fingers.

“In there,” he said. “During the questions.”

“How would you know that?”

Cam glanced down the hallway before answering. “Because Ms. Cole looked at your station.”

Mara’s stomach dropped.

Cam shrugged, but his face stayed serious. “That usually means somebody answered like a person instead of a script.”

For a second neither of them said anything.

The hallway around them stayed normal. Lockers sliding open. Shoes squeaking against the floor. Students moving exactly where they were supposed to go.

“Do they actually care if people unplug?” Mara asked quietly.

Cam leaned one shoulder against the wall. “My grandpa says systems always care when people stop depending on them.”

Mara looked down at the floor tiles.

She kept thinking about the journal. About her mom’s older entries and how alive they sounded compared to the newer ones. Like somewhere along the way, her thoughts had gotten smaller and nobody had noticed.

“Does your grandpa know a lot about this stuff?” she asked.

Cam gave her a look. “He thinks he does.”

“That sounds like a yes.”

“It is definitely a yes. Just an annoying one.”

Mara smiled faintly.

The hallway speaker chimed overhead.

Cam looked up immediately.

For one quick second, his face changed. His jaw tightened. His shoulders went still.

Then it was gone.

“Just be careful,” he said.

“With what?”

“With acting different.”

Mara let out a quiet laugh. “Everybody keeps saying that like I joined a criminal organization.”

Cam did not laugh.

That bothered her.

He pushed himself away from the wall and adjusted his backpack strap.

“And don’t answer every question honestly,” he added.

Before Mara could ask what he meant, he walked down the hallway and disappeared into the crowd.

Two days later, a new notification appeared in Mara’s Guide overlay.

Your support tier has been adjusted.

Welcome to Tier 2.

The prompt felt like a polite suggestion, yet held the weight of a command. Mara stopped walking in the middle of the hallway. Students flowed around her without looking up.

What does that mean? she thought.

The Guide answered immediately.

Tier 2 students receive enhanced wellness support, including additional check-ins with school counselors, routine sync monitoring, and guided behavioral support. This adjustment is designed to ensure your continued success.

Mara read it twice.

Lila caught her staring.

“What?” Lila asked.

Mara looked at her. “Did you just get a tier change?”

Lila’s face shifted.

Just a little.

“What’s a tier change?”

So it was not everybody.

It was just Mara.

“Nothing,” Mara said.

Lila glanced around like she wanted to make sure nobody had heard. “Mara…”

“I said it’s nothing.”

Lila’s mouth pressed into a tight line.

“I’ll see you later at the library,” she said, too quickly. Lila had been trying all week to get Mara to study with her after school, like that would prove everything was still normal between them. Mara had finally agreed to meet her in the library the next day, mostly because saying no felt like starting another fight.

Then she walked away.

Mara stood there for another second while the Tier 2 notification stayed in the corner of her vision.

Not blinking.

Not pulsing.

Just waiting.

✦✦✦

That night she opened the journal to the first blank page in the back and wrote:

I had a wellness check on Tuesday.

Ms. Cole said the questions had no wrong answers.

I noticed she watched my face when I lied.

Today I got moved to Tier 2.

Nobody else got moved to Tier 2.

Chapter 10

Mara spent the whole walk home thinking about what Cam had said.

He had lowered his voice when he said it, standing beside the water fountain while students moved around them like nothing unusual was happening.

Just don’t answer every question honestly.

At first, Mara told herself he probably only meant the wellness evaluations. Maybe certain answers triggered extra monitoring. Maybe that was how students got sorted into support tiers. Maybe “honesty” was fine as long as it sounded normal enough.

But the more she thought about it, the more she started noticing how often everyone shaped their answers everywhere else too. In class, at lunch, in messages, with teachers, with friends. Everyone was always saying something close to the truth. Something smoother than the truth. Something that kept the system calm.

By the time she got home, the Guide had already reminded her twice about unfinished assignments and once about replying to Lila’s messages. Usually those reminders blended into the background so completely she barely noticed them. Now every single one felt like a finger tapping the inside of her skull, pulling at her attention before she could even finish whatever thought she was having first.

Her mom was downstairs working, so the apartment stayed mostly quiet except for keyboard sounds drifting faintly from the lower floor. Dad was still at work. Mara stood at the kitchen counter for a minute, watching traffic move below the apartment building in smooth, steady lines.

Everything outside looked calm.

That was the weird part.

School had felt tense all day, but the city never looked tense. The Guide kept things moving. Traffic flowed correctly. Buildings adjusted temperatures automatically. Delivery drones crossed overhead in perfect patterns without anybody even looking up.

Sometimes it felt like the whole world had learned how to smooth itself out before problems could fully exist.

Mara headed upstairs before the Guide could redirect her attention toward homework again. The journal was still sitting on her desk where she had left it the night before. She dropped onto her bed and opened it automatically, flipping past the shorter entries until she reached the older ones again.

She liked those better.

The newer pages sounded rushed. Quick updates. Grocery reminders. Half-finished thoughts that stopped before they really said anything. The older entries wandered all over the place. Her mom would start talking about work, then suddenly switch into a story about getting lost on the way home, or fighting with somebody at church, or sitting in a parking lot trying not to cry before going into a grocery store.

It sounded more like an actual person thinking.

Mara stopped on one of the pages she had already read twice.

Still not totally sure how prayer works.

But talking to God feels different than talking to everybody else.

The Guide immediately pushed a definition for prayer into the corner of her thoughts.

Prayer: a religious practice involving communication with a divine being, often used for reflection, comfort, or request.

Mara stared at it.

That was not even close to what her mom meant.

A message notification interrupted her.

Lila: You alive?

Mara stared at the message longer than she meant to. Yesterday, she probably would have smiled. She probably would have typed something normal back without thinking. But now the words sat there in front of her like another test.

Underneath the message, the Guide quietly suggested responses.

Just tired lol.

Long day.

I’m okay, promise.

All of them sounded normal. All of them sounded like things people said when they did not want anyone to ask a second question.

Mara looked back down at the journal.

The Guide always answers quickly.

God usually doesn’t.

But somehow prayer still feels less lonely.

She still couldn’t stop thinking about that line.

Another message appeared.

Lila: Seriously are you okay?

Mara started typing three different responses before deleting all of them. Her fingers hovered over the response field while the Guide waited beside the conversation, ready with smoother answers if she wanted them.

I’m just tired.

Stress probably.

Long week.

Mara typed: I’m just tired.

The second she sent it, she knew it was not true. Not completely false either. Just close enough to end the conversation.

Lila: Then go to sleep genius.

Mara did not answer right away. She looked at the message and felt suddenly tired in a way sleep would not fix. Lila sounded normal. Maybe that was what bothered her. Everything sounded normal if you kept it shallow enough.

Mara finally typed goodnight and locked the screen.

The room went still again. She looked back down at the journal spread open across her blanket. Her mom’s handwriting slanted sideways in places where she must have gotten distracted while writing. Some words were crossed out completely. One sentence ended halfway down the page before restarting underneath in a different direction.

Nothing about it looked polished.

Maybe that was why Mara trusted it.

She leaned back against the wall and closed her eyes for a second. The evaluation room drifted back into her thoughts again.

There are no wrong answers.

Even though everybody knew there were.

Then Cam’s voice came back, quiet beside the water fountain.

Systems always care when people stop depending on them.

The next Guide notification appeared across her thoughts. Mara muted it before it fully opened. A few seconds later, before she could talk herself out of it, she tried to disconnect completely.

The silence rushed in fast enough to make her dizzy.

For a moment, her whole body seemed to notice the absence at once. No suggestions. No soft prompts. No reminders waiting behind her thoughts. Just air moving through the vents. A door closing somewhere down the hall. Someone laughing far below on the street.

Without the Guide running underneath everything, Mara’s thoughts felt slower and harder to organize. One thought drifted into another without instantly sorting itself into clean answers. It was uncomfortable, but not in a bad way. More like realizing background noise had been playing your whole life and only noticing it after someone finally turned it off.

Mara pulled her knees closer to her chest and looked down at the journal again. Then, quietly, before she could overthink it, she said, “I don’t even know if I’m talking to You right.”
