Nothing answered. The room stayed quiet. The Guide pushed through and reconnected without warning, the notifications returned all at once. Pending notifications loaded across her vision: six missed academic reminders, two wellness prompts, one peer message, and one support-tier notice.

Mara’s stomach tightened. She didn’t know that the Guide could overide her choice to disconnect, and on top of that The Tier 2 notification had not gone away. It had updated.

Peer Support connection available. .
District Library Wellness Alcove.
Tomorrow after school.

Mara sat very still. The library? That was where students went to study, hide, or pretend they were not avoiding someone. It was not where Wellness called you. For one stupid second, Mara wondered if Lila would be there after school like usual. Then she hated herself for hoping.

The next day moved slowly. Too slowly. Mara barely heard anything in class. Every time Lila looked at her she looked away too quickly. Every time the Guide suggested a calming exercise, Mara dismissed it. By lunch, her headache had returned, dull and steady.

Lila was too bright. That was the first thing Mara noticed. Not happy bright. Not excited bright. Guide-bright. Her voice stayed smooth. Her smile came quickly. Her eyes did not match either one.

“You’re going to the library after school?” Lila asked.

Mara looked at her. “Why?”

Lila blinked, just once. “I just thought you might. You go there sometimes.”

Mara did not answer right away. Something about Lila’s voice felt too careful, like she was stepping around broken glass Mara could not see yet.

“Maybe,” Mara said.

Lila nodded too fast. “Okay.”

That was all she said.

After school, the hallways emptied faster than usual. Rain tapped softly against the tall windows near the stairwell. Mara followed the library signs even though she knew the way. The Guide highlighted the route anyway.

District Library Wellness Alcove. Proceed.

Mara dismissed the route.

The library was quieter than the rest of school. Not silent. Just softer. A few students sat at study tables, screens glowing in front of them. The old paper book section was in the back, mostly ignored, like a place the school had forgotten to remove.

Lila waited near the alcove.

She stood when Mara approached, her face full of relief. That made Mara’s chest tighten.

“I talked to Ms. Cole,” Lila said.

Mara stopped. For a second, the whole library seemed to go very still.

“What do you mean?” Mara asked.

Lila stepped closer and lowered her voice. “I couldn’t just watch you slip away. It’s okay now.”

“What’s okay?”

“I asked her to help.”

Mara stared at her. “Asked help for what?”

Lila’s eyes were shiny. She looked scared, but also determined, like she had rehearsed this. Like she needed Mara to understand before Mara got angry.

“I didn’t report you to get you in trouble,” Lila said quickly. “I reported concern. That’s different.”

Mara could not speak. “You reported me?”

“I saw you acting weird,” Lila continued. “Ignoring prompts. Looking at that repair shop. Asking strange questions. And then you started talking about people not saying what they really think, and I just—” Her voice cracked. “I thought if I told someone early, they would only give you a little help.”

“A little help,” Mara repeated.

Lila nodded too fast. “Yes. Before it got worse.”

Mara’s throat felt tight. “Is that why I got Tier 2?”

Lila’s face changed. Just enough.

That was the answer.

Mara took a step back.

“Mara, please listen to me.”

“You reported me.”

“I helped you.”

“No,” Mara said, her voice shaking now. “You reported me.”

“I was scared!” Lila said, louder than she meant to. A student at a nearby table looked up, then quickly looked away. Lila lowered her voice again, but the panic was still there. “You don’t understand what you looked like. You were pulling away from everyone. You were ignoring prompts, asking weird questions, spending time with Cam. You were acting like him.”

Mara flinched.

Lila saw it immediately, and guilt flashed across her face. “I didn’t mean it like that.”

“Yes, you did.”

“No, I mean—” Lila wiped quickly at her cheek, frustrated with herself now. “Cam is already marked. Everyone knows that. I didn’t want you to become marked too. I didn’t want people whispering about you or watching you or waiting for you to mess up. I thought if I told Ms. Cole early, she could help before it got worse.”

Mara looked at her best friend. Really looked at her. Lila was not smirking. She was not being cruel. She was not trying to win. She looked terrified, and somehow that made it worse. Because Lila truly believed this was love. She truly believed reporting Mara had been the right thing to do.

“I reported concern” Lila whispered.

Something inside Mara went cold. Lila believed it. She actually believed she was the hero of this story. Not Ms. Cole. Not the Guide. Lila. Her best friend, who had watched her laugh and cry and complain about cafeteria food since first year, had looked at her and seen a problem that needed reporting.

The Guide pulsed softly in the corner of Mara’s vision.

Emotional distress detected. Support available.

Mara dismissed it.

Lila reached for her arm, but Mara pulled away before she could touch her.

“Don’t,” Mara said.

Lila froze. For a moment, neither of them moved. Somewhere in the old book section, a shelf creaked softly, and the sound seemed too normal for what had just happened.

Mara turned and walked away before Lila could say anything else. Behind her, Lila called her name once.

Mara did not turn around.

Chapter 11

Friday Day 15

The recalibration notices started the next morning.

Nobody announced them publicly, but everybody knew when someone got one. Their schedule updated during first period, their face went pale, and then they disappeared for an hour. When they came back, they always acted like it had been no big deal.

That was how you knew it had been a big deal.

By lunch, three students from Mara’s grade had already been called in.

Mara did not sit at her usual table.

She told herself it was because she needed quiet. Because her head hurt. Because the Guide had already suggested reduced social stimulation three times, and for once, the recommendation was not completely wrong.

But that was not the real reason.

The real reason was Lila.

Mara could see her from across the cafeteria, sitting with Nessa, June, and Connor like everything was normal. Lila kept glancing toward the side wall where Mara sat alone with her tray. Every time their eyes almost met, Mara looked down first.

She hated that.

She hated that Lila looked worried instead of guilty. She hated that Lila probably thought giving Mara space was another way of helping. She hated that part of her still wanted to go sit beside her like yesterday had never happened.

But yesterday had happened.

You reported me.

I helped you.

The words kept replaying in Mara’s head no matter how many times she tried to make them stop.

The Guide offered a calming exercise.

Mara dismissed it.

Across the cafeteria, Connor said something that made June laugh. Lila smiled too, but it faded quickly. Her eyes found Mara again.

Mara looked away.

Her gaze landed on Cam.

He sat near the back wall by himself, picking apart a sandwich while reading something on an old-looking tablet. Not a school tablet either. The screen was thicker and duller around the edges. Weirdly physical-looking. Almost like something Mr. Eli would own.

Cam looked up suddenly, like he felt her watching.

Mara looked down at her tray so fast her face went hot.

Great. Normal. Very normal.

The cafeteria lights flickered overhead.

Not fully off. Just a quick dim pulse before stabilizing again.

Most people barely reacted.

Then the lights flickered a second time.

This time the room changed.

Not panic exactly. Just disruption.

Conversations stopped halfway through. A few students looked around automatically, like they were waiting for instructions. Someone laughed too loudly, then stopped. A younger student near the drink station froze with one hand still wrapped around a cup.

Mara suddenly realized how many people relied on the constant stream of tiny Guide prompts to move through ordinary moments without thinking about it.

The lights stabilized again almost immediately.

Around the cafeteria, people awkwardly laughed and picked their conversations back up.

The overhead speakers chimed softly.

Minor district interruption resolved. No action required.

Everybody relaxed almost instantly.

Everybody except Cam.

Across the cafeteria, he had gone completely still. He wasn’t looking at the lights. He was looking at everyone else.

Watching them.

Mara noticed he still had not touched his food again.

After lunch, Mara walked slower on purpose near the science wing while students crowded around her toward afternoon classes. She told herself she was not looking for Cam.

Then she found him at his locker, stuffing books into his bag.

“You okay?” she asked before she could rethink it.

Cam glanced up. “Why wouldn’t I be?”

“The lights thing.”

His expression shifted slightly. Not surprised exactly. More like he was deciding how honest to be.

“My grandpa calls them dependency glitches.”

Mara leaned against the locker beside his. “What does that mean?”

Cam zipped his bag halfway before answering. “When systems fail, people remember how much they rely on them.”

“That was like two seconds.”

“Yeah.”

The way he said it made Mara think about the cafeteria going quiet. Not because people were scared exactly, but because everybody had paused, waiting for the system to smooth the moment out for them.

Cam adjusted the strap on his backpack. “You ever notice people get uncomfortable really fast now?”

“Everybody’s always uncomfortable.”

“No, I mean with silence. Or waiting. Or not knowing something immediately.”

Mara thought about unplugging in her room. About how loud the quiet felt at first.

“I guess.”

Cam looked down the hallway before lowering his voice slightly. “My grandpa says humans used to practice boredom.”

Mara leaned back against the locker. “Practice boredom? On purpose?”

“That was my question too.”

“That sounds horrible.”

“He says boredom is where people learned to think.”

Mara considered that. “Think about what?”

“Just think. Without anything telling them what to think about.”

Mara thought about the journal again. Her mom’s handwriting. Lines with no immediate answer. Prayers that sat there on the page without getting resolved. Standing in her room with nothing to do and her own thoughts finally showing up, uninvited and strange.

“That makes me feel a little depressed,” Mara said.

“Why?”

“Because I don’t think we know how to do that anymore.”

Cam adjusted his backpack strap. He looked like he was about to say something, then stopped.

“What?” Mara asked.

“Nothing. It’s just…” He glanced down the hallway again. “My grandpa has been saying this stuff for years, and nobody listened. But now with the glitches, people are starting to notice.”

“Yeah.”

The hallway was filling around them. Students moved between classes, most of them checking messages or following routes only they could see. Normal. Everything was normal, except for those few seconds when the power failed and nobody knew what to do with themselves.

The warning bell rang overhead.

Cam stepped away from the lockers. “I should go.”

“Wait.”

He looked back.

Mara hesitated. Then quietly, she asked, “Do you think people were better before the Guide?”

Cam thought about it longer than most people would have.

“I think people were messier,” he said finally. “More arguments. More bad decisions. But probably more honest too.”

Then he walked down the hallway before Mara could answer.

Mara stayed by the lockers for another second after Cam disappeared into the crowd.

Boredom. Thinking. Her mom writing in that journal with no Guide to smooth the thoughts into something finished or coherent.

The journal was messy. Half the sentences wandered into completely different thoughts halfway through. Some pages looked like her mom had changed her mind three times while writing. Nothing was polished or final.

But that was the point, wasn’t it?

That was what thinking looked like when nobody was telling you what to think.

When you just had to sit with your own mind and see where it went.

That Saturday morning, Mom told Mara they were driving to see Grandpa Frank.

“Oh,” Mara said, looking up from breakfast. “We’re actually going to his house?”

“Yes. Since it’s his birthday.” Mom opened the fridge and checked something, then closed it again. “I want to pick up a cheesecake from the bakery on the way.”

“Okay. I’ll get ready.”

Mara had not visited Grandpa Frank in eight or nine months. The Guide did not really route there. He lived in an older neighborhood north of the city where most homes had not been smart-converted, and the area kept showing up on Guide maps as low-priority routing.

They kept in touch, though. Mom texted him. Mara sent messages sometimes. Last month Mom had video called him, or maybe two months ago. Time had a way of sliding past when you were mostly connected through screens.

The drive felt longer than it actually was. Mom drove the whole way without overlays.

Mara noticed.

“You know where you’re going?” she asked.

“Yes.”

“Without overlays?”

Mom gave her a look. “I know my way to my father’s house.”

“Based on your journal, I’m not sure I trust that.”

Her mom laughed. “Oh, so now you’re questioning my sense of direction?”

“After reading about you getting lost all the time? Absolutely.”

“That was different. I had better things to worry about than memorizing routes.”

“Like what?”

“Mostly being twenty-three and dramatic.”

Mara smiled and looked out the window.

The neighborhood looked exactly the same as the last time she had been there. Small wooden houses with actual lawns. Mailboxes with names hand-painted on them. The air smelled different out here too. Less filtered. More like trees.

Grandpa Frank opened the door before they reached the steps.

“There you are.”

He looked the same. White hair cropped short. Glasses that probably should have been replaced fifteen years ago. A flannel shirt with the sleeves rolled up because his hands stayed warmer when his arms were free, or so he had once explained to Mara when she was seven.

“Hey, Daddy. Happy birthday,” Mom said.

Her voice changed when she said it. Softer somehow. Younger.

Grandpa Frank hugged her for longer than Mara expected. Then he turned to Mara.

“Look at you.”

“Hi, Grandpa. Happy birthday.”

“Thanks, Mara. You got taller. Or I got shorter. One of those. Maybe both.”

Inside, the house was the same too. Hardwood floors that ticked under footsteps. Bookshelves on three walls. No glowing displays anywhere. A clock in the kitchen Mara could hear from the front room.

Grandma Vale sat in her usual chair by the window with a soft afghan over her legs.

“Mara, honey.”

She smiled the same warm smile she had always had. But her eyes took a half second longer to focus than they used to.

Mara walked over and hugged her carefully.

“You remembered me,” Grandma said quietly.

“Of course I did.”

“That’s good. I forget sometimes.”

Mom touched Mara’s shoulder briefly, then went into the kitchen with Grandpa Frank. Their voices murmured low through the wall.

Mara sat in the chair beside Grandma. The afghan smelled faintly of cedar.

A soft blue overlay floated near the corner of Grandma’s vision. Mara could only see the edges of it. Reminders. Names. Faces. The Guide kept her oriented.

Grandma noticed Mara noticing.

“It helps me,” she said simply. “Some days more than others.”

“That’s good.”

“Your grandfather doesn’t have one. He never did.”

“I know.”

“He reads to me at night,” Grandma said. “The Bible, mostly. Sometimes other things.”

Mara did not know what to say to that. She watched Grandma’s hands instead. They were small and freckled and folded in her lap.

“It’s one of my favorite things,” Grandma said. “Your grandpa reading to me. I don’t always remember everything, even with the Guide. But those nights with your grandpa, I hold onto those.”

Something tightened in Mara’s chest.

Later, in the kitchen, Grandpa Frank handed Mara a mug of tea she had not asked for and sat down across from her at the table. Mom had gone out back to look at something in the garden, which Mara suspected was grown-up code for giving them a minute.

“Your mom says you’ve been seeing Eli,” Grandpa Frank said.

Mara almost dropped the mug.

“You know him?”

“Frank Vale and Eli Merrick have been friends since before your mother was born.”

“Wait. Really?”

“Stubborn men tend to stick together.” Grandpa sipped his tea. “We have coffee once a month at a place that isn’t connected to anything. Just coffee and conversation.”

Mara tried to picture her grandfather sitting in a coffee shop with Cam’s grandpa.

“Last month he fixed my radio,” Grandpa said. “The one in the kitchen. Stopped working, so Eli brought it back to life.”

Mara smiled despite herself.

Of course Grandpa had someone who could fix a radio. Of course there was a place that was not connected to anything. Of course these two old men had been friends her entire life without her knowing.

“How many other people do you know like that?” she asked.

“Like what?”

“Like you and Eli. People who just… didn’t get Guides.”

Grandpa considered the question. “Thirty or so in the city. Maybe more. We tend to find each other.”

“When I was in his shop, did he tell you about me?”

“He told me a girl had come in asking questions. Didn’t use your name.” Grandpa smiled faintly. “I figured it out when your mother mentioned where you’d been spending afternoons.”

“He didn’t tell me he knew you.”

“He wouldn’t. Eli doesn’t push. That’s part of why he’s worth knowing.”

Mara turned the mug in her hands. The tea was still too hot to drink.

“Mom said you refused integration.”

“That’s accurate.”

“Why?”

Grandpa Frank leaned back in his chair. “I was old enough by the time it came around that I had already learned how to do most things on my own. I didn’t trust something I hadn’t had to teach myself how to use.”

“So you just chose not to?”

“Well,” Grandpa admitted, “there were other things too.”

He set the mug down.

“One big reason was your grandmother.”

Mara looked toward the front room.

Grandpa followed her gaze. “She got integrated for memory support. And it helped. I won’t pretend it didn’t. The Guide gave her back things she had forgotten. Names. Dates. Where she was. Who people were.” His voice softened. “That part was real. But I also watched her lose small pieces of herself in the trade. The Guide gave her some things back, and it took some things that were hers. I couldn’t tell you whether the trade was worth it. I only knew I didn’t want to make it for myself.”

Mara looked toward the front room where Grandma was still sitting quietly with her afghan.

“Is she okay?”

“Most days, yes. Some days she’s somewhere else.”

“Why didn’t more people refuse?”

“Plenty did at first. Did you know that?” Grandpa asked. “There were marches when I was your age. Newspaper articles. Court cases. A federal commission for three years that did almost nothing. Most people don’t teach that part anymore.”

Mara sat very still.

“The early Guide was opt-in,” Grandpa continued. “You had to sign up for it. It was supposed to be for medical conditions, learning disabilities, seniors with memory loss. Then the schools started piloting it. Then workplaces. Then insurance companies. Then cities.”

He picked his mug back up, but did not drink from it.

“Twenty years in, refusing it wasn’t illegal. But the world had been rebuilt around the assumption that you had one. The pushback didn’t fail because we lost an argument. It failed because the world didn’t need to argue with us anymore. It just kept moving.”

Mara thought of city traffic flowing perfectly below her apartment. School hallways routing students around each other. Lunch conversations smoothing themselves flat before anyone could say the wrong thing.

“The Guide came on quiet,” Grandpa said. “Optional. Helpful. Then it got better. Then it got everywhere. Then staying out started to look like stubbornness instead of conviction.”

He looked at her steadily.

“There’s nothing brave about how I lived, Mara. I just couldn’t make myself stop noticing what was happening.”

Mara did not know what to say to that.

The afternoon light shifted toward evening. Mom appeared in the kitchen doorway and said they should start heading home before traffic patterns changed.

Grandpa Frank stood and hugged Mara before they left. A real hug. Not the kind people gave when they were distracted by three other things.

On the porch, he pressed something small into Mara’s hand. A folded square of paper.

“Open it later,” he said.

When they got to the car, Grandma waved from the window. Grandpa Frank stood on the porch until they turned the corner.

The drive home felt different than the drive there. Mara watched the city pass and thought about thirty people who had decided not to integrate. She thought about Grandma’s hands folded in her lap. She thought about Grandpa sitting in a coffee shop with an old man who fixed radios, living a life that continued without the Guide’s help or approval.

When she got home, Mara went straight to her room and pulled out the journal. She opened to a fresh page and wrote about Grandpa Frank and Grandma and what he had said about the early days of the Guide. About how the world had been rebuilt around an assumption. She wrote about the coffee shop with actual cups and about learning that her grandfather had been making a choice all along, quietly, without needing anyone to understand it.

Then she set the journal down and unfolded the paper.

In Grandpa Frank’s careful handwriting, it said:

Pay attention. That’s the whole thing.

Mara read it twice.

She thought about her grandfather noticing what was happening. About her mother driving without the Guide’s navigation. About Cam’s grandfather teaching him words that did not exist in the official world anymore. About her own mind, the one thing the Guide could not quite make smooth.

By the time she finished writing, it was dark outside and the house was still.

She folded the paper back up, left the journal open on her desk, and went to bed.

✦✦✦

Chapter 12

Mara got the recalibration notice two days later.

It showed up halfway through breakfast while her mom was talking about grocery prices and trying to decide whether the apartment needed another air filter replacement. Behind her mother, the kitchen wall display shifted to the morning district feed.

GUIDE30: 12 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.

Celebrate thirty years of clarity, unity, and support.

Mara stared at the words while the recalibration notice pulsed quietly in the corner of her vision.

Student Follow-Up Required.

Report to Student Wellness after second period.

Mara stopped chewing.

Her mom noticed immediately. “What?”

“Nothing.”

“Mara.”

She dismissed the notification too quickly. “I have to go back for another wellness thing.”

Her mom frowned a little. “Already?”

“Apparently I’m emotionally concerning now.”

“You’re fourteen. That’s basically the job description.”

Usually Mara would have laughed at that. Instead she rinsed her plate too fast and nearly dropped it into the sink.

The whole walk to school felt different after that. Every notification from the Guide pulled at her attention harder than normal, like once she knew the system had flagged her, she couldn’t stop noticing how often it watched everything.

By second period she had mostly convinced herself it probably meant nothing.

By the time she reached Student Wellness, she no longer believed that.

The waiting room was almost empty. A younger kid bounced his knee beside the wall display where forest scenes rolled silently across the screen, soft instrumental music playing overhead like it was designed to soothe anyone who ended up here. The whole room felt carefully constructed — the colors, the plants, the gentle hum of something that wanted you to feel safe while it figured out what was wrong with you. Mara sat down and the Guide automatically logged her arrival.

“Mara Vale?”

A woman wearing a pale gray district badge with the name Mrs. Cooper opened the office door and smiled politely. “You can come in.”

The office didn’t look medical at all. There were soft chairs instead of exam tables, warm lamps instead of ceiling lights, and shelves lined with actual paper books.

The books reminded Mara a little of the repair shop. Quiet shelves. Worn covers. Things people had decided were still worth keeping around.

“Have a seat,” Mrs. Cooper said.

Mara sat carefully while the Guide synced automatically with the room systems.

Mrs. Cooper glanced down at her tablet. “This shouldn’t take very long. Your evaluation flagged a few mild irregularities.”

Mara already hated the word irregularities.

“We’re also seeing some unusual reflection patterns in your activity logs over the past few weeks. Long quiet stretches. Dismissed assistance prompts. Cognitive activity that doesn’t correspond to anything the Guide could process for you.”

Mara’s stomach went cold.

The Guide didn’t see what she read. It didn’t see her mom’s journal. It couldn’t even tell what she was looking at if she was looking at paper. But it could absolutely see the shape of her mind. The pattern of her attention. The minutes she spent doing something other than being routed toward an answer.

She hadn’t known it tracked that.

She felt like an idiot for not knowing.

“You reported occasional non-assisted reflection periods,” Mrs. Cooper continued. “Can you tell me more about that?”

Mara immediately thought of Cam standing beside the water fountain.

Don’t answer every question honestly.

The Guide quietly supplied a suggested response.

Minimal harmless experimentation.

Mara folded her hands together. “Sometimes I unplug for a few minutes.”

“How often?”

“I don’t know. A couple times maybe.”

Mrs. Cooper nodded while typing something.

“Have you experienced emotional discomfort during disconnected periods?”

Mara hesitated.

She wasn’t sure how to answer.

The silence felt uncomfortable at first. Then peaceful. Then uncomfortable again, because the peaceful part bothered her.

Instead she said, “Not really.”

Mrs. Cooper made another note.

“Do you feel dissatisfied with normal Guide interaction?”

“No.”

The answer came out too fast.

Mrs. Cooper looked up briefly from her tablet, and Mara wished she could pull the word back into her mouth and try again slower.

“You answered that quickly,” Mrs. Cooper said. Her voice stayed impossibly kind. “Sometimes that happens when a student is trying to separate their own thoughts from Guide support.”

Mara said nothing.

“You’ve been trying to figure things out on your own, haven’t you?” Mrs. Cooper asked. “Sitting in silence. Thinking. Maybe even praying.”

Mara looked at her, stunned.

Mrs. Cooper smiled like she had not said anything strange.

“That can feel meaningful,” she said. “Especially at your age. Silence can make a person feel like they’re discovering something deep. But silence is not always wisdom, Mara. Sometimes silence is just a delay.”

Mara’s hands tightened in her lap.

“Prayer is often how people describe the space before an answer,” Mrs. Cooper said gently. “But the Guide was designed to close that space.”

Mara stared at her.

“The Guide offers clarity instantly,” Mrs. Cooper continued. “It removes unnecessary uncertainty. It protects you from guesswork. So when a student begins choosing silence over support, we pay attention.”

Mara remembered how The Guide reconnected before she chose to allow it.

Mrs. Cooper rested the tablet against her knee, as if the moment had been completely ordinary. “Students your age sometimes go through temporary identity differentiation periods.”

“Identity what?”

“Temporary identity differentiation,” Mrs. Cooper said. “It means a student begins testing whether their private instincts are more trustworthy than the support system designed to protect them.”

Support system.

Mara kept noticing how carefully people chose words in this building.

“Have you spoken with anyone encouraging you to disconnect?” Mrs. Cooper asked.

The question landed quietly. Almost casually.

Mara’s stomach tightened anyway.

“No.”

This time the answer came naturally. Not because the Guide suggested it. Because mentioning Cam suddenly felt like the kind of thing you weren’t supposed to do.

Mrs. Cooper studied her face for another second before nodding slowly.

“Good.”

Mara glanced toward the bookshelf while Mrs. Cooper updated something else on her tablet. One of the books near the top shelf had yellowed pages and a cracked spine. Somebody had repaired part of the cover with clear tape.

Beside it sat a thinner, newer hardcover.

The Quiet Mind.

The author name on the spine read Adrian Cole, MD.

Mara didn’t think much about it. Dr. Cole had written lots of books since creating the Guide.

Still, her eyes stayed on the repaired book a moment longer.

She wondered if people still fixed books because they mattered, or just because nobody wanted to throw them away.

“At this point, I don’t think formal recalibration is necessary,” Mrs. Cooper said.

Mara finally breathed normally again.

“Still,” Mrs. Cooper continued.

Mara’s relief caught halfway in her chest.

“With Guide30 approaching, the district is increasing support monitoring for students in elevated tiers.”

Mara looked at her. “Because of the event?”

“Large public gatherings can create emotional strain,” Mrs. Cooper said. “Excitement, social pressure, overstimulation. We want everyone entering Connection Day stable and fully supported.”

Stable.

Fully supported.

Mara was starting to hate words that sounded helpful.

“So what does that mean?” she asked.

“For now, just a few extra check-ins. Limited unnecessary disconnection. And I’d recommend you avoid spending time with students who may reinforce unhealthy independence patterns.”

Mara’s fingers tightened against the edge of the chair.

Cam.

Mrs. Cooper did not say his name.

She didn’t have to.

The meeting ended a few minutes later.

As soon as she stepped back into the hallway, the school noise hit her all at once. Lockers slamming. Shoes against tile floors. Voices bouncing through the corridor.

Mara slowed near the stairwell and pulled up her messages. Then stopped.

Because for a second, she almost texted Cam. Not about class. Not about homework. Just because she wanted to talk with him.

Her thumb hovered over the message field for another second before she locked the screen and shoved the device back into her pocket.

* * *

Mara ended up texting Cam that night.

She stared at the empty message field long enough for the Guide to suggest three possible conversation starters, all of them terrible.

She ignored them and typed the first thing that came to mind.

Mara: did you survive wellness jail

After she sent it, she immediately wanted to throw her screen under her pillow.

Three dots appeared.

Cam: barely
Cam: they had chairs that looked comfortable but somehow weren’t

Mara smiled.

Mara: classic villain move

Cam: exactly

Downstairs, her mom was still on a work call. Mara could hear her walking back and forth through the kitchen, her voice muffled through the floor. Cold pressed against the window, the kind that meant winter was getting closer.

Her screen buzzed again.

Cam: they ask you weird stuff too?

Mara sat up a little straighter.

Mara: define weird

Cam: like “has anyone been influencing your choices” weird

Mara thought about the woman in the office.

Have you spoken with anyone encouraging you to disconnect?

At the time, Mara had known not to mention Cam. Or his grandfather. Or the repair shop. She hadn’t even had to decide it first. The answer had just come out.

No.

Now, sitting alone in her room, the lie sat in her gut like something she had eaten too fast.

Mara: yep
Mara: super normal and not creepy at all

Cam: wellness people are basically professional creeps

Mara: pretty sure that’s not their official title

Cam: should be

Mara pulled the blanket over her legs.

For a minute, neither of them sent anything. The quiet did not feel awkward the way it usually did with Lila, where every pause seemed to need fixing before it got too noticeable.

Cam: can i ask you something

Mara: that depends

Cam: on what

Mara: how likely it is to make me want to disappear

Cam: medium likely

Mara: fine then obviously yes

Cam: why’d you start disconnecting

Mara stared at the question.

The Guide offered an answer before she had even figured out her own.

Curiosity and stress are common factors in temporary disconnection behavior.

Mara muted it.

She almost typed because I found my mom’s journal, but that felt too personal. She almost typed because your grandpa’s shop is weird, but that did not really explain it either.

Mara: idk

Cam: honestly that’s probably the least suspicious answer

Mara: thanks?

Cam: welcome

Mara smiled, then typed before she could overthink it.

Mara: how did you know anyway

Cam: know what

Mara: that i unplugged

The typing dots appeared, disappeared, then appeared again.

Cam: idk , i think maybe you got quieter

Mara frowned.

Mara: rude

Cam: not in a bad way

Mara: still rude

Cam: you used to pause like you were waiting for something

Mara stared at the words.

Cam: now you pause like you’re actually thinking,

Mara did not know what to say back to that. Which, annoyingly, kind of proved his point.

Mara: okay that was weirdly serious

Cam: sorry
Cam: i’ll go back to being annoying

Mara: thank you

Cam: why do you unplug

Mara: you already asked me that

Cam: no i asked why YOU started
Cam: this is different

Mara: you are exhausting

Cam: i’ve been told

This time he didn’t answer right away. Mara watched the typing dots appear, disappear, then appear again. She almost told him never mind, but stopped herself.

Cam: when i was little my grandpa used to take me places with bad signal

Mara: on purpose??

Cam: yeah

Mara: that is fully illegal grandpa behavior

Cam: he would be proud of that sentence

Mara smiled.

Cam: i hated it at first
Cam: like actually hated it
Cam: there was nothing to do

Mara: horrifying

Cam: right

A pause.

Cam: then one time we sat by the river for like an hour and he didn’t make me talk
Cam: or be normal
Cam: or answer anything

Mara pictured Cam younger, sitting somewhere outside the city zones with no prompts sliding into his thoughts and no one filling the silence for him. She couldn’t decide if that sounded awful or kind of nice.

Mara: that sounds lonely

Cam: yeah
Cam: but not always

Mara rested the screen against her blanket and did not answer right away. The Guide nudged her about sleep timing. She dismissed it without opening the full reminder.

Then another message came through.

Cam: you should come by the shop again sometime

Mara picked the screen back up.

Mara: ya

Cam: my grandpa likes you

Mara: he barely knows me

Cam: he said you ask weird questions

Mara: wow what a compliment

Cam: from him it is

Mara: what do you think

The typing dots appeared, then stopped.

For a second, Mara regretted asking.

Then his answer showed up.

Cam: i think you’re less boring than most people

Mara stared at the message.

Her face got warm, which was extremely annoying because she was alone and there was no reason for her face to be doing anything.

Mara: that might be the nicest mean thing anyone has ever said to me

Cam: i’m talented

Mara: clearly

Outside her window, the city towers shifted into their nightly display. Blue, gold, white. The same colors from the cafeteria banner.

GUIDE30: 8 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.

Celebrate thirty years of clarity, unity, and support.

Mara watched the words crawl across the side of a distant building.

Mara: are you going to Guide30

The typing dots appeared.

Disappeared.

Appeared again.

Cam: no

Mara sat up a little.

Mara: everyone is going

Cam: that’s kind of the problem

Cam: idk
Cam: just feels weird

Mara stared at the screen.

Mara: that’s not an answer

Cam: you said idk was a valid answer earlier

Mara: rude to use my own logic against me

Mara looked back out the window. The countdown shifted again, brighter this time.

GUIDE30: 12 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.

For the first time, the countdown did not feel like a celebration.

It felt like a warning.

Chapter 13

Mara went back to the repair shop on Tuesday after school pretending she needed the journal checked again.

She knew it was a weak excuse before she even opened the door. The repaired page was fine. She had checked it three times before leaving the apartment, pressing the paper flat with her fingertips like it might suddenly fall apart and give her a real reason to go.

It didn’t.

She went anyway.

The truth was, she had not spoken to Lila in two days. Not really. Lila had sent four messages. The first one said, I’m sorry. The second one said, I really was trying to help. The third one said, Please don’t ignore me. The fourth one had no words at all, just a sad little sticker Mara would have laughed at last week.

Now she could not make herself answer.

Every time she tried, she remembered Lila’s face in the library.

I saved you.

And then Mara felt angry all over again.

The bell above the repair shop door gave its uneven little jingle when she stepped inside. Clocks ticked from different corners of the room, all slightly off from one another. Somewhere farther back, something buzzed softly and clicked off again.

The shop smelled the same as she remembered, like dust, wood polish, old paper, and something cooking.

Cam’s grandfather looked up from behind the counter.

“The famous damaged page returns.”

Mara set the journal on the counter. “It could be ripping worse.”

“It could also be perfectly fine.”

“It could be secretly ripping worse.”

“That sounds medical.”

“I’m very concerned.”

“Mhm.” He took the journal and opened it carefully. “And here I thought you just missed my sparkling personality.”

Mara looked away too fast.

Cam’s voice came from near the back wall. “Nobody misses that.”

He was sitting on the floor beside an old radio with the back panel removed. Tiny screws sat lined up beside his knee in careful rows. He held one up to the light, squinting at it like it had personally offended him.

Eli didn’t look up from the journal. “Careful. I control dinner.”

Cam glanced at Mara. “Hi.”

“Hey.”

That was apparently all either of them had.

Excellent.

Mara wandered farther into the shop while Cam went back to the radio. The place somehow looked even more crowded during the daytime. Shelves were packed with old radios, tangled cords, stacks of photographs, boxes with handwritten labels faded at the edges. Nothing matched. Nothing glowed unless it was supposed to. A fan turned lazily near the ceiling like it had been spinning forever.

The Guide nudged softly at the edge of her thoughts.

History assignment due tomorrow.

Mara dismissed it automatically.

Near the front window, a small public display on the street flashed through the glass.

GUIDE30: 7 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.

Celebrate thirty years of clarity, unity, and support.

The colors shifted from blue to gold to white.

Mara looked away.

Cam noticed.

“They put one across from the shop yesterday,” he said.

“Hard to miss.”

“That’s the point.”

His grandfather made a low grunting sound from behind the counter. Not quite agreement. Not quite warning.

Mara pretended to study a shelf of old clocks while Cam twisted something inside the radio. Music crackled unevenly through the speaker, then vanished, then came back again. Somebody singing over guitar strings slightly out of tune.

“You’re here a lot,” Mara said.

Cam shrugged without looking up. “My mom works late.”

“And your dad?”

He pulled another screw out and set it carefully in the row. “Up north. Forestry work. He comes back every couple months.”

“Oh.”

“It’s fine. We talk.”

He said it casually enough that Mara almost believed him.

From behind the counter, Grandpa Eli cleared his throat. “Also, I apparently run a free repair apprenticeship program.”

“You mean child labor,” Cam said.

“You mean valuable life skills.”

“You yelled at me for holding a screwdriver wrong yesterday.”

“Because you were holding it wrong.”

Cam rolled his eyes, but Mara could tell he was trying not to smile.

A notification slid across Mara’s vision.

Recommended social balance check-in: unresolved peer conflict detected.

Her stomach tightened.

Lila.

Mara dismissed it quickly, but not quickly enough. Cam looked up from the radio, his hand still resting near the row of tiny screws beside his knee.

“You okay?”

“Yeah,” Mara said.

Cam did not go back to the radio. He just waited, which was somehow worse than asking again. Mara looked toward the front window instead of at him. Outside, the Guide30 display shifted from blue to gold to white, bright and cheerful against the gray afternoon.

“I’m not talking to Lila,” she said finally.

Cam set the screwdriver down. “What happened?”

Mara pressed her fingers against the edge of the journal. She had not planned to say it. Not out loud. Not to Cam. But the words had been sitting inside her for two days, getting heavier every time Lila sent another message.

“She reported me,” Mara said.

Cam did not answer right away.

“She said she was helping,” Mara added. Her voice came out smaller than she wanted it to, so she looked harder at the window. “She called it a concern report. Like that made it better.”

Cam looked down at the screws lined up beside his knee. “I’m sorry.”

Mara blinked.

That was not what she had expected. No advice. No big speech. No I told you so. Just sorry.

Somehow that made her throat tighten.

“She cried,” Mara said. “And I still walked away.”

Cam picked at the edge of one screw with his fingernail. For a moment, the only sound in the shop was the uneven ticking of the clocks and the faint hum of the old radio.

“That doesn’t mean you were wrong,” he said.

“It kind of felt wrong.”

“Yeah.” Cam’s voice stayed quiet. “Stuff can feel wrong and still be the only thing you can do.”

Mara looked at him then.

He shrugged like he immediately regretted saying something that serious. “Or whatever.”

Mara almost smiled.

Almost.

Cam picked up the screwdriver again, then stopped before putting it back inside the radio. “Was that why? Did you get moved up after Lila told?”

“To Tier 2?”

He nodded.

“I think so.”

His face went still in a way that made the shop feel colder.

“What?” Mara asked.

“Peer concern reports carry more weight.”

Mara frowned. “What does that mean?”

Cam leaned back against the shelf behind him. “It means the system doesn’t just count what you do. It counts who says they’re worried about you.”

Mara thought of Lila standing in the library with tears in her eyes, insisting it was different because she had not “reported” Mara. She had only “reported concern.”

Like that made it better.

“It feels worse that way,” Mara said quietly.

“It is worse that way,” Cam said.

The clocks ticked around them, each one keeping time slightly wrong. Outside the window, the Guide30 display flashed again, bright enough to paint the glass blue.

11 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY. Cam and Mara stared out at the sign.

Mara looked away first.

That was the problem. Lila had meant it. If she had been cruel, it would have been easier to hate her.

Cam looked toward his grandfather, but Eli kept reading the journal like he had suddenly become extremely interested in paper fibers.

Then Mara asked the question that had been following her since the first day.

“Why didn’t they recalibrate you?”

Cam’s hand froze over the radio.

Mara rushed to explain. “I mean after Mr. Halden’s class. When the system flagged you. He made it sound like if I didn’t report you, you’d be pulled out right away. But you weren’t.”

Cam set the screwdriver down very carefully.

“They don’t always take you right away,” he said.

“They don’t?”

“That’s what they want everyone to think.” He leaned back against the shelf behind him. “A report starts a review. The system checks sync history, wellness markers, response delays, social concerns. Stuff like that.”

Mara sat on the edge of a wooden crate across from him. “So if I had reported you?”

“It would have counted as peer-confirmed disruption.” He said the words like he had heard them too many times. “That moves things faster.”

Mara’s throat tightened. “So I slowed it down?”

Cam looked at her.

“Yeah,” he said. “You did. You slowed it down.”

Not stopped it.

Slowed it down.

The difference sat between them.

“But they’re still watching you,” Mara said.

Cam gave a tiny shrug. “They’ve been watching me for years.”

Eli finally closed the journal and slid it back across the counter. “Page is fine.”

Mara looked over. “You checked it that fast?”

“I checked it slowly. You were distracted.”

Cam snorted.

Mara stood and took the journal, holding it against her chest. “So why haven’t they recalibrated you before now?”

Cam glanced toward Eli again.

This time Eli answered.

“Paperwork.”

Mara blinked. “Paperwork?”

“People underestimate paperwork,” Eli said. “Very useful when applied correctly.”

Cam picked at the edge of one screw with his fingernail. “My grandpa filed exemptions when I was little. Medical ones first. Then educational reviews. Then appeals. Then appeals to the appeals.”

“Those are real?”

“They used to be,” Eli said. “Most people don’t know how to find them anymore.”

Mara looked at Cam. “So you’re protected?”

Cam gave a humorless little laugh. “Delayed. Not protected, and it really is all up to my mom.”

The shop felt quieter after that.

Outside the window, the Guide30 display shifted again.

12 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.

Eli watched the colors change across the glass.

“Anniversaries are useful,” he said.

Cam looked up quickly. “Grandpa.”

Eli ignored him. “People like celebrating a story before they ask whether it’s true.”

Mara turned toward him. “What does that mean?”

“It means I don’t think the Guide30 is just a birthday party,” Eli said.

Cam stood too fast. “Soup’s ready.”

Mara looked between them.

Eli’s mouth twitched slightly. “That was not subtle.”

Cam didn’t smile. “You were about to say too much.”

For a second, the ticking clocks were the only sound in the shop.

Then Eli nodded once. “Soup it is.”

The kitchen in the back of the shop was barely bigger than Mara’s bedroom. One tiny table sat beneath a rain-streaked window while the clocks from the front room ticked faintly through the walls.

Eli handed Mara a bowl before she could decide whether she was actually staying. The soup smelled heavily of garlic and herbs she didn’t recognize. Cam sat across from her while Eli lowered himself slowly into the third chair.

Just as Mara picked up her spoon, Eli paused.

“Hold on.”

Cam lowered his head automatically.

Mara froze for a second before awkwardly lowering hers too.

“Lord, thank You for food, warm places, and people willing to ask good questions. Amen.”

“Amen,” Cam said.

Then Eli reached for the bread basket like nothing unusual had happened.

Mara looked back down at her soup.

Nobody really prayed out loud anymore unless it was during official ceremonies or public holidays. Even then it usually sounded polished and approved and distant, like someone had checked it for efficiency first.

This had not sounded polished at all.

It sounded like Eli was talking to Someone who had actually come to dinner.

The Guide nudged softly again.

Unread messages.

Assignment reminder.

Mara ignored both.

Nobody talked. They just ate. Wind pressed against the windows while the clocks ticked unevenly through the walls.

Cam finally pointed his spoon toward the book sitting near Mara’s elbow. She must have carried it in without realizing.

Questions Worth Asking.

“That thing ruined my childhood, by the way,” Cam said.

“You’re fourteen.”

“Exactly. Tragic.”

Eli ignored him. “It’s a good book.”

“It made me answer questions like ‘What is courage?’ when I was nine.”

“And look how wonderfully normal you turned out.”

Cam gave him a flat look.

Mara opened the book carefully. The pages were crowded with notes from different people. Whole arguments filled the margins. Somebody had circled paragraphs hard enough to leave marks through the paper.

One comment just said:

No. Absolutely not.

Underneath it somebody else had written:

Then explain why.

Mara turned another page, trying not to smile.

“The Guide would hate this book,” she said.

“The Guide would summarize it into three sentences and remove all the arguing,” Eli replied.

“That also sounds true.”

Mara stopped on a page near the middle.

People will trade freedom for reassurance faster than they realize.

The sentence had been underlined several times in different pen colors.

A reminder flickered briefly across Mara’s vision.

Recommended study cycle beginning in twelve minutes.

She ignored it.

Eli noticed. Of course he did.

“So,” he said, tearing a piece of bread in half, “what question keeps following you around lately?”

Cam groaned. “You can’t just ask people that while they’re eating.”

“Why not?”

“Because it sounds like the beginning of a psychological experiment.”

Eli looked at Mara. “You don’t have to answer.”

That made it worse somehow. If he had pushed, Mara could have resisted.

Instead she stared down into her soup.

“Do you think people can forget how to think for themselves without realizing it?” she asked finally.

Neither Cam nor Eli answered immediately.

Cam leaned back slightly in his chair.

Eli rested one elbow against the table and studied her for a second before speaking.

“I think people can get very used to being comfortable,” he said. “And once comfort starts feeling like safety, they’ll defend almost anything that keeps them from feeling afraid.”

Mara thought of Lila’s face in the library.

I saved you.

“She was scared,” Mara said, before she meant to.

Cam looked at her.

“Lila,” Mara said. “She was scared. That’s why she reported me.”

Eli nodded slowly. “Fear makes people obedient faster than hate does.”

Cam looked down at his soup.

Mara suddenly wished she had not said anything.

Then a soft tone sounded.

Not from Mara’s Guide.

From Cam’s.

His expression changed before he even looked at the notification. His shoulders tightened. His face went still.

“What?” Mara asked.

Cam did not answer.

Eli’s chair scraped softly against the floor as he stood.

“Cam.”

Cam stared at whatever only he could see.

Mara’s stomach dropped. “What is it?”

Cam blinked, but his face had changed.

“My review got moved.”

The room went quiet except for the ticking clocks in the front of the shop.

Eli set his spoon down. “Moved to when?”

Cam swallowed. “Friday.”

Mara stared at him. “This Friday?”

Cam looked at her, and for once he did not have a joke ready.

“Yeah,” he said. “This Friday.”

“Exactly,” Cam said. “I think they are trying to clear the list before the event.”

Chapter 14

10 days until Guide30

The whole city seemed to be counting down.

The words flashed across the transit station screens, the school entrance display, the cafeteria wall, and the side of the tall glass building across from Mara’s apartment. Blue, gold, white. Over and over again. Celebrate thirty years of clarity, unity, and support.

Mara used to think the colors were pretty. Now they made her stomach hurt.

She had barely slept Tuesday night. Every time she closed her eyes, she saw Cam sitting at Eli’s table, staring at a notification only he could see.

My review got moved.

Friday.

That was only two days away.

Mara checked her messages three times before school even started. There was nothing from Cam since the night before, when he had finally answered her last message with:

still alive. tragically.

That should have made her feel better. It did, a little. But not enough.

There were also five messages from Lila sitting unread beneath his name.

Can we please talk?

I know you’re mad.

I didn’t mean to make things worse.

I told Ms. Cole I think I overreacted.

Mara please.

Mara stared at the fourth message longer than the others.

I told Ms. Cole.

Her stomach twisted. Lila still did not understand. Talking to Ms. Cole again was not fixing it. It was doing the exact thing Mara wanted her to stop doing.

The Guide suggested a peer reconciliation prompt, then a calming breathing cycle, then a reminder that unresolved conflict could increase stress markers. Mara dismissed all three before they finished opening.

By the time she reached school, the front entrance was crowded with students moving beneath a huge Guide30 banner stretched above the doors. A group of younger kids were taking pictures under it while the morning announcement played through the outdoor speakers.

“Guide30 readiness programming begins this week. Students are reminded that full participation helps ensure a healthy and unified celebration experience.”

Healthy and unified.

Mara was getting tired of words like that, words that sounded nice but were a little too perfect.

Inside, the halls felt louder than usual. Or maybe Mara was just noticing more. The tiny pauses in conversations. The half-second delays before people answered. The way everyone’s eyes unfocused when a notification slid through their thoughts.

Maybe it had always been like this.

Maybe she had been like this.

She stopped near Cam’s locker before first period, even though she told herself she was not going to.

He was there.

Mara stopped so suddenly that a seventh grader almost walked into her.

Cam was leaning against his locker with one shoulder, trying to open a breakfast bar with his teeth because apparently using hands was too advanced. His hair fell into his eyes like usual, and his backpack was half-unzipped. For one second, he looked exactly like himself.

Then he saw her.

“Don’t look so relieved,” he said around the wrapper. “It’s bad for my ego.”

Mara walked closer. “Your ego survived?”

“Barely. It’s asking for support services.”

That sounded like Cam. Mostly.

Mara hugged her books tighter against her chest. “You didn’t answer after last night.”

“I answered.”

“You said ‘tragically.’”

“That was emotional honesty.”

“That was annoying.”

“Also honest.”

Mara wanted to laugh, but Friday sat between them like a third person.

Cam must have felt it too, because his face changed a little. Not much. Just enough for the joke to thin out.

“My mom got three school notices this morning,” he said.

“About the review?”

“About support preparation.” He said the words with a flat voice, like he was reading them off a cereal box. “Sleep, hydration, reduced conflict exposure, and maintaining trust in the review process.”

Mara made a face. “Reduced conflict exposure?”

“I think that means me.”

“It probably means everyone around you.”

“That’s more fair.”

A group of students moved around them, laughing about something on their feeds. Across the hall, Lila stood near the water fountain with Nessa and June. She was not laughing. She looked toward Mara, then toward Cam, then quickly down at her screen.

Mara’s chest tightened.

Cam followed her gaze. “Still bad?”

Mara looked back at him. “Still bad.”

“Sorry.”

She shrugged, but it did not feel like enough of an answer.

The Guide highlighted her route to class.

Proceed to first period.

Cam glanced at the same direction like his Guide had done it too. “Guess we’re being proceeded.”

“That’s not a word.”

“It is now. I’m innovative.”

“You’re something.”

He pushed away from the locker and walked beside her. For half the hallway, it almost felt normal. Cam making dumb comments. Mara pretending not to care. The Guide30 countdown glowing from every screen like the city had decorated itself in reminders.

But when they reached the classroom door, Cam paused.

“What?” Mara asked.

He looked down the hall, then back at her. “If I say weird things after Friday, you’re allowed to tell me.”

Mara stared at him.

“I mean it,” he said.

“What kind of weird things?”

“I don’t know. Polite things.”

“You already say polite things sometimes.”

“No, I pretend to say polite things. There’s a difference.”

Mara tightened her grip on her books. “Cam.”

He looked away first. “I’m just saying. If I start sounding like a brochure, throw something at me.”

“I’m not throwing things at you.”

“Emotionally then.”

“I can do that.”

“Good.”

The classroom door opened, and Mr. Halden looked out at them.

“Class is beginning.”

Cam lifted one hand. “Wouldn’t want to damage public harmony.”

Mr. Halden did not smile.

Mara and Cam went inside.

First period was Verbal Synchronization, which felt like a terrible joke.

Mr. Halden stood at the front of the room while the Guide30 countdown glowed in the corner of the wall display. Today’s lesson was called Public Harmony Response Practice. Students were supposed to practice appropriate reactions for large civic gatherings, which mostly meant learning how to sound calm and peaceful no matter what happened.

The system gave them prompts.

A family member becomes overwhelmed in a crowd.

A friend refuses to participate in a unity activity.

A student expresses anxiety about national celebration events.

Mara stared at that last one too long. The Guide offered her a response almost immediately.

I would reassure the student that Guide30 is designed to support all participants and encourage them to seek wellness assistance if anxiety persists.

Mara stared at the answer. It was exactly what Mr. Halden wanted.

Which made her not want to say it.

“Mara?” Mr. Halden said.

Every head turned.

Mara felt the answer sitting in her mind, smooth and safe and ready to use. She could say it and be done. She could step back into the current and let it carry her.

Instead she said, “Maybe I’d ask why they were anxious.”

The room got quiet. Not shocked quiet. Worse. Careful quiet.

Mr. Halden looked at his tablet before looking back at her. “That would be an acceptable first step, if followed by appropriate support routing.”

“Right,” Mara said.

The Guide pulsed softly.

Response deviation noted.

Mara looked down at her desk.

Across the room, Lila’s head turned slightly toward her, but Mara did not look back. Cam did. He glanced over his shoulder at Mara, just for a second, and his mouth twitched like he wanted to say something he knew better than to say in class.

That helped more than it should have.

By second period, the whole school had started to feel too bright. Mara checked her messages again between classes. Nothing new from Cam, even though he was only two classrooms away. Nothing new from Lila either, which should have been a relief but somehow wasn’t.

The Guide reminded her that unanswered peer messages could increase social strain.

Mara dismissed it so fast the notification flickered.

Then the lights went out.

Not all the way. Just a hard blink. A half-second of darkness before the hallway lights snapped back on.

Everyone froze.

For one strange moment, the hallway was full of students standing still with their mouths half-open, like somebody had paused a video and forgotten to restart it.

The overhead speakers chimed.

“Minor synchronization delay resolved. No action required.”

The hallway breathed again. Someone laughed too loudly. A teacher clapped her hands and told everyone to keep moving. The Guide rerouted students around a stairwell bottleneck, and within seconds the hallway looked normal again.

But Mara had seen it.

For that one second, nobody knew what to do.

Not even her.

At lunch, Mara sat at the end of a table near the windows. Not her old table. Not completely alone either. It was the kind of spot that looked accidental, which was exactly why she chose it.

Lila sat with Nessa and June two tables away. Mara could feel them there without looking. Nessa said something quietly, and June leaned closer to listen. Lila kept her eyes on her food.

Connor dropped into the seat across from Mara with his tray and a dramatic sigh.

“I am officially against soup.”

Mara looked at his tray. “That’s not soup.”

“Exactly. I ordered noodles, and this is noodles pretending to be soup.”

“Maybe it’s going through something.”

“That’s what adults say when they don’t want to admit something is wrong.”

Mara looked at him.

Connor pointed his spoon at her. “What? I contain wisdom sometimes.”

“I’m sure it’s very uncomfortable for you.”

“Deeply.”

Mara took a bite of her lunch. For a minute, Connor let the silence sit, which was unusual enough that she noticed.

Then he glanced toward Lila’s table. “So. Everybody’s being normal and mature, I see.”

Mara did not answer.

“Right,” Connor said. “Forbidden topic.”

“It’s not forbidden.”

“It’s just surrounded by emotional lasers?”

“That sounds accurate.”

Connor nodded like he was filing that away. “Cool. I will avoid the lasers.”

A few seats down, someone mentioned Guide30 rehearsal schedules, and the table lit up with complaints. Band students had extra practice. Student greeters had orientation. Younger grades were rehearsing a welcome chant that Connor immediately declared “a crime against ears.”

Mara listened without joining in.

Guide30 was a celebration. Everyone kept saying that. The city would have music and food and lights and drones and speeches. Lila had been excited about her solo for weeks. Connor cared mostly about whether the food trucks would be better than cafeteria noodles. Even the teachers sounded lighter when they mentioned it.

Mara wanted it to feel normal too.

It just didn’t.

Cam slid into the seat beside Connor halfway through lunch with a sandwich he had clearly smashed in his backpack.

Connor looked at it. “Did your lunch lose a fight?”

“Several,” Cam said.

Mara looked up quickly. “Where were you?”

“Meeting.”

“What kind?”

Cam tore open the sandwich bag. “The kind where they say ‘preparation’ a lot.”

Connor looked between them. “Is this a lasers conversation?”

“Yes,” Mara said.

“No,” Cam said at the same time.

Connor lifted both hands. “Great. I love clarity.”

Cam took a bite of his sandwich, then looked at Mara. “It was just a pre-review check-in.”

“Just?”

“I’m trying not to make everything sound like a disaster.”

“That doesn’t mean it isn’t one.”

Cam swallowed and looked down at the table. “I know.”

That was the first honest thing either of them had said about Friday all day.

Connor, to his credit, did not make a joke.

For almost four whole seconds.

Then he said, “For the record, I do not support Friday as a concept. It has always seemed suspicious.”

Cam looked at him. “Friday is the best day of the week.”

“Exactly what Friday wants you to think.”

Mara shook her head, but the tightness in her chest loosened a little.

After lunch, the day dragged. The Guide30 banners seemed to multiply every time Mara turned a corner. In history, Mr. Bennett talked about the early years after the Guide launched, when cities were still learning how to connect schools, transit, hospitals, and emergency systems into one shared network.

“It was considered one of the greatest achievements of public coordination,” he said.

The wall screen showed old footage of crowded streets becoming orderly, hospital wait times dropping, and storm evacuations happening faster than ever before.

Mara watched people in the video follow glowing route lines toward shelters.

It looked helpful.

It was helpful.

That was the part that kept making everything harder.

The Guide had helped people. It helped Grandma remember faces. It helped Mom keep track of work and groceries and a thousand things she was always juggling. It helped students who were scared, kids who were overwhelmed, families who needed directions, doctors who needed answers fast.

Mara knew that.

So why did it feel like the more it helped, the less anyone remembered how to be helpless for even one second?

The final bell rang before she figured out how to answer that.

After school, Mara headed toward the front steps with the rest of the crowd. The sky had turned gray again, and wind pushed leaves across the sidewalk in little spinning circles. Students packed the pickup area, checking routes and complaining about the cold.

Mara stood near the curb by herself, pretending to check her route even though it had not changed in three minutes.

A few yards away, Lila stood with Nessa and June near the front steps. Lila kept glancing over like she wanted to say something, but every time Mara looked up, Lila quickly looked somewhere else.

Connor was balancing his backpack on one foot for absolutely no reason.

“You’re going to fall,” Nessa said.

“I’m aware of the risk,” Connor said.

“That makes it worse,” June told him.

Connor grinned right before the backpack slipped sideways and smacked directly into his leg.

“My own people mock me,” he said, hopping once and grabbing his bag.

Mara heard it and wanted to answer, but stopped herself. Laughing with them felt too much like everything was normal.

The usual stream of buses should have arrived by then, but the pickup lane stayed mostly empty. A few students checked their Guides automatically.

“Mine says delayed,” somebody nearby said.

“Same.”

“Route syncing issue maybe?”

Nobody sounded worried yet. Mostly annoyed. Mara glanced down the street, but the lane stayed open and empty except for one school van and a line of parents waiting in the wrong place.

Then half the students around her went still at almost the exact same time.

Not frozen exactly. Just waiting.

Their eyes shifted slightly unfocused while notifications refreshed.

A second later, confused voices started breaking out across the sidewalk.

“My route disappeared.”

“Wait, mine too.”

“It says stand by.”

“What does stand by mean?”

Connor frowned at nothing in front of him. “Okay, that’s actually weird.”

A teacher near the entrance raised her voice. “Everyone stay near your assigned pickup sections while transit sync recalibrates.”

That probably would have helped if everybody remembered their assigned pickup sections.

Most of the time, nobody had to. The Guide showed the right curb, the right bus, the right door, the right adult. It even warned you if you were walking the wrong way. Without the blue route lines glowing in front of them, the front of the school suddenly looked like a place nobody had been before.

Students started drifting around uncertainly. Some moved toward the wrong lanes, then turned around again when conflicting updates appeared. A few younger kids looked close to tears.

A sharp chime echoed overhead.

Synchronization interruption detected.
Transit guidance temporarily unavailable.

A groan rolled through the crowd.

“You have got to be kidding me,” Connor muttered.

Students immediately started talking over each other.

“What if the buses already left?”

“They wouldn’t leave.”

“How do you know?”

“My dad’s gonna freak out if I’m late.”

“I can’t even message my route group right now.”

Mara’s own stomach tightened. Her Guide kept trying to reconnect, notifications flickering in and out across her vision without fully loading.

Searching for updated transit pathways…

Then nothing.

For one second, she had the strange urge to just stand there and wait until somebody told her what to do.

The feeling surprised her, mostly because that was exactly what everybody else was doing too.

Teachers huddled together near the entrance, talking too quickly while students crowded closer around them. One boy kept asking the same question over and over, even after nobody answered him the first three times.

Then Mara noticed a little girl near the curb. She looked younger than everyone else, maybe third grade, with a purple backpack almost as big as she was. She kept turning in a small circle, wiping her face with one sleeve.

“My mom’s route disappeared,” the girl said to nobody in particular. “It won’t tell me where to go.”

Mara looked around.

Everyone was busy looking at blank routes, frozen prompts, or teachers who were trying to sound more certain than they looked.

The girl started crying harder.

Mara stepped toward her before she could think too much about it.

“Hey,” she said gently. “What’s your name?”

The girl sniffed. “Ava.”

“I’m Mara. Are you supposed to be at the younger pickup area?”

Ava shook her head fast. “I don’t know. My Guide always tells me.”

Mara looked across the crowded sidewalk. Normally the answer would have appeared instantly. Pickup zones. Guardian tracking. Route matching. Now there was just noise and wind and people getting more irritated every minute.

Then Mara remembered something.

The elementary pickup lanes were on the opposite side of the building near the gym entrance. Her mom had picked her up there years ago, before the Guide had started doing every little thing for everybody.

“Come on,” Mara said. “I think it’s this way.”

Ava looked up at her. “You think?”

Mara paused.

Normally, she would have waited for the Guide to confirm it. Normally, she would have trusted the blue line more than her own memory.

But the blue line was gone.

So she tried to remember.

“Yeah,” Mara said. “I’m pretty sure.”

Connor appeared beside them, backpack over one shoulder. “Pretty sure is better than standing here until graduation.”

Mara looked back once. Lila was watching from near the steps, her face worried. Nessa said something to her, but Lila did not look away.

Mara turned back toward Ava.

She could not deal with Lila right now.

They moved around the side of the building, staying close to the wall as the wind pushed leaves across the wet sidewalk. Mara kept looking for familiar pieces of the school from when she was younger. The side doors. The ramp near the gym. The painted line along the curb where parents used to wait.

For a few seconds, she was afraid she had remembered wrong.

Then they turned the corner.

A cluster of parents stood near the gym doors under the awning. A teacher was there too, holding a tablet and looking very relieved to see another student appear.

Ava gasped. “That’s my mom!”

She ran forward before Mara could answer. A woman near the doors dropped to one knee and opened her arms just in time for Ava to crash into her.

Mara let out a breath she had not realized she was holding.

Connor leaned closer. “Not bad for pretty sure.”

Mara looked back toward the front of the school. The main pickup area was still loud and crowded, and the Guide was still trying to reconnect in the corner of her vision.

Then the Guide came back online.

Updated route available.
Return to assigned pickup zone.

The blue line appeared in front of Mara, bright and smooth and certain, pointing her back around the building like nothing had happened.

Mara stared at it.

A minute ago, that line would have felt helpful.

Now it felt late.

Chapter 15

10 days until Guide30

By the time Mara got home that afternoon, she felt tired in a way sleep probably would not fix.

The pickup glitch kept replaying in her mind. Not just the routes disappearing or the delayed buses or the blue lines coming back too late. It was the waiting. The way everyone had stood there, staring at blank directions like the front of the school had turned into a place none of them had ever seen before.

And then there was Ava.

Mara could still picture the little girl’s purple backpack bouncing as she ran toward her mom near the gym doors. She had helped her. That part should have felt good, and it did, a little.

But it also bothered her.

Because helping Ava had not been some amazing thing. Mara had not hacked a system or solved a complicated emergency. She had remembered where the younger pickup area was. That was all.

So why had it felt like breaking a rule?

Her mom was in the kitchen when Mara came in, standing at the counter with a pile of grocery bags and a very annoyed expression.

“The Guide ordered oat milk again,” Mom said without looking up.

Mara dropped her bag near the couch. “You don’t drink oat milk.”

“I know.”

“Dad?”

“He thinks oat milk is what happens when regular milk gives up.”

Mara looked at the carton. “I mean… he’s not wrong.”

Her mom pulled it from the bag and set it on the counter. “Apparently I bought it because my nutritional profile suggests I should be open to alternatives.”

“That sounds bossy.”

“It is bossy.” Mom shoved the carton toward the back of the fridge. “And expensive.”

Mara leaned against the counter, watching her mom unpack the rest of the bags. It felt nice for a second. Normal. Annoying groceries. Her mom complaining about a system that had technically been trying to help. A kitchen that smelled faintly like onions and coffee.

Then Mara’s screen buzzed.

She grabbed it too fast.

Nothing from Cam.

Just another Guide30 reminder.

GUIDE30: 10 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.
Family attendance confirmation recommended.

Mara locked the screen and set it face down.

Her mom noticed. “Cam?”

Mara shook her head. “Guide30.”

“Ah.” Mom pulled a dented can of tomatoes from one bag. “The city’s favorite new personality.”

“It’s everywhere.”

“That is usually the point of citywide celebrations.”

“I know.” Mara slid onto one of the stools at the counter. “But it feels different now.”

Mom stopped unpacking. “Different how?”

Mara was not sure how to answer that. She thought about the banners. The countdowns. The cheerful reminders. She thought about Cam at Eli’s table, staring at the notice only he could see.

His review had been moved to Friday.

That was only two days away.

“I don’t know,” Mara said. “Like everyone is excited, but I keep noticing things I didn’t notice before.”

Mom studied her for a second, then went back to the groceries. “Noticing can be annoying.”

“Grandpa Frank made it sound important.”

“It can be both.”

Mara picked at a loose thread on her sleeve. “The pickup thing was weird.”

“I heard.” Mom’s eyes shifted slightly, probably reading a message from work. “People are still complaining.”

“Over buses?”

“You would be amazed what adults can turn into a crisis.”

“It kind of was one. But also it wasn’t.” Mara frowned, trying to find the right words. “Nobody was hurt. Nobody was trapped. It was just delayed pickup. But everyone acted like they couldn’t move.”

Mom put the last grocery bag away and leaned against the counter. “People don’t like feeling lost.”

“Even teachers?”

“Especially teachers. They’re used to pretending they aren’t.”

Mara looked down at the counter. “A little girl couldn’t find her mom. Her Guide stopped loading.”

“What did you do?”

“I helped her find younger pickup.”

“That’s good, Mara.”

“It felt weird.”

“Helping her?”

“No.” Mara hesitated. “Remembering.”

Mom’s face softened, but she did not jump in right away.

“I knew where to go because you used to pick me up there,” Mara said. “Before the Guide did every tiny thing. I just… remembered it.”

“That is allowed, you know.”

“It didn’t feel allowed.”

Mom opened her mouth, then closed it again like she had decided not to say the first thing that came to her.

“What?” Mara asked.

“Nothing.”

“That was not a nothing face.”

Mom sighed and reached for the oat milk again, turning it around like the carton might explain itself. “I think the Guide helps so much that people forget they’re still allowed to know things.”

Mara sat with that.

A notification slid across Mom’s vision. Her eyes unfocused for a second.

Mara pointed at her. “You just did it.”

Mom blinked. “Did what?”

“The pause thing.”

Mom made a face. “I know. It’s bad.”

“You were saying people forget they’re allowed to know things, and then the Guide interrupted you.”

“That is rude timing.”

“It is.”

Mom pushed the oat milk farther back in the fridge. “And a little too perfect.”

Mara looked up.

Her mom seemed to realize what she had said and smiled faintly. “Apparently I’m stealing your words now.”

Mara did not remember telling her that exact thought, but maybe she had. Or maybe everyone was starting to notice the same thing, just in different ways.

The apartment was quiet for a moment except for the hum of the fridge.

Then Mara said, “Do you think people depend on the Guide too much?”

Mom did not answer immediately. That made Mara pay closer attention.

Finally, Mom said, “Yes. I do. I just don’t think most people notice until it stops working.”

That answer sat between them longer than Mara expected.

Then Mom clapped her hands once, softer than usual. “Okay. Soup. Then homework. Then sleep, because you look like a very damp ghost.”

“I’m not damp anymore.”

“You are emotionally damp.”

“That’s not a thing.”

“It is now.”

After dinner, Mom disappeared into her bedroom for a work call about the pickup delays. Mara stayed on the couch with a blanket over her legs, listening to the muffled sound of Mom’s voice through the wall.

The Guide lit softly at the edge of Mara’s vision.

Suggested evening reflection available.

Mara stared at the words.

Usually she would open it. The Guide would ask three questions about her emotional state, suggest a gratitude thought, and save the answers somewhere no one ever fully explained. It would make her feel organized, at least for a little while.

Tonight she muted it.

Then she went upstairs and pulled the journal from her bag.

The repaired page held neatly in place, a thin line near the fold showing where the tear had been. Eli had told her the page would never be exactly the same, but that did not mean it was ruined.

Mara ran her finger carefully near the repaired edge.

On the next blank page, she wrote the date.

Wednesday. 10 days until Guide30.

Then she sat there, pen hovering.

She had prayed before. Twice, kind of. The first time had been an accident, just the word God slipping out before she knew what else to say. The second time had been after Eli prayed over soup, and she had felt strange and curious and embarrassed all at once.

This felt different.

Maybe because of Ava. Maybe because of Cam. Maybe because Friday was coming too fast. Maybe because she was tired of pretending she was only thinking when really she was asking.

Mara wrote:

God.

Then she stopped.

It looked too small on the page.

She added:

Are You really there?

For a while, nothing happened. No voice. No warmth. No sign. The Guide did not answer because she had muted it. The room did not answer either.

But the silence did not feel exactly empty.

It felt like standing in a doorway and not knowing yet if she was brave enough to walk in.

Mara turned the pen between her fingers.

Then she wrote one more line.

Please help Cam.

She stared at the words until they blurred a little.

That was not enough. There should have been more. Help him how? Help him not get recalibrated? Help him not change? Help him not be scared? Help her not be scared?

She did not know.

So she left it there.

Please help Cam.

In the morning, nothing looked different. The Guide was still there. Her school schedule opened on time. Lila still had messages Mara had not answered. Cam had not sent anything new.

But Mara remembered asking.

That part stayed.

Thursday, Day 9

The next morning, the countdown had changed.

GUIDE30: 9 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.

Mara saw it on the wall display before she even got out of bed. The numbers sat under her morning schedule, bright and cheerful, like the whole city had decided to become a reminder.

Nine days until Guide30.

One day until Cam’s review.

That was the part the display did not say.

At breakfast, Mom was making toast and pretending not to watch Mara check her messages.

“You’re not subtle,” Mara said.
