Mom set a plate in front of her. “Neither are you.”

“There’s nothing from him.”

“Cam?”

Mara nodded.

Mom sat across from her with her coffee. “Maybe he’s trying not to think about tomorrow.”

“That sounds impossible.”

“For you, maybe.”

Mara picked at the edge of her toast. “He joked about it yesterday.”

“Some people joke when they’re worried.”

“Connor jokes when there’s oxygen.”

“Connor may be a special case.”

Mara looked toward the window. Across the street, the building display shifted from blue to gold to white.

GUIDE30: 9 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.

Mom followed her gaze. “That thing is everywhere.”

“I know.”

“Annoying.”

“Very.”

Mom picked up her coffee. “Don’t let a giant blinking sign ruin your whole day before it even starts.”

Mara nodded, but the countdown was still the last thing she saw before she left.

At school, the pickup outage was all anyone wanted to talk about.

By first period, three different versions of the story had already spread. One said the buses had disappeared completely. One said a teacher cried, which Mara was pretty sure was not true. One said a third grader had almost been sent across the city alone until some high schooler saved her.

Connor leaned across his desk before class started. “Congratulations. You are now some high schooler.”

“I didn’t save her.”

“You located a parent during the Great Bus Disappearance. That counts.”

“It was not great. Or a disappearance.”

“History will decide.”

Mara rolled her eyes, but it did not feel terrible. For once, the joke did not make the problem smaller. It made it easier to hold.

Across the room, Lila sat with her hands folded on her desk, looking like she had slept about as much as Mara had. Nessa whispered something to her, and Lila shook her head. June glanced back toward Mara, then quickly looked away.

The group had not exploded exactly.

It had cracked.

That was worse in some ways. Explosions were obvious. Cracks made everyone pretend the wall was still fine.

Mr. Halden started class with a reminder about Guide30 readiness essays, which made Connor whisper, “Nothing says celebration like homework about celebrating.”

Mara pressed her lips together so she would not smile too much.

The essay prompt appeared in front of her.

How has the Guide helped our city become safer, stronger, and more connected?

Mara stared at it.

A week ago, she could have answered in four paragraphs without even thinking. The Guide would have supplied statistics, examples, and a clean conclusion about shared progress. She probably would have gotten a ninety-eight.

Now all she could think about was Ava crying near the curb.

And Cam’s review tomorrow.

The Guide suggested an opening sentence.

For thirty years, the Guide has improved daily life by offering reliable support in moments of uncertainty.

Mara read it twice.

Reliable support.

Mom’s words came back.

Most people don’t notice until it stops working.

Mara opened a blank response box and typed:

The Guide helps people know what to do.

Then she stopped.

That was true.

She added:

But sometimes I wonder if knowing what to do is different from learning how to decide.

The sentence sat there, blinking back at her.

Too much?

Probably.

She almost deleted it.

Then she thought of the journal in her bag and the line she had written the night before.

Are You really there?

Her finger moved away from delete.

She left the sentence where it was.

At lunch, Mara sat at the end of the table near the windows again. Connor sat across from her with a tray full of something orange.

“I have decided this is either pasta or a warning,” he said.

“Could be both.”

“That is the kind of open-minded thinking they want in leaders.”

Cam dropped into the seat beside Connor a minute later.

Mara’s heart jumped before she could stop it.

He looked tired, but he was there. Same messy hair, same half-zipped bag, same way of slouching like chairs were personal enemies.

“Tomorrow,” Mara said quietly.

Cam picked up Connor’s spoon, inspected the orange food, and put it back down. “Wow. You really opened with doom.”

Connor pointed at him. “Thank you. I said warning.”

Cam looked at Mara, then down at the table. “Yeah. Tomorrow.”

“Are you okay?”

“Define okay.”

“That is not an answer.”

“Sure it is. It’s just a bad one.”

That sounded like him.

Mara held on to it.

Cam rubbed one hand over the back of his neck. “My mom’s taking me in the morning.”

“To school?”

“To the review.”

“Oh.”

“She said it’ll be better if I don’t get myself worked up first.”

“Are you?”

“Getting worked up?”

Mara nodded.

Cam looked toward the cafeteria wall, where the countdown glowed above the lunch menu.

GUIDE30: 9 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.

“Not exactly,” he said. “More like I know something is coming and everyone keeps telling me it’s not a big deal, which makes it feel like a bigger deal.”

Mara understood that so much it hurt.

Connor, who had been unusually quiet, cleared his throat. “For the record, adults saying something is not a big deal has never once made it smaller.”

Cam pointed at him. “Exactly.”

“I contain wisdom. People ignore it because of the backpack incident.”

“What backpack incident?” Cam asked.

Mara looked at Connor. “Don’t encourage him.”

Connor sat up straighter. “It was a tragedy in three acts.”

Cam actually laughed.

Not a huge laugh. Not enough to fix anything. But real.

Mara felt her shoulders loosen.

Then Cam’s eyes shifted slightly unfocused.

The laugh faded.

It was only for a second. A notification, probably. Everyone got them. Everyone paused.

But this time Mara watched it happen.

Cam blinked and looked back at his lunch.

“What was that?” she asked.

“Nothing.”

“Cam.”

“Review prep reminder.” He tried to sound annoyed, but it came out thinner than usual. “Maintain calm routines. Avoid unnecessary conflict. Trust the support process.”

Connor made a face. “That sounds like a poster in a nurse’s office.”

Cam pushed his tray away. “Yeah.”

Mara waited for him to joke.

He didn’t.

After lunch, Mara passed Lila near the stairwell.

For a second, they both slowed.

Lila looked like she wanted to say something. Mara knew the look now. The apology was always right there, waiting behind her teeth, but so was the part where Lila still thought she had been helping.

“Mara,” Lila said.

Mara stopped even though she had not meant to.

Lila twisted the strap of her bag between both hands. “I heard you helped that little girl yesterday.”

Mara looked down the hall. “Connor is making it sound bigger than it was.”

“I don’t think it was nothing.”

Mara did not answer.

Lila swallowed. “That’s why I was worried about you before. Because you do things without thinking.”

Mara looked at her then.

Lila seemed to hear herself a second too late. “I mean—”

“No,” Mara said. “You meant it.”

“That’s not what I was trying to say.”

“But it’s what you think.”

Lila’s eyes filled. “I think you’re brave. I just also think brave can get you hurt.”

Mara’s anger rose fast, partly because Lila sounded scared and partly because she still sounded sure.

“I’m not a problem you have to solve,” Mara said.

“I know.”

“Do you?”

Lila looked down.

The Guide pulsed softly.

Support peer interaction available.

Mara dismissed it.

“I have class,” she said.

This time, Lila did not follow.

By the end of the day, Friday felt too close.

Mara checked her messages after the final bell, even though Cam was only a hallway away. Nothing new. Just the same review reminders on her own schedule feed because she was still connected to his support circle from the shop visit.

She was not sure if that was an accident or if the Guide thought knowing more would make her calmer.

It did not.

When she got home, she went straight upstairs and opened the journal.

The page from the night before was still there.

God.
Are You really there?
Please help Cam.

Mara sat on the edge of her bed with her pen in her hand.

After a minute, she added:

And help me not be mad at Lila forever.

She stared at the sentence.

Then she quickly wrote under it:

I am still mad though.

That felt more honest.

The Guide lit softly at the edge of her vision.

Suggested evening reflection available.

Mara muted it.

Then she looked down at the journal again and whispered, “You can answer whenever.”

The room stayed quiet.

Mara waited anyway.

Chapter 16

By Friday morning, Mara had checked her messages before her feet even touched the floor.

Nothing from Cam.

She stared at his name anyway, like maybe if she looked long enough, a message would appear because he could feel her waiting through the screen.

It did not.

The wall display beside her bed glowed softly with her morning schedule.

GUIDE30: 8 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.

Eight days until the whole city stood under blue and gold lights and pretended countdowns made everything more exciting.

One day until the weekend.

One day until everybody else could sleep late or rehearse or complain about family attendance confirmations.

Today until Cam’s review.

That was the only countdown Mara cared about.

She got dressed too fast, forgot to smooth her hair, then fixed it badly after the Guide suggested she had six minutes available for appearance optimization. That made her want to mess it up again on purpose, but she didn’t have the energy.

At breakfast, Mom slid a plate of toast toward her and looked at her phone instead of Mara, which meant she was absolutely watching Mara.

“Subtle,” Mara said.

Mom looked up. “What?”

“You’re pretending not to stare at me.”

“I am not staring. I am monitoring with maternal concern.”

“That sounds worse.”

“It is worse.” Mom set her phone down. “Any word?”

Mara shook her head. “No.”

“Does his review start this morning?”

“I think so. His mom was taking him.”

Mom’s face softened. “That’s probably why he hasn’t answered.”

“I know.”

But knowing something did not make it feel better. Mara picked at the edge of her toast until crumbs gathered on the plate.

Mom watched her for a second, then said, “Did you write in the journal again last night?”

Mara looked up quickly. “Why?”

“Because you left it open on your desk when I came in to say good night.”

Mara felt her face get warm. “You read it?”

“No.” Mom’s voice went firm enough that Mara believed her. “I just saw it was open.”

“Oh.”

“I’m glad you’re writing in it.”

Mara looked down. “I don’t know if I’m doing it right.”

“Writing?”

“Praying.”

Mom was quiet for a second.

The kitchen felt very still.

Mom was quiet for a second.

Then she said, “Honey, prayer isn’t a school assignment.”

Mara looked down at her toast. “It feels like I’m doing it wrong.”

Mom reached across the table and touched her hand. “You do know, God isn’t grading your words- right? ”

Mara swallowed. “I just wrote, ‘Please help Cam.’”

“That’s a good prayer.”

“It doesn’t feel like enough.”

Mom squeezed her hand once. “Sometimes the smallest prayers are the most honest ones.”

Mom reached across the table and brushed a crumb away from Mara’s sleeve. “Sometimes you pray because you know what to say. Sometimes you pray because you don’t.”

The Guide chimed softly in Mara’s vision.

Departure recommended in four minutes.

Mara dismissed it.

Mom noticed but did not comment. She stood and picked up her coffee. “Text me if you hear from him.”

“I will.”

“And Mara?”

“What?”

“If you feel worried all day, that doesn’t mean you’re doing something wrong.”

Mara swallowed. “Okay.”

“It just means you care about someone.”

That followed Mara out the door and down the stairs and all the way to school.

At the entrance, the Guide30 banner had changed overnight.

GUIDE30: 8 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.

Lila was standing beneath it with Nessa and June. Nessa was talking quickly, probably about rehearsal or assignments or whatever normal people talked about when their friend was not about to be recalibrated. June nodded along, but Lila looked distracted.

When Mara walked past, Lila looked up.

For a second, Mara thought she might say something.

She didn’t.

Mara kept walking.

Her Guide immediately offered a peer repair prompt.

Mara dismissed it without reading.

First period was history, which meant Mara was supposed to care about coastal relocation timelines, early Guide infrastructure, and how shared response systems reduced panic during emergencies.

She tried.

She really did.

But every few minutes, her eyes dropped to the corner of her display where Cam’s message thread sat closed and silent.

No new messages.

Mr. Bennett talked about old evacuation routes and how, before the Guide, families had to follow public instructions from radio stations, traffic officers, and emergency volunteers. The class reacted like he had described people navigating by moonlight and bird noises.

Connor raised his hand. “So people just guessed?”

Mr. Bennett smiled. “They used maps. Signs. Public announcements.”

“Right,” Connor said. “Advanced guessing.”

A few people laughed.

Mara thought of Ava near the curb, crying because her route had disappeared. She thought of herself trying to remember the younger pickup area and how strange it had felt to trust her own memory.

Mr. Bennett moved to the next slide.

“Of course, the Guide made large-scale response much faster and safer. Once route coordination became automatic, city delays dropped by nearly sixty percent.”

That was true. Mara knew it was true.

But she also knew how fast everyone had fallen apart when the routes disappeared for less than an hour.

Both things could be true at the same time.

She hated that.

By second period, still nothing from Cam.

By third period, still nothing.

At lunch, Mara sat near the windows again. Connor dropped into the seat across from her with a tray of square pizza that looked personally offended.

“Good news,” he said. “Lunch is technically solid today.”

Mara looked at the pizza. “Technically?”

“I’m not a scientist, but I think cheese should bend less.”

Mara looked back at her screen.

Connor followed her gaze. “No word?”

She shook her head.

He pushed his tray away a little. “Sorry.”

The word came out awkward, like Connor did not use it often and was not sure where to put it.

Mara appreciated it anyway.

“Thanks.”

For a minute, they sat without talking. Connor tapped one finger against the edge of his tray, then stopped himself like he remembered noise might be annoying.

Across the cafeteria, Lila sat with Nessa and June. Nessa was talking with both hands, serious and fast. Lila kept looking toward Mara’s table. Not in the old way, like she expected Mara to look back and understand everything without words. More like she knew she had lost that and did not know how to ask for it again.

Then Nessa looked over too.

Mara looked away.

Connor noticed because Connor noticed everything he pretended not to notice.

“So,” he said. “Our friend group is doing amazing.”

Mara gave him a look.

“What? I said amazing. That’s positive.”

“It’s not amazing.”

“No, it’s aggressively not amazing.” Connor picked at the corner of his pizza. “It’s like if a group project became a crime scene.”

Mara almost told him to stop.

Then she didn’t.

Because that was exactly what it felt like.

“Nessa thinks Lila did the right thing,” Connor said more quietly.

Mara’s stomach tightened. “She said that?”

“Not like that. But yeah.”

“Of course she does.”

Connor hesitated. “Nessa’s brother was recalibrated when he was little.”

Mara looked up.

“Tobias?” Connor asked. “You know him, right? Tall. Always looks like he’s apologizing to furniture.”

“I know who Tobias is.”

“Nessa says it helped him a lot. Like, he used to panic about everything. Crowds, tests, music recitals, all of it. After recalibration, things got easier.”

Mara looked back toward Nessa’s table. Nessa was still talking, and Lila was listening with her hands wrapped around her water bottle.

“That doesn’t mean Lila was right,” Mara said.

“I didn’t say it did.”

“Then why say it?”

Connor looked uncomfortable. “Because I think maybe everybody thinks they’re helping.”

Mara did not answer.

That made her angrier than if he had picked a side.

It also made her less angry.

Which was annoying.

The Guide pulsed softly.

Emotional regulation support available.

Mara dismissed it so hard her vision flickered.

Connor watched her face. “Was that a Guide thing?”

“Yeah.”

“What’d it say?”

“That I’m emotionally annoying.”

“I mean, same, but rude.”

Mara let out a tiny breath that was almost a laugh.

Connor pointed at her. “That counts. I am accepting credit.”

Before she could answer, the cafeteria display changed.

GUIDE30: 8 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.
Final week readiness begins Monday.

Mara stared at the words.

Final week.

Monday.

Cam would be different by Monday. Or maybe he wouldn’t. Maybe the review would be nothing. Maybe everyone was making too much of it.

But deep down, she did not believe that.

Not anymore.

After lunch, Mara passed Lila near the hallway to science.

This time, Lila did speak.

“Mara.”

Mara stopped, but she did not turn all the way around.

Lila took a small step closer. “I heard Cam’s review is today.”

Mara turned then. “How?”

Lila looked guilty immediately, which answered the question before she said anything.

“Ms. Cole mentioned there were multiple students receiving additional support before Guide30,” Lila said. “She didn’t say his name. I just… figured it out.”

“You figured it out.”

“I’m worried about him too.”

Mara stared at her.

Lila’s face crumpled a little. “I know you don’t believe me.”

“I believe you’re worried,” Mara said. “That’s kind of the problem.”

Lila flinched.

Mara hated how sharp it sounded, but she did not take it back.

“I didn’t mean—” Lila started.

“You keep saying that.”

Lila looked down.

The hallway moved around them. Students walked past, laughing, complaining, checking routes, letting the Guide steer them to class. Mara’s own Guide highlighted the fastest path to science.

Proceed to class.

She ignored it.

Lila hugged her tablet against her chest. “I thought if adults knew what was happening, they could help you.”

“I know.”

“I really thought that.”

“I know.”

“That doesn’t make it better?”

Mara looked at her for a long second.

“No,” she said. “Not yet.”

Lila nodded like she had expected that answer and still hated hearing it.

“I hope Cam is okay,” she whispered.

Mara did not know what to do with that, so she walked away.

Science class was a blur. So was math. The day kept moving because days were rude that way. They did not stop just because something important was happening somewhere else.

By the final bell, Mara felt like she had been holding her breath since breakfast.

She checked her messages as soon as she stepped into the hall.

Nothing.

Outside, the pickup area had extra staff after yesterday’s delay. Teachers stood near the curb with tablets, and temporary signs marked bus sections in actual letters and numbers, not just Guide overlays.

Connor noticed at the same time she did.

“Look at that,” he said. “Physical signs. Revolutionary technology.”

Mara looked at one of the signs taped crookedly to a pole.

BUS SECTION C.

It was not pretty. It was not smooth. It was not optimized.

But everyone could see it.

For some reason, that made her feel better.

Then her screen buzzed.

Mara stopped walking.

Cam.

Her heart jumped so hard it almost hurt.

i’m fine

That was all.

Two words.

No joke. No complaint about wellness jail. No weird comment that somehow made everything less terrible.

Just:

i’m fine

Connor must have seen her face change. “What?”

Mara did not answer. She typed back immediately.

Mara: what happened?

The typing dots appeared. Disappeared. Appeared again.

Cam: it was fine

Mara stared at the words.

Fine.

There it was again. Too short. Too clean. Too not Cam.

Mara: where are you?

The dots appeared.

Cam: home

Mara: are you going to the shop?

This time, the pause lasted longer.

Cam: don’t come tonight

Mara’s fingers went cold.

Mara: why

The dots appeared. Disappeared.

Cam: just don’t

Mara stood in the middle of the sidewalk while students moved around her toward buses and waiting cars. The temporary paper sign above Bus Section C flapped in the wind.

Connor’s voice was quieter than usual. “Is he okay?”

Mara looked down at the message again.

i’m fine

it was fine

don’t come tonight

just don’t

“No,” she said.

Her Guide immediately offered a calming cycle.

Mara dismissed it.

Then she opened her journal app by mistake, realized what she had done, and closed it again.

She did not want the Guide’s reflection questions.

She wanted the paper journal at home.

She wanted Eli’s kitchen table and the soup prayer and Cam making jokes he clearly thought were better than they were.

She wanted God to answer fast, just this once.

Her screen buzzed again.

For half a second, she thought it was Cam.

It was the Guide.

Peer support recommended: Lila Arven.

Mara stared at the words until they blurred.

Across the pickup area, Lila stood beside Nessa and June, watching her with a worried face.

Mara looked back at Cam’s message.

don’t come tonight

Then she locked her screen.

Friday had not fixed anything.

It had only made Monday feel closer.

✦✦✦

Chapter 17

Saturday morning, Mara woke up to somebody pounding on her bedroom door.

“Mara!”

She opened one eye and immediately knew something was wrong. Sunlight was already pouring through her curtains, bright and rude and way too late.

Her mom pushed the door open halfway. “Why are you still asleep?”

Mara grabbed her screen off the nightstand.

11:42 AM.

Her stomach dropped. “What?”

“You’ve seriously been asleep this whole time?”

Her mom walked farther into the room holding a coffee mug, but she did not look calm enough for coffee. “Everything’s been messed up all morning. Half my meetings disappeared and then came back scheduled at different times.”

Mara checked her alarm history again.

Blank.

That made no sense. “The Guide doesn’t miss alarms.”

“I know.”

Her mom sounded unsettled too, which somehow made everything worse. Adults were allowed to be annoyed with the Guide. They were allowed to complain about oat milk and bad directions and unnecessary reminders. They were not supposed to sound nervous about it.

Mara shoved the blankets off and pulled on yesterday’s sweatshirt while notifications kept rearranging themselves in front of her.

Transit delay detected.
Please disregard previous transit warning.
Schedule conflict resolved.
Correction pending.

“Ugh.”

Her mom rubbed her forehead. “That is basically everybody today.”

Mara muted the notifications completely. The silence felt amazing for about two seconds. Then it felt stressful. Because now she had no idea what information was real. Because now she had no idea what information was real.

Downstairs, the kitchen screen was playing a local news stream while Mara shoved bread into the toaster too hard.

“…officials continue describing the disruptions as temporary synchronization instability,” the reporter was saying. “Residents are encouraged to remain calm while systems stabilize.”

Behind the reporter, footage showed crowds gathered outside a transit station while workers in yellow vests tried to answer questions from frustrated commuters. Then the broadcast cut to a press podium downtown. Dr. Adrian Cole stood beneath the Lumen seal, looking more tired than Mara had ever seen him look on a public feed.

“We are committed to full restoration before the Guide30 celebration,” Dr. Cole said. “This city has come too far to be set back by temporary instability.”

Mara stared at him.

People looking tired on official screens felt wrong.

“Your dad got stuck downtown earlier,” Mom said while opening the fridge. “Routing couldn’t stabilize.”

Mara frowned. “Couldn’t people just drive normally?”

Mom looked over the refrigerator door at her.

Mara opened her mouth to argue, then stopped.

Because honestly, maybe that sentence was part of the problem.

Notifications started chiming again in the corner of her vision. One after another after another.

Mara groaned. “I’m starting to hate that thing.”

Mom gave a tired little laugh. “You and most of the city right now.”

A few minutes later, Mara checked her messages. Connor had sent sixteen, most of them in all caps.

Connor: I MISSED SOCCER PRACTICE
Connor: MY GUIDE TOLD ME IT WAS STILL FRIDAY
Connor: MY DAD ENDED UP AT THE WRONG GROCERY STORE
Connor: MY GRANDMA GOT SENT TO A CHURCH SERVICE THAT WASN’T EVEN TODAY
Connor: WE ARE NOT EQUIPPED FOR THIS AS A PEOPLE

The last one would have been funny on a normal day. Today, it mostly made her stomach feel tighter.

Then another message appeared underneath.

Connor: okay but seriously people are freaking out

That part was true.

Underneath Connor’s thread, June had sent a few messages too.

June: is anyone else losing connection completely??
June: please tell me it’s not just me
June: sorry. nevermind. it’s everyone.

Mara almost replied to the last one.

She didn’t.

Instead, she checked Cam’s thread.

Nothing new.

The last message was still from yesterday.

just don’t

Mara stared at it while the toast popped up behind her.

Mom followed her gaze. “Still nothing?”

“No.”

Mom closed the fridge slowly. “Do you want to go by the shop later?”

Mara looked up so fast it almost hurt. “I thought you said I shouldn’t.”

“I said you shouldn’t sneak around because you’re worried. That is different from going somewhere with your mother knowing exactly where you are.”

“So I can go?”

“If the systems settle down, and if I drive you.”

Mara nodded before Mom could add more conditions. “Okay.”

“And if Cam is there and asks you to leave, you leave.”

“I know.”

“I mean it.”

“I know.”

Mom studied her for a second. “You can talk to Eli. But you are not responsible for fixing Cam.”

Mara looked down.

“I know,” she said, even though she was not sure she did.

By afternoon, most systems were supposedly restored, but nobody really relaxed. Mara kept checking the time every few minutes like she expected it to suddenly change again. Mom tried using the Guide route to Merrick Repair and Restoration, but the line shifted twice before they had even left their street.

Finally Mom turned off the route display.

Mara looked at her. “You know how to get there?”

“I know streets, Mara.”

“I didn’t mean—”

“I know what you meant.” Mom kept her eyes on the road. “And yes, that probably says something about both of us.”

The shop looked busier than Mara had ever seen it.

Two people stood outside under the crooked sign, waiting to get in. The front window had a handwritten note taped to the glass.

MAPS AVAILABLE.
LIMIT TWO PER CUSTOMER.

Mara stared at it.

Mom parked near the curb. “Well. That’s new.”

Inside, the bell over the door jingled almost constantly.

Merrick Repair and Restoration looked like the whole city had suddenly remembered old things existed. Stacks of folded maps covered one side of the counter. Boxes of batteries sat near the register. A display of flashlights leaned dangerously beside a crate full of notebooks and pens. Someone had dragged out a cardboard sign that said PRINTED CALENDARS, and three adults were arguing over whether undated ones were better.

Eli stood behind the counter, calm in the middle of all of it, folding a map for an older woman in a raincoat.

“I’m telling you,” a man near the register was saying, “people forgot how to function before screens told them where to turn.”

Eli smiled politely. “Looks like they’re getting a refresher course.”

The man grumbled something under his breath and bought two maps anyway.

Mara stepped farther inside, searching the shop before she meant to.

Cam was at the back counter.

For one second, relief rushed through her so fast she almost forgot everything else.

He was there. Same dark hair. Same old sweatshirt. Same half-zipped backpack leaning against the leg of the workbench. He was sorting batteries into small bins while a customer asked him whether flashlights needed “special kinds.”

“No,” Cam said. “Regular batteries should work as long as the size matches.”

His voice sounded normal.

Almost.

The customer held up two packages. “Which is more reliable?”

Cam glanced at the labels. “Both are acceptable for short-term emergency preparation.”

Mara stopped walking.

Acceptable. Short-term emergency preparation.

Cam did not talk like that.

He looked up then and saw her.

For a second, something changed in his face. Something quick and real, like a light flickering behind a curtain.

Then he smiled.

Not a Cam smile. Not exactly. It was smaller. Polite.

“Hey,” he said.

Mara walked toward him carefully, like moving too fast might scare away the part of him she had just seen. “Hey.”

“You came.”

“You told me not to come last night.”

“I know.”

“So obviously I came today.”

That should have earned at least an eye roll.

Instead, Cam looked down at the batteries and lined up three packages by size. “Today is different.”

Mara waited.

He did not add anything.

Around them, the shop stayed loud. A woman near the front asked Eli if paper maps needed updates. Someone else wanted to know if a flashlight could be solar and battery-powered at the same time. The bell jingled again.

Mara lowered her voice. “Are you okay?”

Cam gave the same little shrug from his messages. “I’m good.”

Good.

Not alive against all odds. Not surviving wellness jail. Not please send snacks and a lawyer.

Good.

Mara hated that word.

“What happened yesterday?”

“The review?” he asked.

“Yes, the review.”

“It was fine.”

Mara stared at him. “That’s what you said.”

“Because it was.”

He looked calm. That was the problem. Cam had never looked calm in a way that made Mara nervous before.

“They adjusted some support settings,” he said. “It’s not as dramatic as it sounds.”

“I didn’t say it was dramatic.”

“You were thinking it.”

“Because you sound weird.”

His hand paused over the batteries.

For a second, his face tightened.

Then it smoothed again.

“I don’t think that’s a helpful way to say it.”

Mara blinked.

“What?”

Cam looked uncomfortable, but he did not take it back. “I just mean maybe don’t make it sound like something is wrong with me.”

Mara felt the words hit harder than she expected.

“I’m not.”

“You kind of are.”

“I’m worried about you.”

“I know.” Cam looked toward the front window, where his mother stood just outside on the sidewalk talking to someone Mara did not recognize. “Everybody is.”

The way he said it made Mara feel guilty, which annoyed her because she was not sure she had done anything wrong.

Eli appeared beside them with a stack of notebooks tucked under one arm. “Cam, your mother is ready when you are.”

Cam nodded once. “Okay.”

Just okay.

Mara looked from him to Eli. “He’s leaving?”

“My mom wants me home before the system load increases again,” Cam said. He sounded like he was repeating something someone else had already said. “They recommended lower-stimulation environments for a few days.”

Mara looked around the shop. “This is lower stimulation?”

Cam’s mouth twitched. Just barely. “Today? No.”

There he was.

Only for a second.

Then his eyes shifted slightly unfocused. He blinked, and his hand went to the strap of his backpack.

“I should go,” he said.

Mara stepped closer. “Cam.”

He looked at her.

She wanted to say something important. Something that would make him snap back or laugh or tell her she was being dramatic in the old way. Something that would prove Friday had not stolen anything she could not help him find again.

Instead she said, “Are you coming back?”

“To the shop?”

Mara nodded.

Cam glanced at Eli before looking back at her. “Probably not this week.”

“Why?”

“My support plan recommends reduced exposure to noncompliant environments.”

Mara stared at him.

Cam’s face shifted, like he heard it too late.

“That means here,” Mara said.

“I know.”

“You’re saying it like it makes sense.”

“It does make sense.”

Eli’s expression changed, but he said nothing.

Cam adjusted his backpack. “This place makes me want to argue with things.”

“That’s not bad.”

“It can be.”

Mara did not know what to say to that.

Cam looked down, then back at her. For a second, his voice dropped lower.

“I’m still me, Mara.”

She swallowed.

“I know.”

But she did not know. Not all the way.

Cam gave a small nod, like he wanted to believe her believing him. Then he walked past her toward the door. His mother opened it from outside, and the bell gave its uneven jingle as they left together.

Mara watched through the window as Cam crossed the sidewalk with his mother. She said something to him and pointed toward the car.

Cam nodded and followed her.

That bothered Mara more than it should have. Yesterday’s Cam would have at least made a face. He would have mouthed help or rolled his eyes or pretended the sidewalk was taking him hostage.

This Cam just went.

Then he looked back once.

Only once.

It was fast, but it was enough.

His face did not look polished then. It looked sad.

The door closed behind him.

Mara stood there until Eli gently set the notebooks on the counter beside her.

“He’s different,” she said.

“Yes.”

Eli did not soften it. Mara was grateful and hated it at the same time.

A customer called from the front. “Do you have any more city maps?”

Eli closed his eyes for half a second. “Apparently, I am now in the map business.”

He went to help the customer, and Mara stayed near Cam’s empty workbench. The little music box was still there, half fixed and open, its tiny pieces arranged in a careful row. A pencil lay beside it, bitten flat on one side.

Mara touched the edge of the workbench.

For the next twenty minutes, she helped sort pens because standing still felt worse. Black pens in one tray. Blue pens in another. Red pens in a cracked mug near the register. Mom came inside after her call and helped Eli tape up a new sign that said CASH ACCEPTED IF SYSTEM PAYMENTS DELAY.

“This is very old-fashioned,” Mom said.

Eli handed her another piece of tape. “Old-fashioned is having an excellent day.”

Mara would have smiled if her chest had not felt so tight.

Finally, the rush thinned. Eli locked the front door for five minutes, flipping the sign to BACK SOON while three people outside groaned dramatically.

“People are upset,” Mara said.

“People are scared,” Eli corrected.

“Because the Guide forgot to wake them up?”

“Because the Guide failed to do something they believed it could not fail to do.”

That sounded closer to the truth.

Mara leaned against the counter. “Can Cam still unplug?”

Eli took off his glasses and rubbed the bridge of his nose. “Not the way he could before.”

“What happens if he tries?”

“He gets prompted. Then redirected. Then his mother gets notified if he keeps trying.”

Mara’s hands went cold. “So now it tells on him?”

“The official term is enhanced support transparency.”

Mara stared at him. “For trying to turn it down?”

Eli nodded once.

“That’s not support,” Mara said.

“No,it’s not” Eli said quietly.

For some reason, that made Mara want to cry.

“What if he likes it?” she asked.

Eli looked at her.

“What if he really does feel better?” Mara asked. “What if he’s tired of fighting everything and this makes it easier?”

The ticking clocks filled the silence between them.

Finally Eli said, “Then we listen to him.”

Mara looked up fast. “What?”

“We listen to him,” Eli said again. “We do not decide Cam is gone just because he is different. And we do not decide he is fine just because he is quieter.”

Mara swallowed.

“That’s hard.”

“Yes,” Eli said. “Most true things are.”

Mara picked up a loose pen and set it carefully into the blue tray.

“I prayed for him,” she said.

“I’m glad.”

“It didn’t stop anything.”

“No.”

“That’s not exactly a great advertisement for prayer.”

Eli’s eyes softened. “Prayer is not a button you press to make the right thing happen.”

“I know that.”

“Do you?”

Mara frowned at him.

Eli lifted both hands. “It is a fair question.”

She looked away.

His voice stayed gentle. “Most of us want God to work like the Guide. Fast answer. Clear route. Problem solved before we have to feel too much.”

Mara thought about her journal. Please help Cam. Please help Cam still be Cam. Are You really there?

“That would be easier,” she said.

“Yes,” Eli said. “But easier is not always the same as better.”

Mara looked toward the window. Cam and his mother were gone now. Only the crooked shop sign moved slightly in the wind.

“I don’t know how to listen for God,” she said.

“Neither do I, sometimes.”

“You’re old.”

“Yes. Thank you.”

“I mean, shouldn’t you be good at it by now?”

Eli’s smile reached his eyes this time, just barely. “You would think.”

Mara felt a little embarrassed. “Sorry.”

“No, it’s a good question.” He picked up the little music box from Cam’s bench and turned the tiny key once. The music box clicked but did not play. “I think listening to God is less like getting a message and more like learning a voice.”

Mara watched him set the music box down carefully.

“That’s broken,” she said.

“For now.” Eli pushed it gently back into its place on the workbench. “Still worth fixing.”

Mara looked at him.

He did not explain the metaphor, which made her grateful. She would have hated that.

Mom’s eyes shifted slightly, like she was reading something only she could see.

Then she looked at Mara. “We should head home soon.”

Mara nodded, but she did not move right away.

“Do you think he’ll come back?” she asked Eli.

“To the shop?”

Mara nodded.

“I think Cam is still Cam,” Eli said. “But it may be harder for him to remember that for a while.”

Mara held onto that, even though it hurt.

Outside, the line of customers had grown again. One man knocked lightly on the window and held up two fingers like he was begging for maps.

Eli sighed and reached for the door. “The map business calls.”

Mom put an arm around Mara’s shoulders as they stepped onto the sidewalk.

“You okay?” Mom asked.

Mara looked back through the shop window. Eli had already returned to the counter, unfolding a paper map for the man who had been waiting outside.

“No,” Mara said.

Mom did not tell her she would be.

For once, Mara did not pull away from her arm.

On the drive home, the Guide suggested the fastest route twice. Mom ignored it both times because the first road was backed up and the second had a temporary closure the system had apparently missed.

Mara watched her mother turn down a side street without waiting for the glowing line to approve it.

“How did you know this way?” Mara asked.

Mom glanced at her. “I lived here before the Guide was this bossy, remember?”

Mara leaned against the window.

The sky outside was turning pink and gold above the buildings. For a few minutes, neither of them talked.

That night, Mara opened the journal again.

Saturday. 7 days until Guide30.

She wrote slowly.

The Guide forgot to wake people up today.

Then she stopped, because that sounded silly. Like a person forgetting. Like the Guide had rolled over and slept in.

She crossed out forgot and wrote failed.

The Guide failed to wake people up today.

She stared at the sentence.

Then she added:

Everyone got scared.

I did too.

She thought of Cam’s face through the shop window. The polite smile. The careful words. The one scared look he gave her before he left.

After a moment, she wrote one more line.

God, please help me listen even when You are quiet.

She waited.

No answer came.

But the quiet did not feel as empty as it used to.

Chapter 18

On Monday morning, school felt like everyone was trying very hard to act normal.

It was not working.

The Guide30 banners were still up. The countdown still glowed across the front entrance in bright blue and gold.

GUIDE30: 5 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.

Usually, people stopped to take pictures under it. Today, most kids barely looked at it. They were too busy telling each other what had happened over the weekend.

“My alarm went off at noon.”

“My dad’s route sent him to the dentist.”

“Our fridge ordered forty-two yogurts.”

“My cousin’s Guide told her she had school on Sunday.”

“My grandma printed directions.”

That last one came from Connor.

He found Mara before first period, waving a folded sheet of paper like evidence.

“Printed them?” Mara asked.

“On paper.” Connor shook the page once. “Like a pioneer.”

“Did they work?”

“That’s the worst part.” He lowered his voice. “They did.”

Mara looked around the hallway. Kids were laughing, but not like usual. Their eyes kept flicking toward the edges of their vision, checking schedules, routes, times, reminders.

Mara was doing it too.

She hated that.

Near the lockers, Nessa was talking fast while June stood beside her looking worried. Lila was with them, but she was quieter than usual. Her hair was pulled back messy, and she kept blinking at something only she could see.

For a second, Mara almost walked over.

Then Lila looked up.

Their eyes met.

Mara looked away first.

Connor followed her gaze and sighed. “You two are exhausting.”

“Thanks.”

“I mean it.”

Mara adjusted the strap of her bag. “Noted.”

Nessa’s voice got louder as they passed.

“I’m just saying, it makes sense,” she said. “Guide30 is huge. They’re probably testing something.”

June frowned. “Testing what?”

“I don’t know. Extra crowd routing. Performance sync. Emergency backup stuff.”

Connor slowed down. “Or the Guide is haunted.”

Nessa gave him a look.

“What?” Connor said. “It explained my grandma ending up at the wrong church.”

“That was routing instability,” Nessa said.

“That is exactly what a haunted Guide would call it.”

June looked nervous. “Do you think it could happen during Guide30?”

Nobody answered right away.

That was answer enough.

The first bell rang, and everyone started moving, but the hallway felt different now. Not panicked. Just off. Like the whole school was waiting for the Guide to trip over itself again.

Then Cam walked in.

Mara saw him before he saw her.

He came through the front doors with his backpack on both shoulders and his hair still damp, like he had actually followed a morning routine. He paused under the Guide30 banner and looked up at the countdown.

Five days.

Mara waited for him to make a face. To roll his eyes. To mutter something about countdowns needing a hobby.

He didn’t.

He just looked at it, then kept walking.

“Hey,” he said when he reached them.

“Hey,” Mara said.

Connor lifted one hand. “Welcome to Monday. The Guide tried to ruin the weekend, but we survived.”

Cam smiled a little. “The system seems to be stabilizing.”

Connor stared at him. “That was not the correct answer.”

Cam looked confused. “What?”

“You were supposed to say something normal, like Mondays are illegal.”

“Oh.” Cam gave a small laugh, but it sounded late. “Right. Mondays are illegal.”

Mara looked at him carefully.

Cam’s eyes shifted for half a second. A prompt, probably. Then he straightened the strap on his backpack.

“Do you think they’re testing something for Guide30?” Mara asked.

“Probably,” Cam said.

“Probably?”

“It’s a citywide event. More people connected at once. More live routing. More performance systems.” He glanced toward the banner again. “There are going to be adjustments.”

Adjustments.

Mara waited for him to hear himself.

He didn’t.

Connor looked at Mara.

Mara looked away.

The second bell warning chimed.

Cam checked something only he could see. “Class starts in two minutes.”

Connor blinked. “That has never bothered you before.”

Cam’s mouth tightened for one second. Then he shrugged.

“I’m trying something different,” he said.

He walked away before Mara could ask what that meant.

By lunch, the weekend stories had gotten bigger.

Someone said an entire train stopped because every passenger got a different arrival time. Someone said a wedding party split into three groups because the Guide sent each side to a different entrance. Someone said their uncle tried to drive without routing and hit a trash can, which Connor said was not the Guide’s fault and probably not the trash can’s fault either.

The funny stories were easier to tell.

The scary ones got quieter.

A girl at the next table said her little brother’s medical reminders disappeared for almost two hours. Nobody made a joke after that.

Mara pushed her food around her tray.

“What if Nessa’s right?” June asked from the other end of the table. She had come over with Lila and Nessa, but everyone was sitting in a way that made it clear the group was still not normal.

Nessa looked relieved to be asked. “I’m not saying it’s good. I’m just saying maybe it means they’re working on something big.”

“For Guide30?” Connor asked.

“Probably. All the drones, the bands, the crowd routes, the safety zones, the family check-ins. That’s a lot.”

“Great,” Connor said. “Love when the thing telling everyone where to stand is also working on figuring itself out.”

Lila did not laugh.

She was looking at the table, one hand wrapped around her water bottle. “Our rehearsal sync was off last week too.”

Mara looked up before she could stop herself.

Lila’s eyes flicked toward her, then away.

“The solo?” Nessa asked.

Lila nodded. “My cue jumped. Just for a second.”

“That happens,” Nessa said quickly. “They fix that stuff.”

“But it doesn’t happen. That’s the problem.” Lila said, twirling a strand of hair around her finger.

Cam sat across from Mara, lining up the edge of his napkin with his tray.

Mara noticed.

Connor noticed too.

“I don’t trust your lunch setup,” Connor said.

Cam looked down. “It’s just lunch.”

“No. That sandwich is too centered.”

Cam shrugged. “I’m trying not to make unnecessary messes.”

The table went quiet for half a second.

Not long enough for anyone else to notice.

Long enough for Mara.

Nessa glanced at Cam and smiled like she was relieved. “You seem better.”

Cam looked up. “Thanks.”

Thanks.

That was all.

Lila’s eyes moved from Cam to Mara. Something worried crossed her face, but she did not say anything.

Mara looked down at her lunch.

After lunch, Mara had Applied Response. The lesson was supposed to be about Guide30 public safety, which meant every example sounded a little too close to real life.

Mr. Halden stood at the front while the wall display showed a picture of smiling families under blue and gold lights.

“During citywide events,” he said, “cooperation is essential. The Guide helps reduce confusion by giving clear instructions to each participant.”

Mara stared at the prompt on her desk.

If a public event experiences a temporary Guide issue, what is the safest citizen response?

The Guide offered an answer immediately.

Remain calm. Follow updated instructions. Avoid independent movement and stay in your assigned area unless directed by a teacher, safety worker, or official Guide alert.

Remain calm. Follow updated instructions. Avoid independent movement unless directed by an authorized support channel.

Mara read the last sentence twice.

Avoid independent movement.

She thought of Ava crying near the pickup area. She thought of the gym doors. She thought of the little paper maps stacked at Eli’s shop. She thought of Mom turning down side streets without waiting for the glowing line to approve it.

If everyone waited for updated instructions, nothing would happen until the Guide decided what should happen.

Mara typed:

Sometimes people need to look around and help whoever is right in front of them.

The answer box blinked.

Response may not meet cooperation standards. Revise?

Mara hesitated, but then submitted her response.

At the end of class, Mr. Halden called her name.

“Mara, the wellness office needs to see you before dismissal.”

Connor looked over.

Lila looked over too.

Mara stood up and grabbed her bag before either of them could say anything. She pushed open the school wellness office door, staring at the poster on the door that showed three smiling students under the words SUPPORT IS STRENGTH.

Ms. Renner, the student wellness liaison, sat behind the desk. Mara had seen her in the halls before. She was the kind of adult who always wore soft colors and comfortable shoes and looked like she knew where the tissues were.

“Hi, Mara,” Ms. Renner said. “Have a seat.”

Mara sat. Ms. Renner tapped her desk display. “Your support team has noticed a pattern.” Mara’s hands tightened on her bag.

“Repeated dismissal of Guide prompts. Higher stress readings. Peer conflict. Unusual responses in class.”

Mara stared at her. She knew what that meant. She had ignored the Guide. She was stressed. Lila had reported her. And she had stopped giving the answers everyone wanted.

Those sounded like the words from Cam’s review. Not exactly the same.

Close enough.

“This is not punishment,” Ms. Renner said.

Mara went still.

That was definitely the same.

Ms. Renner continued, but Mara heard the words like they were coming from the end of a long hallway.

“We would normally recommend a review before a major public event like Guide30, especially with the stress indicators we’re seeing.”

Mara looked up. “Before?”

Ms. Renner’s face softened. “There isn’t an available opening this week.”

A notification opened in the center of Mara’s vision.

Wellness Recalibration Recommendation
Student: Mara Vale

Based on a six-week pattern of sync irregularities, elevated independence indicators, repeated support dismissals, and increased stress markers, your support team has issued a formal recalibration recommendation.

Scheduled review: Monday following Guide30
Parental consent required at this stage

Please discuss this recommendation with your family.

Mara read it once.

Then again.

Wellness Recalibration Recommendation.

Monday following Guide30.

The same “support” kind Cam got.

Ms. Renner was saying something about support before stress became harder to interrupt. Mara barely heard her.

Guide30 was Saturday.

Her review was Monday.

Two days after.

That meant Guide30 was not the finish line anymore. It was just the thing standing between her and what came next.

Mara tried to dismiss the notice.

It minimized, but did not disappear.

Formal recommendation pending family review.

She tried again.

The notice moved to the side of her vision and stayed there, small and patient.

Like it could wait.

“Mara?” Ms. Renner said.

Mara stood.

“You should take a minute.”

“I don’t want a minute.”

Ms. Renner glanced at the notice again before closing it. For the first time, she looked less like someone reading from a screen and more like someone who had read the same kind of notice too many times.

“Your parents will receive the full version too,” she said.

Mara nodded because she could not think of anything else to do.

“You are not in trouble,” Ms. Renner added.

Mara looked at her.

“That’s what everyone keeps saying.”

Ms. Renner did not answer right away.

That was worse than if she had.

The hallway was mostly empty now. Dismissals had started, and students were already moving toward buses and pickup zones.

Mara walked slowly because running would make it look like she was scared. She was scared. The notice stayed at the edge of her vision.

Formal recommendation pending family review.

Across the hall, Cam stood at his locker, organizing his books into a neat stack.

Mara stopped.

He looked up. “You okay?”

Mara shook her head.

Cam took one step toward her. “What happened?”

For one second, he sounded like himself. Worried. Real.

Then his eyes flicked slightly, and his shoulders settled into that careful calm she hated.

“You should find an adult,” he said. “Or use the support prompt.”

That was the part that hurt.

Not that he asked if she was okay.

That part was Cam.

It was how fast the Guide seemed to arrive after.

“They scheduled me,” she said.

Cam froze.

“When?” he asked, but his voice had already changed.

Mara swallowed.

“Monday after Guide30.”

Cam’s eyes flicked, probably to a prompt. His jaw tightened before his face could smooth itself out again.

“A review?” he asked quietly.

Mara nodded.

For one second, he looked scared.

Then the calm started coming back, like a curtain being pulled into place.

Mara stared at him.

Cam swallowed. “I think” His voice dropped. “I don’t know what I think.”

That sounded like him.

Scared, but him.

Mara nodded once, then walked toward the exit before she started crying in the hallway.

Outside, the Guide30 countdown covered the front display.

GUIDE30: 5 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.

Students streamed beneath it, laughing too loud, checking routes, comparing weekend glitches, pretending today had not changed anything.

Mara stood at the top of the steps.

Five days until Guide30.

Seven days until Monday.

For the first time, she was not only scared for Cam.

She was scared for herself.

Chapter 19

Monday Night
5 days until Guide30

Mara knew Mom had seen the notice before she even opened the apartment door.

The kitchen light was on, even though it was still afternoon. Dad’s shoes were by the entry, which meant he was home early. That almost never happened unless something was wrong, or unless one of his meetings had been canceled, which never happened.

Mom was sitting at the kitchen table with an old tablet in front of her. Dad stood behind her chair, one hand resting on the back of it. Neither of them was talking.

The tablet was open in front of them, and a paper notebook sat beside it. A paper notebook and pen. The little blue Guide summary box was minimized in the corner of the screen.

Mom never minimized the summary box.

Mara stopped just inside the door. “You got it.”

Mom looked up from the tablet. “Yes.”

The old tablet on the table showed the parent version of the recommendation. The parent notice was longer than the one Mara had seen at school.

It had headings and subheadings and a list of things the support team had noticed.

Increased prompt dismissal.
Elevated stress markers.
Response deviation.
Social disruption.

Mara stared at the last one.

Social disruption sounded a lot cleaner than lost her best friend.

Wellness Recalibration Recommendation
Student: Mara Vale
Scheduled review: Monday following Guide30
Parental consent required at this stage

Mom had not tapped acknowledge.

The button sat at the bottom of the notice, bright blue.

Acknowledge Receipt.

Mara noticed Mom’s hand resting beside the tablet. Not touching it. Not even close.

Dad leaned over the table and read the line again.

“Parental consent required at this stage,” he said.

He did not say it like he was reading. He said it like one of the words had caught on something.

“What stage?” he asked.

Mom scrolled down.

Then up again.

Then she tapped the little help icon beside the line. A small box opened with one sentence.

Consent requirements may vary by support level.

Dad waited.

Mom waited too, like maybe more would load.

Nothing did.

Mara pressed her hands flat against her knees under the table.

Mom closed the box. “That’s all it says.”

Mom usually knew what things meant. Not everything, but enough. She knew how to read forms and find hidden fees and tell when a school message was trying to sound nicer than it was. She knew when to take something seriously and when to ignore it because some committee had gotten too excited about bullet points.

But now she was looking at the words parental consent required at this stage like they had a trapdoor underneath them.

Dad sat down beside Mom. “Mara, did they explain anything else?”

“Ms. Renner said they wanted to get me in before Guide30, but there wasn’t time.”Mara pressed her hands flat against her knees under the table.

Mom’s eyes moved back to the tablet.

Dad let out a slow breath through his nose. “They wanted to do it this week?”

Mara nodded. “She said before a major public event. Because of stress indicators.”

“Stress indicators,” Dad said. He read the line again, slower this time.

“She had a hard day. That’s not the same thing as needing recalibration.”

Mara looked at the table. There was a grocery receipt beside the tablet, half-covered by Mom’s notebook. The receipt had oat milk on it again.

Again. Dad hated oat milk. Mom did too. Yet the Guide thought it knew best.

Mom pushed the tablet away a few inches, like she needed space from it. “Mara, I need to ask you something. Did Cam get the same kind of notice?”

Mara nodded.

Mom closed her eyes for half a second.

“His was Friday,” Mara said. “The review. And now…” She stopped because the rest was too hard to say in a way that sounded normal.

Dad leaned forward. “Now what?”

Mara looked down at her hands. “He says he’s fine, but he’s different.”

Neither of them answered.

“That’s the scary part,” she said.

Mom’s face changed, not a lot, but enough.

Mara swallowed. “He says things like the system is stabilizing. He says temporary instability. He says stuff like that now. He still looks like Cam, and sometimes he sounds like Cam for a second, but then it’s like he remembers how he’s supposed to sound.”

The kitchen was quiet except for the hum of the fridge.

Dad rubbed a hand over his mouth. “Okay.”

Mom looked at him.

He shook his head a little, like he was stopping himself from saying more.

Mom stood up and walked to the sink, then turned around without doing anything there. “The Guide has helped us,” she said.

Mara looked up.

Mom’s voice was steady, but it was not easy. “I’m not going to pretend it hasn’t. It helps me with work. It helped when your grandmother wandered off that time at the market and we found her in six minutes instead of six hours. It reminds me about appointments and medicines and bills and things I forget when life gets too full. It has probably kept more people safe than we even know.”

Mara nodded slowly.

She knew all that. That was part of why everything felt so tangled.

Mom came back to the table and sat down. “But I don’t like that I don’t know what this is. I don’t like that I’m reading five pages and still can’t explain exactly what they want to do to you. And I really don’t like words that sound gentle but don’t actually answer the question.”

Dad pulled the tablet toward him and scrolled through the parent notice. “It says review. It says recommendation. It says support adjustment. It does not say what happens in the room.”

“That’s what I asked,” Mara said. “Ms. Renner said they want to add support before stress gets harder to stop.”

Mom pressed her lips together.

Dad looked at the notice again. “That doesn’t really explain anything.”

“No,” Mom said. “It doesn’t.”

A soft chime opened at the edge of Mara’s vision.

Family support conversation detected.
Would you like help starting a calm discussion?

Mara dismissed it.

Mom noticed. “The Guide?”

Mara nodded. “It wants to help us talk about this.”

Dad looked at the tablet, then at Mom.

“We can talk without it,” he said.

Mara sat back in the chair. “Grandpa told me to pay attention.”

Mom looked at her.

Not fast. Slowly.

“What did you say?”

“In the journal.” Mara twisted the strap of her backpack around her hand. “Your journal. You wrote about him saying it. Pay attention. That’s the whole thing. Or maybe he said it to me too. I don’t know. It keeps coming back.”

Mom was quiet for a long moment.

Dad looked between them but did not interrupt.

Finally Mom said, “He used to say that when I wanted him to just tell me what to do.”

Mara looked up.

“I hated it,” Mom said. “I would ask him a question, and instead of giving me an answer, he would say, ‘Slow down and pay attention.’ It made me so mad.”

“Why?”

“Because I wanted instructions. He wanted me to notice.” Mom looked back at the notice on the tablet. “And most of the time, I already knew there was something I was trying not to see.”

Mara watched Mom reach for the notebook beside the tablet. Who knew where she found it. . The cover was bent at the corner, and one of the pages had a coffee stain shaped like Florida.

Mom opened it to a blank page.

Dad glanced at her. “You’re writing it down manually?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I don’t want a Guide summary.” Mom picked up a pen. “I want to know what I read, not be told what I just read.”

That was the moment something changed. Mara felt it. Mom was not just reacting now. She was looking. Dad sat down fully and pulled his own chair closer. “All right. Start with the parent notice.” For the next hour, the kitchen table slowly disappeared under pieces of the problem.

Mom wrote down phrases from the notice. Dad opened the parent portal on his own tablet and tried to find the appeal process. Mara sat between them, still in her school sweatshirt, Mara sat between them, still in her school sweatshirt, while Mom read the notice line by line and Dad opened every link that looked like it might explain something.

Most of the links did not.

The official pages were full of soft words.

Support alignment.
Healthy response pathways.
Emotional smoothing.
Reduced distress markers.
Guardian transparency.

Mom read one paragraph twice, then put the tablet down and rubbed both hands over her face.

“What?” Mara asked.

“This says almost nothing.”

“It sounds like it says things.”

“That is how I know it says almost nothing.”

Dad turned his tablet around. “The parent portal says we can request a review conference.”

“When?” Mom asked.

Dad tapped the page. “Estimated response time is five to seven business days.”

Mom looked at him.

Guide30 was in five days.

Mara’s review was in seven.

Dad’s jaw tightened. “I know.”

Mom wrote something in the notebook, harder than she needed to. The pen left a dark line under the word review.

Mara looked from Mom to Dad. “Can you just say no?”

Dad looked at Mom.

Mom did not answer fast enough.

“At this stage,” Mara said.

Mom closed the notebook halfway, then opened it again. “I’m not clicking anything tonight,” she said.

Mara looked at the blue button. “So what are we doing?”

Mom looked tired, but her voice was firm..

“We keep looking,” she said. “I don’t understand this yet, and I’m not going to pretend I do.”

Mara stood up from the table and went to the window. Outside, the city was already glowing with Guide30 colors. Blue lights wrapped around the street poles. Gold banners hung from the building across the road. A public display near the corner flashed the countdown every few minutes.

5 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.

The last few weeks, everyone had been talking about Saturday like it was the big thing coming.

But now, Saturday was starting to feel like a wall someone had painted bright colors on so she would not notice Monday standing right behind it.

Mara heard Dad’s voice was quieter behind her talking to her mom.. “Maybe we call your father.”

Mom responded so softly Mara couldn't hear her.

Mara turned around. “Grandpa?”

Mom looked at the notebook, then at Mara. “He is going to say he warned me.”

Dad shook his head. “No, he won’t.”

“He might think it.”

“He is allowed to think things.”

Mom gave him a tired look, but she reached for her phone. She did not ask the Guide to summarize the situation. She did not use an auto-generated explanation. She called him herself.

Grandpa Frank answered on the fourth ring.

His voice came through a little rough and too loud, like he was holding the phone too close to his mouth. “Hello?”

“Dad,” Mom said. “It’s me.”

“I know who it is. Your name comes up.”

Mom closed her eyes.

Mara would have laughed another day.

Not this one.

Mom put the call on speaker and set the phone in the middle of the table. She explained the notice. Not quickly. Not with panic. She read parts of it aloud, then stopped and said what she did not understand. Dad added the part about the parent portal. Mara stood by the window and listened.

Grandpa was quiet for a while after they finished.

Then he said, “Did you acknowledge it?”

“No,” Mom said.

“Good.”

Grandpa continued, “Don’t sign what you don’t understand.”

“It’s not signing. It’s just acknowledging receipt.”

“Then don’t acknowledge what you don’t understand either.”

Dad looked at Mom and lifted one eyebrow like he was trying not to smile.

Mom did not smile.

“Dad,” she said, “the Guide has helped a lot of people.”

“I know.”

“I mean it. I’m not trying to become one of those people who thinks every new thing is bad just because it’s new.”

“I know that too.”

“I just don’t know what this means, I mean what are they going to do?.”

Grandpa’s voice got softer. “Then there it is.”

Mom looked down.

“There what is?” Mara asked before she could stop herself.

“The part to pay attention to,” Grandpa said. “Not the part where you already know what you think. The part where you don’t know.”

Mara looked at Mom.

Mom was staring at the notebook.

Grandpa cleared his throat. “When something is good, people stop asking what else it is, they stop asking if there could be unknown consequences. That’s where trouble starts.”

Nobody spoke for a moment. “You are right Dad, thanks. I we need to see what actually could go wrong” Mom said as she ended the call with a promise to update Grandpa at what they find.

After the call, Mom stayed in her chair for a long time. The kitchen light made her look tired in a way Mara did not like. Finally, Mom pulled the tablet back toward her. “I’m going to search outside the Guide index.”

Dad looked up. “Can we?”

“We can try.”

Mara sat down again.

The next searches were slower. Messier. Less polished. Half the pages were old. Some did not load right. Some led nowhere. One article looked promising until Dad realized it was written by someone selling sleep patches. Mom wrote anyway, crossing things out when they turned useless.

Mara watched the words collect in the notebook.

Recalibration
support adjustment
distress markers
guardian consent
independence indicators
Guide implant
neural interface
support layer

Support layer.

Mom circled that one.

“Why that?” Mara asked.

Mom scrolled back to the paragraph where she had found it. “Because this says recalibration may involve adding or adjusting support layers.”

“What does that mean?”

“I don’t know yet.”

Mara wanted to hate that answer, but Mom was already searching again.

Dad leaned closer to the tablet. “If it’s a layer, that means it’s added on top of something, right?”

Mom kept reading. “Maybe.”

“So it doesn’t replace what’s already there.”

“Maybe.”

Mara looked from Dad to Mom. She did not want to ask the question, but it came out anyway. “So Cam isn’t erased?”

Mom looked up from the page.

“No,” she said carefully. “I don’t think erased is right.”

“What is?”

“I don’t know.” Mom’s eyes moved back to the page. “But if something is added, maybe something can be lowered. Or removed. Or adjusted. Maybe paused too. I don’t know yet.”

Mara stared at the circled words in the notebook.

Support layer. That was not enough to fix anything, but it did open up some more questions. It did not erase Mara’s Monday review but it was closer to understanding that this calibration might not be as permanent as it seemed. Maybe even be optional in some way.

.Dad searched the author of the article and found a name attached to an older medical archive.

Dr. Samira Voss.
Neural Interface Specialist.
Former Lumen Pediatric Support Consultant.

Mom read the name outloud.

“Former,” Dad said.

Mom wrote it down.

Mara leaned over the notebook. “Is former good or bad?”

Mom did not look away from the page. “I don’t know. I suppose it could mean either, or it could just mean she left.”

“That is not an answer.”

“No,” Mom said. “But it might be a place to start.”

Most of the article was hard to understand, but one line made Mom stop.

Some recalibration support layers may be lowered, paused, or reviewed with guardian request and proper access records.
Mara read it twice.

Lowered. Paused. Reviewed.

“Did Eli know this?” she asked. “ He would have done anything for Cam.”

Mom did not answer right away. “Maybe he knew parts of it. But he wouldn’t have Cam’s records. And he isn’t Cam’s guardian.”

They found a clinic name next.

Bayline Neural Care.
Independent interface review and adjustment.

The site was plain. No bright blue banners. No smiling families. No Guide30 countdown in the corner. Just office hours, a contact form, and a paragraph that said they reviewed neural support settings for families seeking second opinions.

Mom copied the clinic name into the notebook by hand.

For some reason, watching the pen move across the paper made it feel more real than saving it.

Dad filled out the contact form. He kept the message short.

Our daughter has received a Wellness Recalibration Recommendation scheduled for Monday following Guide30. Guardians are seeking an independent explanation of what recalibration changes, what support layers may be added, and whether those settings can be reviewed before consent.

Mom read it twice before he sent it.

“Add that we have not acknowledged the notice yet,” she said.

Dad typed one more sentence.

We have not acknowledged or consented to the recommendation.

Mom nodded.

Dad pressed send.

Nothing happened.

No music. No confirmation that mattered. Just a small message on the page.

Request received.

Mara stared at it.

She had wanted something bigger. A real answer. A person calling immediately. A door opening. Something to keep Monday from arriving.

Instead they had a clinic name, a sent form, and a notebook full of words that only half made sense.

Mom must have seen her face.

“This is not fixed,” Mom said.

Mara looked at her.

“I’m not going to pretend it is,” Mom continued. “I don’t know what they did to Cam. I don’t know yet what they want to do to you. I don’t know how hard it is to challenge it. But we are not going to sleepwalk into this because the words sound good.”

Mara swallowed.

Dad reached across the table and turned the tablet so the notice faced him instead of her. “We keep looking tomorrow.”

“Tomorrow?” Mara asked.

“And the next day,” Mom said.

Dad nodded. “As long as it takes.”

Mara looked at both of them.

The notice was still open. Monday was still coming. Nothing had been fixed.

But Mom had not clicked acknowledge.

For the first time since the wellness office, Mara didnt feel so alone.

Later, Mara went upstairs and pulled Mom’s old journal from her desk drawer.

She did not have a specific page that she was looking for, so she opened randomly to a folded corner near the middle. Mom’s handwriting looked younger there, messier and more slanted, like she had written fast because she had been annoyed.

Dad told me I move too fast.

I told him everyone moves fast now.

He said, “That doesn’t mean they know where they’re going.”

Then he told me to pay attention.

I rolled my eyes, but I wrote it down anyway.

Mara read it twice.

Then she took out her own pen.

Under Mom’s old words, in the white space at the bottom of the page, Mara wrote:

They scheduled me for Monday after Guide30.

She stopped.

The words looked strange inside Mom’s old journal, like two times had gotten folded together. Mom as a girl. Mara now. Grandpa’s voice between them.

She did not know how to pray about this. Not in a way that sounded right. Not in a way that was brave.

So she wrote what she had.

God, please help us find what we need before Monday gets here, tbh I am really scared.

She waited.

No answer came. Mara stared at the page for a while. Then she looked at what she had already written and added one more line underneath it.

Help me notice if You already are.

She did not know if that counted as a good prayer.

It was the only one she had.

But downstairs, the kitchen light was still on.

Mara picked up the journal and walked quietly to the top of the stairs. From there, she could see Mom at the table with the notebook open again. Dad stood at the counter, reheating coffee he probably would not drink. They were talking softly, pointing at something on the tablet, going back over the words one more time.

Mom picked up the pen and wrote another note.

Mara closed the journal and held it against her chest for a second before putting it back in the drawer.

It was not a miracle exactly, but it felt like her prayer mattered. Maybe that was something.

Chapter 20

Tuesday, 4 days until Guide30

By Tuesday morning, the kitchen table looked like it had become a command center.

Not the exciting kind from movies. The tired kind, with cold coffee, half a banana nobody had finished, Dad’s tablet, Mom’s old tablet, two notebooks, three pens that did not match, and one official parent notice still waiting to be acknowledged.

Mom had written across the top of one notebook page in capital letters:

WHAT DOES RECALIBRATION CHANGE?

Underneath it, the page was already crowded.

Support layers
Guardian transparency
Emotional smoothing
Reduced distress markers
Dismissal limits?
Can settings be lowered?
Who has access?

Mara stood in the doorway with her backpack on, reading the list upside down.

Dad was at the counter making toast and reading something at the same time, which meant the toast was definitely going to burn. Mom sat at the table, still in the sweatshirt she wore when she had been awake too late, clicking through an old medical archive that looked like it had been designed before anyone cared what websites looked like.

“You’re still looking?” Mara asked.

Mom glanced up. “We said we would.”

The toaster popped. Dad looked over too late.

“Again?” Mom asked.

Dad lifted the toast carefully. One side was almost black. “It’s still structurally bread.”

Mara took it from him anyway and scraped the burnt part into the sink. Normal things felt strange now. Toast. School. Mom’s coffee. Dad in the kitchen before work. The Guide30 countdown glowing from the wall display like nothing had changed.

GUIDE30: 4 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.

Four days until Saturday.

Six days until Monday.

The numbers had started pairing themselves in Mara’s head. Every cheerful Guide30 reminder came with the other countdown hidden inside it.

Dad set a plate in front of her. “Bayline answered the contact form.”

Mara stopped scraping toast. “Already?”

“An automated reply,” Mom said. “Then a real one very early this morning.”

Mara came to the table.

Mom turned the old tablet so Mara could read.

Bayline Neural Care
Thank you for contacting our office. Independent review may be possible for minors with guardian requests. To begin, please send:

  • the recalibration notice
  • the support level listed on the notice
  • any settings changed during the review
  • parent or guardian access information

For urgent concerns, please request the student’s full Guide record from your district wellness office.

Mara read it twice.

“What’s a support level? I didn’t see anything on the notice.”

“That’s what we need to find out,” Mom said.

Dad leaned back against the counter. “The parent portal says we can request records.”

“That’s good.”

“It also says estimated response time is five to seven business days.”

Mara looked at the Guide30 countdown again.

“That’s not good.”

“No,” Dad said. “It is not.”

Mom wrote something in the notebook. Her handwriting looked sharper than usual, like every letter was annoyed.

Mara sat down slowly. “What about Cam?”

Mom did not answer right away.

Dad folded his arms. “We can’t request Cam’s records. His mother would have to.”

Mara thought of Cam at the shop, walking out with his mother. Thought of the way he had said noncompliant environments like it was a normal thing to call his grandfather’s repair shop.

“Would she?” Mara asked.

Mom’s eyes stayed on the notebook. “I don’t know.”

That was starting to become the answer for too many things.

Mara picked at the edge of the scraped toast. “Eli might know how to talk to her.”

“I’m going to call him today,” Mom said. “Not to pull him into something without asking. Just to ask what he knows.”

The Guide chimed softly.

Departure recommended in six minutes.

Mara dismissed it.

Dad noticed. So did Mom. Neither of them said anything.

That helped.

At school, the Guide30 countdown had changed everywhere.

GUIDE30: 4 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.

It flashed above the front entrance, across hallway displays, on cafeteria screens, and in the corner of Mara’s vision whenever the Guide thought she needed a reminder. The city was still getting ready, even after Saturday. Maybe especially after Saturday.

That was what everyone kept saying.

“They’re probably doing a huge update before the event,” Nessa said near the lockers. “My cousin said the drones are going to sync with everyone’s Guides during the final song.”

Connor looked horrified. “Everyone’s Guides? Like all at once?”

“Maybe not all at once,” Nessa said. “But groups. Sections. Crowd flow. Performance cues.”

“That sounds like a great way to send my grandma to a different church again.”

June hugged her tablet tighter. “Do you think that’s why everything glitched?”

“Probably,” Nessa said. “Big systems have problems before big launches. That’s normal.”

Mara did not know if Nessa was trying to convince them or herself.

Lila stood beside Nessa, staring down at her hands. Her fingers moved slightly, like she was practicing notes against her leg.

“Is your rehearsal today?” June asked.

Lila nodded. “After school. Full stage sync.”

“You’ll be fine,” Nessa said quickly.

Lila nodded again, but it did not look like agreement. It looked like not wanting to talk about it.

Mara started to walk past.

“Mara,” Lila said.

Mara stopped before she could talk herself out of it.

Lila looked at Nessa and June, then back at Mara. “Can I talk to you later?”

Nessa’s eyebrows lifted.

Mara felt suddenly aware of everyone near the lockers, everyone pretending not to listen.

“About what?” Mara asked.

Lila swallowed. “Not here.”

That answer did not make Mara want to say yes. It made her want to leave.

But Lila looked scared in a way Mara recognized. Not sad. Not guilty. Scared.

“Fine,” Mara said. “After rehearsal.”

Lila nodded once.

Connor waited until they were halfway to class before he spoke. “That was either progress or the opening scene of a disaster.”

“Thank you.”

“I provide emotional labeling.”

“You provide noise.”

“Also true.”

Mara did not laugh, but she did feel a tiny bit less alone walking into class.

Cam was already in first period.

That was new.

Cam sat at his desk with his hands folded on top of it. His bag was zipped and tucked under his chair. Nothing spilled out. Nothing leaned sideways. Nothing looked like Cam had dropped it there two seconds before the bell.

He looked up when Mara came in and gave her a small smile.

“Hey,” he said.

“Hey.”

She took the seat beside him because it would have been weirder not to. For a minute, neither of them said anything. Mr. Halden was at the front sorting the day’s materials while the wall display showed another Guide30 safety prompt.

Cam tapped his fingers against the desk, then stopped.

That bothered Mara more than the tapping.

“You can tap,” she said quietly.

Cam looked at her. “What?”

“Making a beat with your fingers on your desk. It’s fine.”

“Oh.” He glanced down at it. “It’s distracting.”

“You always tap.”

“Yeah.” Cam’s hand moved toward the desk, then back to his lap. “I’m trying not to.”

Mara did not know what to say.

Cam looked at the front of the room. His face was calm, but not comfortable. That was the part people missed. They saw calm and thought it meant better.

Mara was starting to see the effort under it.

“Does it feel better?” she asked.

Cam did not pretend he did not know what she meant.

He kept looking at the wall display. “Sometimes.”

That answer landed harder than no would have.

Mara’s throat felt tight. “Sometimes?”

Cam’s fingers curled under the edge of his desk. “It’s easier.”
