The classroom noise seemed to fade around them. Students talking. Chairs scraping. Mr. Halden clearing his throat. The Guide30 prompt glowing in perfect blue letters.

“What is?” Mara asked.

Cam blinked once, slow. “Everything.”

For a second, he sounded relieved.

Then his eyes shifted slightly, and his shoulders straightened.

“I mean, it’s easier to focus,” he said.

The sentence came out smooth. Too smooth.

Mara looked down at her desk.

She wanted to tell him that easier did not always mean better, but Eli had already said that, and repeating it would only make Cam feel watched. So she said nothing.

In Applied Response, the class practiced Guide30 readiness situations. Not emergencies this time. People problems.

Mr. Halden said the week before a major public event could bring up stress, conflict, and “support-resistant behavior.” Mara hated that phrase immediately.

The prompt appeared in the center of her vision.

A friend seems upset about Guide30 and says they do not want to follow their assigned event plan. What is the best first response?

The Guide offered an answer immediately.

Encourage your friend to follow the approved plan. If concern continues, submit a peer support note so Wellness can help.

Mara stared at the answer.

A peer support note.

That was what Lila had done. Maybe not with those exact words, but close enough.

Mara wanted to type something else.

Ask why they are upset.
Sit with them.
Do not report them before you even listen.

Her fingers hovered.

Then her Monday reminder notice pulsed faintly at the edge of her vision.

Formal recommendation pending family review.

Mara looked across the room. Cam was already finished, sitting straight with his hands folded on the desk.

She deleted the first word she had typed.

Then she copied the Guide answer.

Encourage your friend to follow the approved plan. If concern continues, submit a peer support note so Wellness can help.

The response box turned green.

Accepted.

Mara looked away from the screen.

This time, doing what the Guide wanted did not make her feel safer.

It just made her understand Lila a little more.

At lunch, Lila did not sit with Mara. But she did not sit comfortably with Nessa and June either. She kept checking something, then closing it, then opening it again.

Mara tried not to watch.

She failed.

Connor noticed, because of course he did. “You could go over there.”

“No.”

“She could come over here.”

“She won’t.”

“Then I guess we stare across the cafeteria forever and become local legends.”

Mara gave him a look.

Connor held up both hands. “Fine. I will eat my suspicious pasta in silence.”

“You don’t know how.”

“That’s fair.”

Cam sat down beside them with a tray that was still too neat. He had pudding today, unopened, placed perfectly beside his sandwich. Connor noticed but did not comment this time.

That made Mara like him more.

Nessa walked by their table on the way to throw something away. She slowed near Cam.

“My brother said the first week after support adjustment is the hardest,” she said.

Cam looked up.

Mara stiffened.

Nessa’s face softened. “But he said it helped. Eventually.”

Cam nodded. “Yeah. I think it is.”

Mara stared at her lunch.

Nessa left.

Cam opened his pudding carefully, peeling the lid back halfway and folding it down.

“I know you hate when people say that,” he said quietly.

Mara looked at him.

“When they say it helped,” Cam said. “I can tell.”

“I don’t hate it.”

“You do.”

She wanted to argue, but she didn’t.

Cam looked down at the pudding like it had suddenly become very interesting. “I don’t know what to do with it either.”

“With what?”

“If it helps and also doesn’t.” He pushed the spoon into the pudding but did not eat any. “That sounds stupid.”

“No,” Mara said. “It doesn’t.”

Cam’s eyes flicked to hers.

For one second, there he was again. Tired. Confused. Cam.

Then the bell warning chimed, and he blinked like something had tugged him back.

“We should go,” he said.

Mara nodded, even though she wished he would stop saying that.

After school, Mara waited near the music wing because Lila had asked her to talk and Mara had said yes before she could think of a reason not to.

The hallway smelled like floor polish and old instrument cases. Behind one door, the band was running the Guide30 opening again. The music started beautifully, then stopped after six measures.

Someone groaned.

A teacher said, “Again from measure twelve.”

Mara leaned against the wall and tried not to feel like she was waiting outside trouble.

Lila came out ten minutes later with her performance jacket folded over one arm. Her face was flushed, and her eyes were too bright.

“Are you okay?” Mara asked before remembering she was still mad.

Lila looked surprised by the question. “I don’t know.”

They walked a little ways down the hall without talking. Mara did not know where they were going. Away from the music room, maybe. Away from Nessa and June. Away from anyone who would try to help too fast.

Lila stopped beside a trophy case full of old robotics awards.

“Wellness sent me something,” she said.

Mara’s stomach dropped. “About you?”

Lila shook her head.

The answer was already on her face.

“About me,” Mara said.

Lila nodded and looked down at the jacket in her arms. “A peer support input request.”

Mara’s mouth went dry.

“What did it ask?”

“If I had noticed increased isolation. Stress behavior. Resistance to support. Stuff like that.” Lila’s fingers tightened around the jacket. “It had boxes for me to check off.”

Boxes.

Of course it had boxes.

Mara stepped back. “And?”

“I didn’t submit it.”

Mara stared at her.

Lila’s eyes filled, but she did not cry. “I started to. I thought maybe I was supposed to. And then I kept thinking about last time.”

The trophy case lights flickered beside them.

Mara looked at her own reflection in the glass. She looked pale and angry and tired.

“You said you thought you were helping last time,” Mara said.

“I was.”

“And now?”

Lila swallowed. “Now I don’t know who gets helped when I answer questions about you.”

She wanted to say thank you, but the words felt too simple. Too easy. She was still hurt. Lila not submitting one form did not undo Monday, or the library, Ms. Cole or the way Mara had felt when she realized her best friend had turned her worry into a report.

Lila wiped one cheek quickly with her sleeve. “You don’t have to forgive me right now.”

“Good,” Mara said, because it came out before she could make it nicer.

Lila gave the smallest nod.

Mara regretted the sharpness, but not enough to take it back.

Behind them, the music started again. This time Lila’s cue came through the wall, a clear note rising above the others.

When Mara got home, Mom was on the phone at the kitchen table, writing in the notebook while Dad stood near the counter with his arms folded.

Mom looked up when Mara came in and lifted one finger.

“Yes,” Mom said into the phone. “I understand you can’t discuss another minor’s record. I’m asking about the process. If a support layer was added during a recalibration review, who can request an independent adjustment?”

Mara dropped her backpack slowly beside the door.

Dad glanced at her and mouthed, Bayline.

Mara’s heart started beating faster.

Mom listened for a long time.

Then she wrote three words in the notebook.

Guardian. District. Emergency.

“Thank you,” Mom said. “Yes, we’ll send the documents tonight.”

She ended the call and sat still for a second.

Mara walked to the table. “What did they say?”

Mom turned the notebook so Mara could see.

Guardian request
District authorization
Emergency medical review

“These are ways support layers can be reviewed,” Mom said.

“Reviewed like changed?”

“Possibly changed. Possibly lowered. Possibly paused. She was careful with her words.”

“Who was it?”

“Not Dr. Voss. Someone from her office. But they said Dr. Voss will look at the documents if we send them.”

Dad leaned against the counter. “We need Mara’s full support record. We also need the classification of whatever they’re recommending for Monday.”

Mara looked at the notebook. “Can we get it before then?”

Mom and Dad looked at each other.

“We’re trying,” Dad said.

Mara nodded.

Mom reached across the table and covered Mara’s hand with hers. Not a quick squeeze. She left it there.

“I talked to Eli,” Mom said.

Mara looked up.

“He said Cam’s mother is scared and overwhelmed, and the school is telling her Cam is improving.”

“She believes them?”

“I think she wants to.” Mom’s thumb moved once across Mara’s hand. “He also said he would talk to her if he can. Not push. Talk.”

Mara looked down.

Lila’s words came back.

I don’t know who gets helped when I answer questions about you.

Cam’s words came back too.

If it helps and also doesn’t.

The whole thing felt tangled in a way Mara could not pull apart.

Dad sat across from her. “We’re not going to pretend this is simple.”

“I know.”

“And we’re not going to let them rush us because their calendar is full.”

Mara looked at him.

Dad’s voice stayed quiet. “That part I do know.”

Later, after dinner, Mara took Mom’s journal upstairs and opened to the page she had written on the night before.

They scheduled me for Monday after Guide30.

God, please help us find what we need before Monday gets here.

She read the words and thought about the day.

Mom had found Bayline. Dad had found the records request. Lila had not filled out the boxes. Cam had said something that sounded like him, even if it only lasted a second.

None of it was enough.

But it was something.

Mara picked up her pen and wrote underneath:

Today Lila didn’t answer the form.
Cam said it helps and also doesn’t.
Mom found three ways.
I don’t know what any of that means yet.
God, please keep helping us.

She stopped and looked at the last line.

The Guide always answered right away. Sometimes before she even asked.

A chime. A prompt. A warning. A correction.

God did not do that.

There was no box in the corner of her vision. No countdown. No red warning if she asked the wrong thing. No voice telling her to calm down.

But Mara did not feel watched in the same way.

She felt quiet.

Not fixed. Not suddenly brave. Just quiet enough to breathe.

The Guide made her feel like she had to answer correctly.

Talking to God did not.

She looked back at the page and added one more line.

Please stay with me while we figure it out.

Downstairs, Mom and Dad were still talking quietly at the table.

Mara could hear the low murmur of their voices through the floor, steady and tired and still going.

For the first time all day, Monday didn’t scared her.

Because it did not feel like it was coming alone.

Chapter 21

Wednesday, 3 days until Guide30

By Wednesday morning, Mara had learned that waiting for answers was its own kind of work.

Mom and Dad were still looking. That was the phrase they used now. Looking. Not fixing. Not solving. Not making everything better before breakfast. Looking.

The kitchen table had not been cleared in two days. Mom had moved the fruit bowl to the counter so there would be more room for the notebook, Dad’s tablet, the old tablet, printed pages, and a list of questions that kept getting longer instead of shorter.

Mara read the top few lines while eating cereal.

What is a support layer?
Who authorizes changes?
What is the difference between review and recalibration?
Can guardian consent be refused?
Can consent be bypassed?

The last one made her spoon stop halfway to her mouth.

Dad noticed.

“We don’t know that it can,” he said.

“But you wrote it down.”

“Because if there’s a question we don’t like, we still need the answer.”

Mom was standing at the counter, scrolling through a response from Bayline Neural Care. She looked like she had slept, but not enough. Her hair was twisted into a messy knot, and she was wearing the same sweatshirt from Monday night.

“The clinic says they can’t review anything without the support layer classification,” Mom said. “They also said the district office has to release the full record to guardians.”

“So ask the district,” Mara said.

“We did.”

“And?”

Mom looked at Dad.

Dad leaned against the counter with his coffee. “They acknowledged the request.”

Mara waited.

“That’s it?” she asked.

“That’s it so far.”

Her Guide pulsed at the edge of her vision.

Departure recommended in eight minutes.

Mara dismissed it and ate another bite of cereal even though it tasted like cardboard.

Mom saw the little blink in her eyes. “Was that the Guide?”

“Leaving reminder.”

Mom looked at the wall clock, then at the old tablet, then at her own Guide display only she could see. “You do need to leave soon.”

Mara wanted to be annoyed, but Mom was right. That was another irritating thing about the Guide. Sometimes it was right.

Before Mara left, Mom stopped her near the door.

“I’m calling Bayline again today,” Mom said. “And I’m going to try the district office, not just the portal.”

“Will they answer?”

“I don’t know.”

Mara nodded.

Mom touched her shoulder. “I know that’s a terrible answer.”

“It’s the answer everyone keeps having.”

Mom’s hand stayed there for another second. “Then we keep asking.”

School looked more finished every day.

That was the only way Mara could think to describe it. The banners were no longer just at the front entrance. They hung from the second-floor railings and cafeteria ceiling. Blue and gold guide-lines had been projected onto the floors to show where students would stand during Friday’s final sendoff assembly. A huge display near the office counted down in hours now, not just days.

GUIDE30: 3 DAYS UNTIL CONNECTION DAY.
CITYWIDE SYNCHRONIZATION EVENT BEGINS SATURDAY.

The word synchronization had started showing up everywhere.

Mara did not like it.

At her locker, Connor was reading a Guide30 info page with the face he usually saved for math.

“It says there’s going to be a full-city connection moment,” he said when Mara came up.

“What is that?”

“I was hoping you knew.”

Mara leaned closer. The page in Connor’s vision was not visible to her, but he read part of it aloud.

“At the height of the celebration, participants will experience a shared guidance sequence designed to demonstrate thirty years of connection, safety, and unity.”

Mara stared at him.

Connor lowered his voice. “That sounds like everybody’s Guide is going to hold hands.”

“That is the weirdest way you could have said that.”

“But not wrong.”

Mara looked toward the banner again. Full-city connection moment. Shared guidance sequence. The words sounded like something adults thought sounded beautiful because they had never had to sit in a wellness office and be told their Monday was already scheduled.

Nessa appeared beside them with June and Lila.

“It’s probably just a synchronized light cue,” Nessa said. “My cousin said every section gets different colors and music prompts. It’s supposed to be amazing.”

“Your cousin knows a lot,” Connor said.

“He works event setup.”

“He also thought VIP entrance meant Very Important Pigeons.”

“That was one time.”

June looked nervous. “Do you think the recent glitches were because of the connection thing?”

Nessa hesitated. “Maybe. But big events always have testing issues.”

Mara glanced at Lila.

Lila was staring at the display, not joining in. Her rehearsal jacket was folded over one arm, and she kept pressing her thumb into the seam like she was trying to rub a hole through it.

“Full rehearsal today?” Mara asked.

Lila looked surprised Mara had spoken to her. “Yeah. After school.”

“Solo?”

Lila nodded. “They said all cue issues are fixed.”

Connor shifted his backpack. “For what it’s worth, I think if anyone can survive being betrayed by a backing track, it’s you.”

Lila looked at him.

“That was supposed to be supportive,” he added.

“It sort of was,” June said.

Lila’s mouth moved into something almost like a smile, but it did not last long.

The rest of the morning passed without anything big happening.

That should have helped.

It didn’t.

The announcements were normal. The teachers were normal. The Guide30 reminders were normal. But Mara kept waiting for something else to go wrong, and by lunch, her shoulders hurt from sitting like she was bracing for it.

At lunch, Cam sat beside her with a tray that was still too neat.

Today his sandwich was wrapped halfway instead of all the way. There were crumbs on his tray. Mara noticed them before she noticed anything else, which made her feel ridiculous.

Connor noticed too, but he was smart enough not to say it.

Cam picked up his sandwich, then set it down again. “My mom wants me home right after school.”

Mara looked at him. “No shop?”

He shook his head.

“Do you want to go?”

Cam stared at the tray for a while. “Yes.”

That answer came too quickly to be smoothed.

Mara waited.

Cam’s eyes shifted, and his fingers pressed against the edge of the table. “But it’s probably better if I don’t.”

“There it is,” Connor muttered.

Cam looked at him. “What?”

“Nothing.”

“No, what?”

Connor looked uncomfortable for the first time in a while. “It just sounds like somebody else finishes your sentences now.”

The words landed hard.

Mara expected Cam to get mad. Part of her wanted him to get mad. Old Cam would have said something sharp or sarcastic. He would have turned Connor’s comment into a joke and made the table breathe again.

Instead, Cam looked down.

“I know,” he said.

Mara stopped moving.

Connor’s face changed.

Cam swallowed. “Sometimes I know what I want to say, and then it feels like there’s a better thing I’m supposed to say instead. And if I say the first thing anyway, everything gets loud.”

“What gets loud?” Mara asked.

Cam tapped one finger against his temple, then stopped. “Prompts. Reminders. Calm steps. Sometimes my mom gets notified. Sometimes it asks if I need assistance.”

Connor’s voice went quiet. “That sounds awful.”

Cam looked at him. “It’s not awful all the time.”

Mara did not like the way he said it.

Cam took a breath. “Sometimes it helps. That’s what I don’t know how to explain. I’m not as mad. I don’t feel like everything is pushing on me all the time.”

Mara stared at the table.

She had wanted him to say he hated it. She had wanted him to say he wanted it gone. That would have made everything easier.

Cam looked at her. “I know that makes it worse.”

“It makes it confusing,” Mara said.

“Yeah.”

The bell warning chimed before anyone could say more.

After school, Mara almost went straight home.

Then a message from Lila appeared at the edge of her vision.

Can you meet me again by the music wing?

No explanation. Just that.

Mara stood in the hallway for a second, staring at the words. Part of her wanted to ignore it. Part of her wanted to know why Lila was asking.

She went.

This time, she did not have to wait long.

Rehearsal ended early, which was not a good sign.

Students came out in clumps, talking too loudly, carrying instrument cases and complaining about stage marks, timing changes, and how nobody knew where they were supposed to stand anymore.

Lila came out last.

Her face told Mara enough.

“What happened?” Mara asked.

Lila looked down the emptying hallway. “They changed the cue map.”

“The what?”

“The timing for the performance.” Lila shifted the jacket in her arms. “It used to just follow the music. Now it follows the connection sequence too.”

“The full-city thing?”

Lila nodded. “Crowd sections. Drone lights. Speaker timing. Stage marks. All of it is supposed to line up.”

Mara leaned against the wall beside the trophy case. “That sounds like a lot.”

“It is.” Lila’s voice went quieter. “My solo cue moved.”

“Moved how?”

“Two counts earlier.”

Mara waited.

Lila looked at the floor. “Two counts is a lot when everyone is watching.”

Mara did not know enough about music to know if that was true, but she knew Lila well enough to know she was not being dramatic.

“They said it makes the whole event feel unified,” Lila said.

Mara looked toward the rehearsal room. Someone inside played one short note, then stopped.

“But it messed you up.”

Lila nodded once. “Yeah.”

For a moment they both stood there, listening to the faint echo of music from inside the room.

Then Lila said, “I wanted to tell you, they sent me another peer input request.”

Mara’s stomach went cold. “About me?”

Lila nodded.

“What did you say?”

“I didn’t answer it.”

Mara looked at her.

Lila’s fingers tightened around the jacket. “I wanted to. Not because I want you to get reviewed. I just… I kept thinking if I left it blank, maybe that was wrong too. Like maybe if something happened to you, it would be because I didn’t say anything.”

Mara did not answer right away.

Lila’s eyes filled, but she blinked hard and kept talking. “Last time, I thought telling someone was the safest thing. This time I kept reading the questions, and they didn’t feel like they were asking if you were okay. They felt like they were asking me to help prove you weren’t.”

That was the first thing Lila had said that reached Mara without making her want to run.

Mara looked at the floor. “I’m still mad.”

“I know.”

“I don’t know when I won’t be.”

“I know that too.”

Lila nodded like she deserved it, which made Mara feel worse, not better.

The Guide pulsed softly.

Peer reconciliation opportunity detected.

Mara dismissed it.

Lila blinked at something too.

For a second, they looked at each other and understood the same thing without saying it.

Then Lila said, “I’m scared I’m going to mess up Saturday.”

Mara could have said she wouldn’t. That would have been easy and probably useless.

Instead she said, “Then don’t let the cue be the only thing you listen to.”

Lila looked confused.

“I mean, you know the song, right?”

“Of course.”

“So if the cue jumps, you still know the song.”

Lila stared at her.

Mara shrugged, suddenly embarrassed. “That’s all.”

“No,” Lila said quietly. “That’s not all.”

Mara did not know what to do with that, so she nodded and left before the moment got too soft.

At home, Mom was on the phone with Eli.

Mara knew because Mom had the notebook open and was saying, “No, I understand. I’m not asking you to push her. I’m asking if she would be willing to hear from another parent.”

Mom looked up when Mara came in and pointed at the chair beside her. Mara sat.

Dad was at the counter, filling out another request form. He had written the support classification phrases on a sticky note and stuck it to the side of his tablet.

Mom listened for a long time.

Then she said, “Thank you. And Eli? I’m sorry. I know he’s your grandson.”

Mara looked down.

When Mom ended the call, she wrote one name in the notebook.

Cam’s mom.

Then she underlined it once.

“Eli is going to try to talk to her tonight,” Mom said. “Not about us. About Cam. He thinks she might listen if it’s not framed like she made the wrong choice.”

“Did she?” Mara asked.

Mom set the pen down. “I don’t know.”

Mara wanted a stronger answer.

Mom’s face said she knew that.

“She was trying to help him,” Mom said. “That does not mean the help was harmless.”

Dad looked up from the counter. “Bayline wants records. We need yours before Monday, and if anyone is going to help Cam, someone needs his.”

Mara thought of Cam saying sometimes it helped.

“What if he doesn’t want help?”

Mom did not answer quickly. Mara was starting to respect that, even when she hated it.

“Then nobody should force him,” Mom said. “But he deserves to understand what was changed. So does his mother.”

That night, Mara opened Mom’s journal again.

She read the page about Grandpa saying people moved too fast. She turned the page and found a smaller entry near the bottom, written in Mom’s younger handwriting.

Dad said asking questions is not the same as rebelling.

I told him some people act like it is.

He said, “Then ask better questions.”

I rolled my eyes because of course that was his answer.

Then he said, “The right questions make people uncomfortable.”

I hate when he says things that sound annoying but are probably true.

Mara read that one three times.

Then she wrote underneath her own entry from the night before.

Lila didn’t answer the form.

Cam said it helps and also doesn’t.

Mom talked to Eli.

Dad requested records again.

God, please help us ask better questions.

She stopped there.

The house was quiet except for Mom and Dad downstairs, still moving around the kitchen, still opening pages, still writing things down.

Mara closed the journal and turned off her lamp.

She did not feel brave. But she also didn’t feel alone.

Chapter 22

Thursday, 2 days until Guide30

By Thursday, almost everyone had stopped talking about the weekend glitches. The city had explained them away by Monday, and most people seemed relieved to let it. They were not glitches. They were preparations. They were not problems. They were signs that Guide30 was almost here.

Now the school felt like it was counting down to Saturday. Hallway displays flashed celebration reminders between class announcements. Teachers talked through Friday’s rehearsal schedule, assigned seating, performance cues, and what colors each section was supposed to wear.

Connor read the newest message off the display by Mara’s locker.

GUIDE30 FINAL PREPARATIONS CONTINUE.

RESIDENTS MAY NOTICE TEMPORARY ADJUSTMENTS AS CELEBRATION FEATURES ARE ACTIVATED.

He made a face. “Temporary adjustments. That is how I describe my room when my mom says it’s disgusting.”

Mara watched the screen shift to a smiling family under blue celebration lights.

“So we’re all just supposed to believe the glitches were part of the plan, nobody thinks it’s weird anymore? ” she asked.

Connor shrugged. “People believe lots of things when there’s a citywide party coming.”

Nessa appeared beside them with June, holding a folded rehearsal schedule against her chest.

“Friday’s going to be impossible,” Nessa said. “They changed half the section cues again.”

Connor looked at the schedule. “The Guide celebration has homework now?”

“It’s rehearsal,” Nessa said. “And it matters. Saturday is supposed to be perfect.”

June hugged her books tighter. “I’ll be happy when Saturday is over.”

Nessa gave her a look. “Over? That’s when Guide30 actually begins.”

Mara looked toward the music hallway.

Lila was usually there by now.

“Have you seen Lila?” Mara asked.

June shook her head. “Not today.”

Nessa adjusted the folded schedule in her hands. “She’s probably with the performers. They’ve been changing things all week.”

“Where’s Lila?” she asked before she could stop herself.

Nessa glanced toward the music wing. “Early rehearsal. The band has extra call times now.”

“Before school?”

“They need to run the solo with the connection cue.”

Connor’s expression softened. “That sounds horrible.”

Nessa looked at him.

“What?” Connor said. “I can have feelings. Like, I know I have at least three of them.”

Mara headed toward the music wing before she really decided to. Connor followed because Connor followed interesting problems. Nessa and June stayed by the lockers, but Mara could feel Nessa watching.

They reached the side hallway just as the rehearsal room door opened.

Lila came out with the band director and another adult Mara did not recognize, a woman wearing a Guide30 event badge.

“You sounded wonderful,” the woman said. “Just remember to wait for the light cue on Saturday. Once the sequence begins, all eyes will come to your section.”

Lila smiled like she was trying not to smile too much.

“I know,” she said. “I mean, yes. I will.”

The band director handed her a folder. “Get some rest before tomorrow’s rehearsal. Big weekend.”

Lila nodded, still holding the folder against her chest like it was something important.

Connor leaned closer to Mara. “I have never seen anyone this excited about homework with lighting.”

Lila saw them and stopped.

For a second, Mara thought Lila might look away.

She did not.

“You came by?” Lila asked.

Mara shrugged. “Sort of. We were passing.”

Connor looked at her. “We were not passing. We walked directly here.”

Mara gave him a look.

Lila smiled a little, but it faded fast. “Saturday is going to be huge.”

“Yeah,” Mara said. “Seems like it.”

Lila shifted the folder in her arms. “I get to start part of the connection sequence.”

Nessa’s eyes widened. “Seriously?”

Lila nodded, and this time she could not hide the smile. “Not the whole thing. Just my section. But still.”

“That’s amazing,” June said.

Lila glanced at Mara.

Mara knew what she was supposed to say. She also knew Lila actually wanted to hear it.

So she said it.

“That’s really cool, Lila.”

Lila’s smile changed. Not bigger exactly. Just less careful.

“Thanks,” she said.

The first bell rang.

Lila hugged the folder tighter and hurried toward class.

Mara watched her go, feeling glad she had said the right thing and uneasy that she had needed to force herself to say it.

Cam was not in first period.

His desk stayed empty through attendance, announcements, and the first half of the lesson. Mara checked the door every few minutes until Mr. Halden looked at her once, then kept teaching.

When Cam finally came in, he was with a hall aide.

That was new.

He looked calm, but his hair was not as neat as it had been Monday. His backpack was zipped wrong, one side bulging where something had been shoved in too quickly. He took his seat without looking at Mara.

The hall aide handed Mr. Halden a note and left.

Mara waited until Mr. Halden turned back to the board.

“Are you okay?” she whispered.

Cam looked at his desk. “I’m fine.”

Mara nodded, but it did not make her feel any better.

He opened his tablet and stared at the wrong assignment for almost a full minute.

“Cam,” she whispered.

His jaw tightened. “I tried to go to the shop this morning.”

Mara’s heart jumped.

“My mom got a notification before I reached the transit stop.”

Mara sat very still.

“It told her I was deviating from my support plan,” he said. “Then my Guide sent me a calming route home. Then she called.”

“Did you go back home?”

He looked down.

That was answer enough.

Mara wanted to say she was sorry, but the words felt too small.

Cam swallowed. “I hate that I went back.”

There he was.

The realness of it hit so hard Mara could barely breathe.

Then his eyes shifted.

His shoulders straightened.

“But it was probably better,” he said.

Mara gripped the edge of her desk..

Cam stared at his hands, like he had heard himself and could not stop it.

At lunch, he did not sit with them.

He sat at the far end of the table with his food untouched, reading something only he could see. Connor started to say something, then stopped. Mara was grateful. Some days even Connor knew when noise would not help.

After school, Mom picked Mara up instead of letting her take transit.

That was another thing that had changed. Mom did not say she was worried about the routes. She said she had errands nearby, but Mara knew the difference.

Dad was home when they got there. So was Grandpa Frank.

He sat at the kitchen table with a mug of tea and a stack of printed pages he had apparently brought himself. He looked older in their kitchen than he did in Mara’s memory, but his eyes were sharp.

“You printed things?” Mara asked.

Grandpa lifted one page. “People keep acting like paper is dead. Paper is patient.”

Dad looked at Mara from the counter. “Bayline sent a longer response.”

Mom dropped her keys in the bowl by the door and went straight to the table. She had been carrying the answer all the way from the car. Mara could tell.

Grandpa pushed the top page toward her.

The language was still medical and not written for kids, but Mom had highlighted lines.

Recalibration procedures may include modifications to Guide support layers, including prompt frequency, dismissal limits, emotional response smoothing, guardian transparency, and access restrictions.

Mara read dismissal limits twice.

Dad pointed to another highlighted section.

Support layer settings may be reviewed, reduced, suspended, or reclassified through guardian request, district authorization, or emergency medical review.

Mara looked up. “Suspended?”

Mom nodded carefully. “That means turned off temporarily.”

“For Cam?”

“For anyone with a support layer,” Dad said. “If we can get the records and the right authorization.”

Grandpa tapped the paper. “Which they do not make easy.”

“No,” Mom said. “They do not.”

Mara’s thoughts were moving too fast. “So Cam isn’t gone.”

Mom’s face softened. “No.”

“And if they did it to me, it wouldn’t be forever?”

Dad looked at Mom.

Grandpa looked at the table.

Mom moved closer to Mara. “We are going to do everything we can to keep them from doing it to you without a full explanation and without us understanding every part of it.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

“I know.”

Mara waited.

Mom took a breath. “Based on what Bayline sent, recalibration is not supposed to erase anyone. It changes how much the Guide can interrupt, redirect, and push support. That can be adjusted. But I don’t know yet how hard it is once it’s in place, and I don’t know what happens if the district refuses.”

That was not easy.

But it was true.

Mara sat down.

Grandpa looked at her across the table. “The hopeful part is this: added things can sometimes be removed.”

“Sometimes?”

“Sometimes is better than never.”

Mara looked at the highlighted page again.

Reduced. Suspended. Reclassified.

The words were small. Boring, even.

They felt like cracks in a wall.

Mom sat beside her. “Eli called back too.”

Mara looked up.

“He spoke to Cam’s mother. Not much. She didn’t agree to anything yet. But she listened.”

“Does she know it can be adjusted?”

“She does now,” Mom said. “Eli sent her the same article.”

Mara pictured Cam’s mother reading it. Maybe at her own kitchen table. Maybe scared. Maybe angry. Maybe wanting the Guide to be right because the alternative meant she had let them change something in her son she did not understand.

For the first time, Mara felt sorry for her.

Not completely.

But a little.

Grandpa stayed for dinner. The adults talked in low voices about records and permissions and whether a parent request could be expedited. Mara listened until the words blurred together. Then she took Mom’s journal upstairs and opened it on her bed.

She wrote:

Cam tried to go to the shop and the Guide told his mom.

They can suspend support layers. Maybe.

Eli talked to Cam’s mom.

Grandpa says sometimes is better than never.

I hate sometimes.

She paused, then added:

God, please help Cam remember he wanted to go.

That prayer felt different from the others.

Not bigger.

Downstairs, Grandpa laughed at something Dad said. It was a tired laugh, but real.

Mara listened to it through the floor.

For one minute, the apartment did not feel like it was waiting for Monday.

It felt like people were getting ready to fight for it.

Chapter 23

One Day Until Guide30

By Friday morning, the whole school had turned into one long countdown.

Guide30 announcements moved across the lobby walls in blue and gold light. The school had changed the display panels overnight, so every hallway seemed to be counting down at once.

ONE DAY UNTIL GUIDE30.

There were also smaller reminders underneath it.

CHECK YOUR ASSIGNED FAMILY SECTION.

REVIEW YOUR TRANSPORTATION ROUTE.

ACKNOWLEDGE ALL EVENT SAFETY PROMPTS.

Connor stopped in front of the nearest screen and read the last one out loud. “Acknowledge all event safety prompts. That sounds fun. Nothing says celebration like homework from your emergency plan.”

Mara adjusted the strap of her backpack. “At least they didn’t make us wear matching shirts.”

“They tried,” Connor said. “My mom said no because apparently I look bad in gold, which was rude but also true.”

The halls were louder than usual, but not in the normal almost-weekend way. Everyone seemed half at school and half already at the plaza. Students compared section numbers, argued about where the best food stands would be, and complained about early check-in times while pretending they were not excited. Even the teachers had that distracted look adults got when they were trying to act normal but kept checking their own Guides.

Mara tried to ignore the countdown, but it was everywhere. It hovered at the edge of her sight when she passed classroom doors. It sat in the corner of the attendance screen. It even appeared on the lunch menu display beside the terrible breakfast wraps no one ever bought.

Guide30 was tomorrow.

So was the last full day of school before Monday.

Her Guide had not let her forget that part either.

At her locker, Mara opened her bag and shoved a half-finished worksheet into the bottom even though she knew it would come back wrinkled. Connor leaned against the locker beside hers and watched a group of eighth graders practice a chant for Saturday.

“Please tell me we are not chanting,” he said.

“We are definitely not chanting.”

“Good. I have limits.”

“You once sang an entire snack ad during math.”

“That was different. It was stuck in my head, and I chose to share my suffering.”

Mara almost smiled, which was annoying because Connor could usually tell when he had succeeded.

The first bell rang, and Mara’s Guide immediately opened a school route.

GUIDE30 ASSEMBLY.

PLEASE PROCEED TO AUDITORIUM.

A soft blue line appeared along the hallway floor in her vision, turning at the corner toward the auditorium. The same prompt must have opened for everyone else, because the whole hallway shifted direction at once.

Teachers stood near the walls, not really directing anyone, just watching to make sure the students followed what the Guide had already told them to do.

Inside, the auditorium lights were dimmed, and the stage screen glowed blue. Rows filled quickly. Mara ended up beside Connor near the middle, with Nessa and June two rows ahead. Lila was not there, which made sense because the performers had a separate rehearsal block that morning. Still, Mara found herself checking the front rows.

Connor noticed. “She’s probably backstage doing famous person things.”

“She’s singing one song.”

“Exactly. Famous.”

Mara looked toward the stage instead of answering.

The assembly began with Principal Voss standing at the podium, smiling in the careful way adults smiled when they had been given talking points.

“Tomorrow, our city celebrates an incredible milestone,” she said. “Thirty years of Guide support, thirty years of safer choices, stronger connections, and healthier communities.”

The screen behind her shifted through old pictures of the city. The first Guides looked almost clumsy now: wrist cuffs, ear clips, and clear plastic lenses that sat over one eye. People in the pictures were always touching them, adjusting them, looking down at tiny screens or squinting at early route lines.

Nothing like the implant kids now receive when they turn three. The soft overlay that appeared in Mara’s vision now without anyone else seeing it.

There were pictures of classrooms using early learning prompts, nurses helping patients with recovery plans, emergency workers following bright route lines through storm damage, and families standing under the first Guide towers.

Mara knew some of the history. Everyone did. They learned it in school almost every year, usually from videos with soft music and smiling people. Guide had started as emergency support. Then medical reminders. Then school help. Then transit, food, stress, sleep, safety, careers, friendships, conflict, grief. Every few years it had learned to help with something else.

Or tell people what to do about something else.

Principal Voss continued talking about attendance procedures and assigned sections and how students performing on stage should report to their staging areas by four thirty the next afternoon. A few kids clapped when she mentioned the food vendors. More clapped when she said there would be no homework assigned over the weekend “in honor of the celebration.”

Connor leaned toward Mara. “Finally, the Guide supports my actual needs.”

“Your actual needs are no homework and cheese fries.”

“And yet no one has built a system around that.”

After Principal Voss finished, the screen changed to a short video from the city’s Guide30 committee. It showed families arriving at the plaza, drones forming bright shapes over the river, and clips of Dr. Adrian Cole speaking to crowds. His voice filled the auditorium, warm and steady.

“Guidance is not about control,” he said in the video. “It is about care. It is about making sure no one has to face uncertainty alone.”

Mara felt something tighten in her stomach.

Beside her, Connor stopped making jokes.

The video showed a little girl crossing a street safely because her Guide warned her about a turning vehicle. Then an older man smiling as a memory prompt reminded him of his granddaughter’s name. Then a teenage boy sitting outside a classroom, breathing along with a calming pattern until he stood and went inside.

Mara thought of Tobias .

She looked at Nessa. Nessa was sitting up straight, watching the screen like she wanted everyone else to understand what she understood.

Mara did understand some of it. That was the problem. Guide had helped people. It had helped real people with real fear and real pain and real problems. It was easier to be angry at something if it was only bad.

But Guide was not only bad.

That made everything harder.

After the assembly, students spilled back into the hallways with the noisy relief of people who had sat still too long. Mara moved slowly, letting the crowd push around her instead of fighting it. Connor was telling her his plan to survive the celebration by “accidentally” standing near the snack vendors, but Mara only heard half of it.

Then she saw Cam.

He stood near the side hallway by the old trophy case, one hand gripping the strap of his bag. He was not looking at anyone. His eyes moved slightly, like he was reading something in front of him, but his mouth stayed pressed shut.

Mara slowed.

Connor followed her gaze. “You want me to disappear?”

“What?”

“You have the face.”

“What face?”

“The face that says, Connor, please stop being Connor for three minutes.”

Mara did not know what to say to that.

Connor nodded like she had answered. “I’ll go be emotionally unavailable by the water fountain.”

He walked off before she could respond.

Mara stood there for a second, then crossed to Cam.

“Hey,” she said.

Cam blinked and looked at her. “Hey.”

“You okay?”

He gave a small laugh, but it did not sound like he thought anything was funny. “That question is starting to feel like a trap.”

“I can ask worse ones.”

“I know.”

They stood out of the main flow of students, close enough to the trophy case that Mara could see their reflections in the glass. Cam looked tired. Not sleepy tired. More like someone had been making him carry a backpack full of rocks all day and telling him it was helping his posture.

“Did something happen?” Mara asked.

Cam looked down the hall toward the auditorium doors. “Not exactly.”

“That is a very annoying answer.”

“I know.”

He rubbed both hands over his face and then dropped them quickly, like he had remembered he was at school.

“It’s getting harder to tell,” he said.

Mara waited.

Cam’s jaw moved like he was trying to decide whether to keep talking. “When I answer people, I can feel the answer before I say it. Like mine. My actual answer. But then another one comes.”

“What do you mean?”

He glanced at her. “When the second sentence comes.” He looked down the hall. “The first one is mine. I think. Then there’s another one, and it feels safer, so I say it too.”

Mara did not answer right away.

The hallway around them kept moving. Lockers opened and closed. Someone laughed too loudly near the stairs. A teacher told three boys to stop hitting each other with rolled-up Guide30 programs. It was strange how normal everything could look while Cam stood beside her saying something that made Mara’s skin feel cold.

“Does it sound like you?” she asked.

“That’s the worst part.” Cam’s voice stayed low. “It almost does. It uses words I would use. It just makes them smoother.”

Mara thought about every time Cam had answered too calmly. Every time his face had gone blank for half a second before he said the right thing. The safe thing.

“Did you tell your mom?” she asked.

Cam shook his head. “She thinks the support plan is working.”

“What about Eli?”

Cam’s mouth twitched a little at the name. “Grandpa Eli thinks a toaster is suspicious if it has more than two buttons.”

“Then he’ll probably understand.”

This time Cam almost smiled.

Mara looked at his wrist. “Can you message him?”

“I’m supposed to check in with my mom after school.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

Cam looked at her then. The old Cam was still in there, somewhere under the careful face. She could see him getting annoyed at her, which was honestly a relief.

“You’re bossy now,” he said.

“I’ve always been bossy. You were just too busy being mysterious to notice.”

He breathed out through his nose, almost a laugh. Then he opened a message screen and typed with his thumb. Mara did not read over his shoulder. She looked at the trophy case instead and pretended the faded soccer ribbons were interesting.

A few seconds later, Cam lowered his hand.

“I told him I need to talk before tomorrow,” he said.

“Good.”

“You say that like you fixed something.”

“I didn’t.”

“No,” Cam said. “But you interrupted it.”

Mara looked at him.

“The second sentence,” he said. “It was trying to tell me this was unnecessary.”

Mara did not like that at all.

Before she could answer, the warning bell rang. Students around them groaned and started moving faster.

Cam stepped back. “I should go.”

“Cam?”

He paused.

“If the second sentence comes again, maybe don’t say it right away.”

“That’s your whole plan?”

“It’s not a plan. It’s barely advice.”

“Sounds about right.”

He walked away, and Mara stayed by the trophy case a moment longer than she needed to.

At lunch, everyone talked about the celebration. It was impossible not to. Someone had gotten a leaked menu from the food vendors. Someone else claimed the drones were going to form a giant moving face of Dr. Cole, which Connor said would cause him to leave the city forever. Nessa said that was obviously fake because the drone team had better taste than that.

“You know that for sure?” Connor asked.

“Yes.”

“Because your cousin told you?”

Nessa gave him a look. “Because it would be weird.”

“Many things are weird and still happening.”

June picked at her lunch and asked what time everyone was getting there. Nessa opened her event plan before June had even finished the question.

“The Guide says we leave at three forty-two,” she said. “South entrance, section B. It’ll update if transit changes.”

Connor nodded. “Mine says I should get there early enough to find snacks.”

June looked at him. “Your Guide says that?”

“No. My stomach does.”

She found her after school near the music wing.

Lila came out carrying her performance folder against her chest. Her hair was half pulled back from rehearsal, and her cheeks were pink like she had been running even though she had probably just been singing.

“Mara,” she said, sounding surprised and pleased before she could hide either one.

“Hey.”

For a second they just stood there, which used to never happen. Before everything got weird, there had never been empty space between them. They would have filled it with homework complaints or jokes or Lila telling Mara something she had forgotten to tell her earlier even though she claimed it was important.

Now they had to decide where to start.

Lila shifted the folder in her arms. “Tomorrow is going to be so big.”

“Yeah. It seems like it.”

“We got to see part of the stage layout today. Not all of it, because they said some things are supposed to be a surprise, but the screens are huge. Like, huge huge.”

Mara smiled. “That is a very exact measurement.”

“You know what I mean.”

“I do.”

Lila looked down at the folder, then back up. “I’m not even the main soloist. It’s more like I start one section, and then other voices come in, and then the whole thing builds. But still.” She tried not to smile and failed. “I get to start it.”

“That’s really cool, Lila.”

Lila’s smile changed. It got smaller, but more real.

“Thanks,” she said.

Mara meant it. That surprised her a little. She could feel all the other things too, the knot about Guide and the worry about Monday and the weirdness between them, but underneath that, she was glad for Lila. Lila loved singing. She loved being good at something. She loved the kind of moment where people turned and listened.

“Are you coming?” Lila asked.

The question came out too fast, like she had been trying not to ask it.

Mara looked at her. “Yeah.”

“With your family?”

“And Connor, apparently.”

Lila smiled. “Of course Connor.”

“He invited himself into our section. I’m not sure if he has an actual ticket.”

“I’m glad you’ll be there,” Lila said.

Mara looked at the floor for a second. “Me too.”

There were more things they could have said. Bigger things. Sorry things. But the hallway was full of students and instrument cases, and the band director was calling for someone to come back for a missing jacket, and maybe some conversations needed more space than a school hallway could give.

Lila twisted the end of her jacket sleeve around one finger. “I have to go. My mom is making me rest my voice tonight like I’m a professional opera singer.”

“That sounds annoying.”

“It is,” Lila said, but she looked happy about it.

Mara watched her leave, then headed toward the front entrance.

Dad picked her up instead of letting her take transit. He did not explain why right away. That was usually how Mara knew something had happened. Dad was not bad at serious conversations, exactly. He just treated them like heavy boxes he had to find the right grip for before lifting.

They were halfway home before Dad said, “I received your support record.”

Mara turned from the window. “You did?”

“Yes.”

“All of it?”

“I think so.”

“What did it say?”

Dad kept his eyes on the road. “It made you sound like a problem.”

Mara’s stomach dropped.

The record would have everything in it. The dismissed prompts. The route changes. The day she stopped for Ava near the curb. The times she went to the shop. The Applied Response notes. Maybe even the parts where she had written too honestly during reflection checks.

“So you’re mad?” she asked.

“At you?” Dad looked over, surprised. “No.”

Mara watched his face carefully. “Then at what?”

“At the way they wrote it,” he said.

She looked back out the window.

Dad’s voice stayed calm, but she could hear something underneath it. “Helping Ava was listed as a support disruption. Visiting Eli’s shop was listed as outside influence. Asking for more time before recalibration was listed as avoidance.”

Mara pressed her thumb into the seam of her backpack strap.

“That’s what I was afraid of,” she said.

Dad nodded once. “Me too.”

Mara looked back out the window. The city was already filling with people arriving for the weekend. Street crews were setting up extra railings near the transit stops. Guide30 flags hung from light poles, snapping in the wind.

Dad said, “Your mom and I should have asked for it sooner.”

Mara did not know what to do with that.

“We trusted the summaries,” he continued. “The parent updates. The progress language. It all sounded…” He searched for the word. “Responsible.”

“It always does,” Mara said.

Dad nodded once. “Yes. It does.”

They drove another block before Mara asked, “What happens now?”

“We keep asking questions.”

“That’s not really an answer.”

“It is the one I have today.”

Mara leaned her head against the window. Normally she would have hated that answer. Today she liked that he did not pretend to have more than he did.

At home, Mom had printed nothing, because nobody printed anything anymore unless they were Grandpa Frank. Instead, she had three screens open at the kitchen table and a look on her face that made Mara set her backpack down quietly.

“I’m not going to make you go through all of this tonight,” Mom said before Mara could ask. “Tomorrow is already a lot.”

“Okay.”

“But I want you to know we saw it.”

Mara stood near the table. “The record?”

Mom nodded. “And we believe you.”

For some reason, that made Mara feel like crying, which was ridiculous because she had not cried when she got the first recalibration notice or when the Applied Response teacher treated her like a problem or when Cam said the second sentence felt safer.

Mom must have noticed because she pushed back her chair, but Mara shook her head quickly.

“I’m fine.”

Mom gave her a look.

“I’m not fine,” Mara corrected. “But not in a needing-a-hug-right-now way.”

Mom sat back down. “Understood.”

Dad came in behind Mara and set his keys on the counter. “Grandpa Frank says we are still required to bring the paper map tomorrow.”

Mom closed her eyes. “Of course he does.”

“He says if the city wants everyone in one place, at least one person should know how to get out without waiting for instructions.”

Mara looked at Dad. “He said that?”

“Pretty much.”

“What did he actually say?”

Dad opened the fridge. “He said, ‘I’m bringing the map.’”

Mara smiled despite herself.

That night, the city outside Mara’s window did not get quiet. Not all the way. She could hear extra transit shuttles humming on the main road and people talking as they walked past their building toward hotels or relatives’ apartments or whatever place they were staying before the celebration. Every so often, the sky flashed blue from a rehearsal drone passing over the river district.

Mara sat on her bed with her journal open.

For a while, she did not write anything.

Her Guide pulsed twice with reminders she ignored. One was about recommended rest before a major event. The other was about Monday review preparation. She dismissed both and turned the wrist screen facedown on her blanket.

Then she picked up her pen.

Tomorrow = Guide30.

Which everyone is acting like is a national holiday, a concert, a history project, and a group assignment all at the same time.

Lila wants me there.

Cam does not know which thoughts are his.

Mom and Dad saw the record and did not freak out at me, which was nice and also made me almost cry like a baby, so that was embarrassing.

Grandpa Frank is bringing a paper map because apparently we are crossing the wilderness.

Mara drew a tiny square map with a dotted line, then added a stick figure labeled Grandpa Frank. She gave him a giant backpack and a serious face.

Then she wrote:

Monday is still Monday.

I keep wishing God would tell me exactly what to do before then.

Not in a mysterious way.

In a normal, obvious way.

Like:

MARA, DO THIS.

MARA, DO NOT DO THAT.

MARA, STOP OVERTHINKING AND GO TO SLEEP.

Actually, that last one might be Mom.

She tapped the pen against the paper until small dots appeared in the margin.

I don’t want the Guide deciding what I think.

But sometimes I don’t know how to think without it jumping in.

That’s the worst part.

It is never quiet.

Not really.

Even when no one is talking, the Guide is still there. Reminding. Suggesting. Warning. Fixing. Finishing sentences before I can.

Maybe that is why praying feels hard.

How are you supposed to listen for God when something else is always talking?

Outside, a shuttle hummed past, and blue rehearsal light flashed across her wall.

Mara looked back at the page and added one more line.

God, help me get quiet enough to hear You.

Chapter 24

Guide30

By Saturday afternoon, the city looked like it had been cleaned, polished, and told to smile.

The streets leading toward the river were closed to regular traffic, so families filled the road instead. Blue and gold light moved across the sides of buildings in slow waves. Guide30 messages shimmered above intersections, changing every few seconds.

WELCOME TO GUIDE30.

CELEBRATING THIRTY YEARS OF SUPPORT.

FOLLOW YOUR ASSIGNED ROUTE FOR THE BEST EXPERIENCE.

Mara walked between Mom and Dad while Connor trailed beside them, already complaining that his event route had taken them past two food stands without stopping.

“That feels personal,” he said. “The Guide knows I saw the pretzel cart.”

Dad adjusted the backpack on his shoulder. “We have snacks.”

“Respectfully, family snacks and event snacks are not the same category.”

Mom smiled, but she kept checking the crowd. Mara noticed because Mom was usually good at pretending not to worry. Today her eyes kept moving from the plaza entrances to the transit platforms to the huge stage rising near the river.

Dad carried water bottles, snack packs, and an extra charger in the backpack. Grandpa Frank walked beside him with the paper map folded under one arm. He had already unfolded it twice, even though the Guide route had been impossible to miss. Bright arrows floated at every corner, and the pavement lights pulsed gently in the direction each section was supposed to go.

Connor pointed at the map. “Sir, I need to ask. Is that for emergencies or decoration?”

Grandpa Frank looked at him. “Both, apparently.”

“I respect that.”

Their assigned section was not close enough to the stage to be special, but it was close enough to see without needing the giant screens. That seemed perfect to Mara. She did not want to feel important at Guide30. She wanted to be there for Lila, survive the ceremony, and get one more day between herself and Monday.

Their section opened onto a wide part of the plaza where the river curved behind the stage. The water kept catching the lights and breaking them into shaky pieces. Food carts lined one side, and families stood in neat clusters where their Guide routes had placed them. A few people brought folding seats even though the event guide had recommended standing for “maximum connection visibility.” Grandpa Frank had muttered something about “maximum leg cramps” when that prompt came through.

The stage was bigger than Mara expected. Two screens towered on either side, and a long platform stretched toward the crowd in a shallow curve. Blue and gold panels shifted across the back like moving water. Above it all, drones waited in the afternoon sky, not doing anything yet, just hovering in rows so straight they looked pinned there.

Connor stared up at them. “That is too many flying objects for one celebration.”

“You’re scared of drones?” Mara asked.

“I’m respectful of gravity.”

Before Mara could answer, her Guide pulsed.

SECTION C-14 CONFIRMED.

FAMILY GROUP COMPLETE.

REMAIN WITH ASSIGNED PARTY.

A smaller line appeared underneath.

MONDAY REVIEW MATERIALS PENDING ACKNOWLEDGMENT.

Mara dismissed it so fast she barely read the whole thing.

Mom’s expression changed at almost the same moment.

Mara looked at her. “You got one too?”

Mom hesitated, then nodded. “Mine says to review the parent materials before Monday.”

Dad’s jaw tightened.

Grandpa Frank looked from Mom to Mara. “Is it asking or telling?”

“It says recommended,” Mom said.

Grandpa Frank grunted. “That usually means telling with nicer shoes.”

Connor leaned toward Mara. “Your grandpa is terrifying, but in a library way.”

“A library way? .”

“He has a paper map and opinions. He belongs to everyone now.”

Mara almost laughed, but Mom was still looking at the place where the prompt had been. Then Mom blinked it away and reached for Mara’s hand.

“I dismissed it,” Mom said.

Mara nodded. She did not trust herself to say anything.

The plaza kept filling. People greeted friends from other sections by waving across the barriers, even though the Guide kept reminding everyone to remain in assigned areas. Younger kids chased little dots of light that danced across the pavement before their parents pulled them back. A group of high school students took pictures with the stage behind them, adjusting their smiles every time the screens changed.

Mara scanned the stage area until she found the student performers.

Lila stood near the front with the other singers, wearing her performance jacket and black pants. Her hair was pulled back, and even from a distance Mara could tell she was trying to stand exactly the way she had been told to stand. She kept glancing out at the crowd, then back toward the stage director, then out again.

“She’s looking for you,” Connor said.

“No, she’s not.”

“Yes, she is. That is definitely the face of someone trying to find one specific person while pretending to be chill.”

Mara looked back at the stage.

Lila’s eyes moved over the crowd and finally landed on their section.

Mara lifted one hand.

Not huge. Just enough.

Lila’s whole face changed. She smiled so quickly that Mara knew she had been nervous about whether Mara would actually come.

Connor made a small noise. “Aw. Friendship repair. Disgusting.”

“Stop.”

“I support it. I’m just emotionally allergic.”

Lila gave one more quick smile before a stage worker directed the performers to move into their opening places.

Mara kept watching her for a second longer.

She was glad she had come. Even with everything else, she was glad.

A few minutes before the program started, Cam arrived with his mother. They were two sections over, close enough that Mara could see them but not close enough to talk unless she wanted to climb over several rows of annoyed families.

Grandpa Eli was not with them.

That bothered Mara right away.

Cam’s mother looked carefully dressed and carefully calm, the way people looked when they had spent extra time trying not to seem nervous. She kept one hand near Cam’s shoulder without actually touching him. Cam stood very still beside her.

Then he looked over and saw Mara.

For a second, his face changed. Not into a smile exactly. More like he had found a window in a room that was too crowded.

Mara raised her hand a little.

Cam gave the smallest nod.

Then his eyes flicked toward something only he could see, and his face smoothed out again.

The opening announcement rolled across the public displays, and a voice filled the plaza.

“Welcome, citizens, families, students, and friends, to Guide30.”

The crowd cheered so loudly that birds lifted from the far side of the river.

Mara cheered too. Not loudly, but enough to blend in.

The program began with music from the city youth orchestra. Then a children’s choir sang a song Mara had heard in three different school assemblies. Connor whispered that the song should legally retire after this, and Mom gave him the kind of look that said she was trying not to smile.

After that came the stories.

The screens showed people from all over the city talking about what the Guide had done for them. A man stood in front of a fire station and said his Guide had noticed the signs of a heart attack before he did. A woman with silver hair touched a photograph of her family and explained that memory support helped her keep names and faces connected. A college student described how panic used to keep him from leaving his apartment, until his Guide helped him practice one small trip at a time.

The crowd listened quietly.

Mara did too.

She thought about Tobias standing in the cafeteria while Nessa explained that recalibration had helped him. She thought about how angry Nessa had been, not because she loved rules, but because she loved her brother.

That was the hard part. Guide had helped people. Real people. It had stepped in during emergencies and filled gaps families could not fill by themselves. It had made life feel possible for people who had been stuck.

Mara could not hate it cleanly.

She wished she could. It would have made everything easier.

The screens changed again, and Dr. Adrian Cole appeared above the stage. The applause rose before he even spoke. He stood on a raised platform near the center, dressed simply, with no flashing lights around him. That almost made him look more important.

“Thirty years ago,” he began, “we asked a question. What if no one had to face uncertainty alone?”

The plaza quieted.

Mara felt Mom’s hand tighten around hers.

“What if guidance could arrive before fear overwhelmed us?” Dr. Cole continued. “What if help could reach the lost, the hurting, the anxious, and the afraid before the moment became too heavy to carry alone? What if connection could be woven into the everyday life of a city?”

His voice was calm and warm. Not like a politician. More like a teacher who never had to raise his voice because everyone already wanted to listen.

Mara understood why people trusted him.

“The Guide has never been about replacing human choice,” he said. “It has been about supporting it. Helping each person make safer choices, calmer choices, more connected choices. It reminds us that none of us was meant to move through life unsupported.”

People around Mara nodded. A woman in front of them wiped under one eye.

Mara looked toward Cam.

He was watching the screen with his hands closed at his sides. His mother was crying quietly.

Dr. Cole turned slightly toward the stage. “Tonight, we celebrate thirty years of guidance. And in a few moments, we will enter the shared connection sequence, a citywide demonstration of what happens when millions of individual paths move together without anyone being lost.”

The crowd erupted.

Connor leaned close to Mara. “I don’t know why, but that sentence made me want to clap and hide under a table.”

“Same,” Mara said.

Mom gave Mara’s hand one more squeeze, then let go as everyone around them shifted to see the stage.

The school performers moved into place. The orchestra settled. The singers formed two lines near the front, and Lila stood a few steps ahead of them at the main microphone.

Mara’s Guide pulsed softly in her vision.

CONNECTION SEQUENCE BEGINNING.

PLEASE REMAIN IN YOUR ASSIGNED AREA.

FOLLOW GUIDANCE PROMPTS FOR UNIFIED EXPERIENCE.

Mara dismissed the prompt.

It returned in the corner of her vision, smaller this time.

PARTICIPATION RECOMMENDED.

She ignored it.

The first notes of the song began.

The drums were low and steady. Strings came in underneath, soft at first, then fuller. Above the stage, the drones moved out of their straight rows and formed a wide circle over the river. The circle widened, broke into smaller rings, then reconnected into a glowing path that seemed to stretch from the stage across the sky.

The crowd grew quiet without being told.

Lila looked small on the huge stage until the gold cue light reached her.

Then she stepped forward.

Mara held her breath.

Lila opened her mouth and sang.

Her voice carried clear and bright across the plaza. It was stronger than it had sounded in the auditorium, like the big stage had not swallowed her up but made more room for her. People near Mara lifted their heads. Someone behind them whispered, “That’s one of the students?”

Even Connor stopped moving.

Lila kept her eyes forward, but Mara could tell she knew the cue had gone right. She knew she sounded good. She looked proud, and for once Mara did not feel weird about being proud of her too.

The screens shifted with the music. Blue lights moved through the crowd sections like ripples in water. Each area glowed for a few seconds, then passed the light to the next. The drones above the river formed a school, then a hospital, then thousands of tiny points that gathered into one bright circle.

For a moment, the whole city seemed to be holding the same breath.

Then something fell out of the sky.

At first Mara thought it was a piece of light.

A spark from one of the drones. A planned effect. Something designed to look dangerous but land exactly where it was supposed to.

Then it dropped too fast.

A drone spun sideways above the river, its blue light blinking wrong. It clipped another drone with a sharp crack and tumbled down toward the water.

Lila was still singing when it hit.

The splash rose white against the gold lights along the river wall.

For half a second, the plaza stayed quiet, like everyone was waiting for the Guide to tell them whether they had just seen what they thought they saw.

Chapter 25

The first drone hit the river so hard that water jumped white against the gold lights.

For half a second, nobody screamed.

Mara thought that was the strangest part later. Not the drone falling. Not the sound. Not the way the music bent around it like the whole song had tripped. It was the silence after. Thousands of people standing in the plaza, heads tilted back, faces glowing blue and gold, all waiting for the Guide to tell them whether they were supposed to be afraid.

Then another drone spun sideways above the stage.

This one did not fall straight down. It clipped the edge of a light tower with a sharp metal crack, bounced once, and dropped behind the stage curtains. A shower of sparks flashed bright enough to make everyone gasp at the same time.

The music stretched.

Lila’s note pulled too long, too thin, until it stopped sounding like singing and started sounding like something tearing. The backing track jumped ahead, snapped backward, then cut out completely. One trumpet kept going for two confused notes. A drum hit once, loud and lonely, then stopped too.

The giant screens behind the stage flickered from Lila’s face to the Guide30 logo to a blank blue field.

All around the plaza, section lights flashed too quickly. Blue. Gold. White. Blue again. The lights were supposed to move in waves, passing from one section to the next like the whole city was connected by one heartbeat. Instead, they jerked across the crowd in broken pieces. One section lit up, then went dark. Another flashed three times and stayed white. Near the back, a whole row of lights died at once.

Mara’s Guide opened a full-center notification.

SYNCHRONIZATION DELAY DETECTED.

REMAIN IN ASSIGNED AREA.

AWAIT: UPDATED INSTRUCTION.

Mom grabbed Mara’s hand.

“What’s happening?” Connor asked, but nobody answered because nobody knew.

Above them, the drones were no longer forming circles. They were trying to. Mara could see that much. A few still moved in their perfect programmed lines, blinking blue and gold, trying to pull the broken shape back together. But others drifted out of formation. One spun in place. Another tilted hard toward the river wall. A third dropped low enough that people in the front rows ducked and covered their heads.

That was when the crowd changed.

Not all at once. Not like a wave in a movie.

It started in pieces.

A woman near Mara stood up too quickly and knocked into the man behind her. Someone shouted, “Move back!” Someone else shouted, “Stay down!” A little boy began crying because his mother had gripped his shoulder too hard. People near the south aisle pushed toward the exit, then stopped because another group was pushing back the other way.

“My route disappeared,” someone said behind Mara.

“Mine says stay here.”

“Mine says north gate.”

“There is no north gate.”

“Yes, there is.”

“No, that’s parking.”

“Where did we park?”

The questions started multiplying. They came from everywhere, rising over the dead music and the broken drone buzz. People asked where the exits were, where their children were, where the family pickup points had moved, whether the river path was closed, whether the parking decks were locked, whether the west stairs were still open. Most of them were not asking another person exactly. They were saying the questions out loud because the place where the answer usually appeared had gone blank or started lying.

Mara’s route line flickered in her vision.

For one second, it pointed left.

Then right.

Then it vanished.

A new message replaced it.

EMERGENCY ROUTING IN PROGRESS.

PLEASE REMAIN CALM.

REMAIN IN PLACE.

The words were clean and steady.

Nothing else was.

On stage, the student performers had frozen in their lines. Some of them still held their microphones near their mouths. Others had turned toward the band director, who was waving both arms and shouting something Mara could not hear. The choir kids in the back row started moving first, bunching toward the side stairs. One of the boys stepped on the hem of another singer’s pants and almost fell. A girl grabbed his sleeve and yanked him upright.

Lila was still at the front microphone.

She was not singing anymore.

Her face had gone white under the stage lights. One hand was pressed to her ear, like her Guide was shouting inside her head. She looked toward the band director, then toward the side stairs, then back at the crowd. She seemed smaller suddenly, swallowed by the huge stage and the blank blue screens behind her.

Another drone hit somewhere behind the stage with a pop like a firecracker.

The performers flinched.

That was enough.

The neat rows broke.

Kids started rushing toward the stairs, because standing still had become impossible. A stage tech tried to hold out his arms and slow them down. Another adult shouted for everyone to stay on the stage until emergency clearance came through. Nobody could tell which adult was right, and the students were scared enough to move anyway.

Lila turned from the microphone.

A taller girl bumped into her shoulder.

Lila stumbled but caught herself on the microphone stand.

Then two younger singers pushed past, crying, trying to get to the side stairs. One of them tripped and grabbed the person nearest to her, and the whole cluster shifted hard toward the front edge of the platform.

Lila was caught in it.

Mara saw her reach for the railing.

She missed.

For one awful second, Lila’s arms windmilled in the broken stage light, her performance jacket bright blue against all the gold and white flashing behind her. Then someone shoved past her, not on purpose, just panic and elbows and too many bodies trying to fit through one narrow space.

Lila slipped sideways off the low stage edge.

She hit the stairs first, then the ground beside one of the big front speakers.

Her microphone rolled across the platform and stopped with a hard squeal of feedback.

The sound ripped through the plaza.

People covered their ears. Tobias, two rows ahead, dropped into a crouch with both hands clamped over his head. Nessa shoved past two chairs to get to him, shouting his name over and over. She wrapped both arms around him from behind and pressed her forehead to his shoulder like she could hold him inside the world by force.

Mara barely saw it.

She was looking for Lila.

Lila was on the ground near the speaker, half-hidden behind a hanging cable and the edge of the stage stairs. One hand moved against the floor. Her other arm was curled tight across her chest.

She did not get up immediately.

Mara’s Guide filled her vision.

DO NOT APPROACH STAGE.

AWAIT AUTHORIZED EMERGENCY RESPONSE.

DO NOT APPROACH STAGE.

The words were so large she had to blink around them to see.

Two event workers moved toward Lila. One made it three steps before the crowd surged against the front barrier and he had to turn back to keep people from pressing into the stage. The other stopped near the stairs, staring at something in his own vision. His mouth moved like he was reading instructions. Then he looked at Lila. Then back at whatever the Guide was telling him.

He did not move.

Around Mara, people waited and pushed at the same time. Some tried to stay in their assigned places, but others were already climbing over rows. A woman shouted for her daughter. A man held his phone up like a flashlight even though it was afternoon. Someone stepped on Mara’s shoe and did not notice.

The Guide was telling everyone to wait.

The Guide was not helping Lila.

Mara thought of Ava by the curb, turning in a circle with her purple backpack because her route had disappeared and nobody else had looked up long enough to see her.

She thought of Cam at lunch, trying to find the sentence that belonged to him before the safer one came.

She thought of the answer she had typed in Applied Response, the one Mr. Halden had not liked.

Sometimes people need to look around and help whoever is right in front of them.

Mara moved before she had time to decide whether moving was brave or stupid. One second Mom’s hand was wrapped around hers, and the next Mara was slipping out of it, pushing sideways through the row as the crowd shifted hard around her. Someone’s elbow knocked her shoulder. A bag strap caught on her sleeve. Chairs scraped and tipped as people tried to stand, sit, turn, obey, leave, and wait all at the same time.

Behind her, Mom shouted her name, and Dad shouted it too, but their voices were swallowed almost instantly by the rising noise of the plaza: crying kids, arguing adults, the broken buzz of drones overhead, the Guide’s calm emergency tone pulsing through everyone’s heads. Mara looked back once and saw only pieces of her family through the moving crowd: Mom’s arm reaching for her, Dad trying to step over a row of chairs, Grandpa Frank blocking two people from shoving toward the jammed exit with the paper map crushed in his fist.

Then the crowd closed between them.

Mara was alone in the middle of bodies and flashing light, with Lila still on the ground near the stage and the Guide ordering her to return to a place she could no longer even see. She ducked under a half-lifted barrier and kept moving. The ground was slick with spilled drinks, and a paper food tray stuck to her shoe for three steps before tearing loose. Someone grabbed at her sleeve, maybe to stop her, maybe just because they were falling, but Mara pulled free and pushed toward the side of the stage.

Connor appeared beside her out of nowhere, breathing hard and carrying one strap of his backpack in his fist like he had forgotten the rest of the bag was still attached to him.

“I don’t know why we’re running,” he said, “but I hate being left out.”

“Lila fell.”

His face changed so fast it almost looked like the lights had gone out behind it.

“Oh.”

They reached the side barrier, where a security volunteer stood with both hands on the metal latch, staring into space. His Guide must have been open. His eyes had that unfocused look, the one everyone got when they were reading something only they could see and forgetting the real world was still in front of them.

By the time Mara and Connor reached the side barrier, Mara’s lungs burned and her shoes were sticky from whatever had spilled across the plaza floor. A security volunteer stood at the opening with both hands on the metal latch, but he was not opening it. He was staring past them and slightly upward, eyes unfocused in the way people looked when the Guide had filled their vision. The barrier was only waist-high, something meant to organize lines on a normal day, but now it felt enormous because he was standing there waiting for permission while Lila was on the ground ten yards away.

“We need to get to the stage,” Mara said.

The volunteer blinked, but not really at her. “No one is cleared.”

He sounded young. Too young to be in charge of anything this loud. His voice shook at the edges, and for a second Mara could see that he was scared too. Not because he did not care. Because he cared and did not know which instruction he was allowed to ignore.

Connor leaned around Mara and pointed toward the stage. “A performer is down. Right there.”

“I know, but emergency routing says—”

“The emergency is right there,” Mara said.

That got through. The volunteer looked at her then, not at her support status, not at an alert, not at the red warning Mara could still feel flashing in the corner of her vision. At her. Then his eyes shifted past her to the stage, where Lila was trying to push herself up with one arm and failing. His mouth opened a little, like the words from the Guide had finally stopped making sense beside what he could see with his own eyes.
