He unlatched the barrier.

“Go,” he said.

Mara and Connor slipped through together, but Connor had to stop almost immediately when a group of younger performers came rushing down from the side platform, crying and half-falling over one another. He grabbed the edge of the barrier and shoved it wider so they could get through without tipping into the crowd. Mara turned back just long enough to see him plant both feet and hold it open with both hands, his face pale but determined.

“Go!” Connor yelled. “I’ve got this!”

Mara ran.

The side stairs were only a few yards away now, but the space between the barrier and the stage was crowded with cables, equipment cases, and people who were trying to move in opposite directions. A stage light swung overhead, throwing blue-white flashes across the ground. Mara dodged around a toppled speaker stand and nearly ran into an adult in a headset who was shouting into the air instead of at anyone real.

Then she saw Cam.

He was already at the base of the stairs.

For a second, Mara could not understand how he had gotten there. The last time she had seen him, he had been somewhere in the crowd with his mother, farther back and to the left. Now he was gripping the stair railing with one hand and pressing the other hand hard against the side of his head, like he was trying to hold himself together. His mother was a few steps behind him, calling his name, but the crowd kept pushing between them.

“Cam, wait!” she shouted.

Cam did not turn around.

His face was pale. His jaw was tight. The fight in him was not big or dramatic. It was small and painful and all over his body: in the way his fingers dug into the railing, in the way his shoulders shook once and then locked, in the way he stared at the stairs like there were two different paths in front of him and only one of them belonged to him.

Mara reached him, out of breath. “Come on.”

Cam looked at her, and for one awful second his eyes were not quite focused on her. “Go back,” he said.

Mara stopped.

It did not sound robotic. That was what made it worse. It sounded like Cam, scared and strained and trying hard to say the safest thing. Then his face twisted, and he squeezed his eyes shut, hitting the railing once with the side of his fist.

“No,” he said through his teeth. “Sorry. That was the second sentence.”

Mara stared at him.

Cam opened his eyes. They were wet, but this time they found her.

“The first one was, help her.”

Then he pulled himself up the stairs.

Mara followed.

Lila was behind the front speaker, curled on her side with one hand wrapped around her ankle. Her performance jacket was dusty at the sleeve, and one side of her hair had come loose from the pins that had held it perfectly in place ten minutes ago. Her microphone had rolled a few feet away and lay on its side, still live enough to send little scratches of sound into the air every time someone stepped too close to the cord. When Mara dropped beside her, Lila looked up with wide, wet eyes like she had not been sure anyone would find her there.

“You found me,” Lila said.

Mara had a hundred things in her head and none of them came out right. “You fell.”

For a second Lila stared at her, and then one shaky breath came out of her that was almost a laugh and almost a sob. It was such a normal Lila sound, even in the middle of all of this, that Mara had to press her hand hard against the floor to keep herself steady.

Cam knelt on Lila’s other side. He was breathing too hard, and his eyes kept shifting like alerts were still flashing across his vision faster than he could dismiss them, but he stayed where he was. One hand hovered near Lila’s shoulder without touching her, like he wanted to help but was afraid of doing the wrong thing.

“Can you move?” Mara asked.

“My ankle hurts,” Lila said, and her voice broke on the last word. “Really bad. I don’t think it’s broken. I don’t know. I don’t know.”

“Okay,” Mara said, even though nothing about this felt okay. She glanced down at Lila’s foot, then immediately wished she had not because she had no idea what she was looking for. “Don’t try to stand up.”

Lila grabbed Mara’s sleeve. Her fingers were cold and tight, twisting the fabric like it was the only solid thing left on the stage.

“Mara, I’m scared.”

Mara looked at her best friend’s face, at the messy hair and smudged stage makeup and tears caught under her eyes. Around them, everything was still too loud: the speakers popping, the crowd shouting, the drones buzzing wrong above the river, the Guide flashing warnings Mara could barely see because her own eyes were filling too.

She wanted an instruction.

She wanted a grown-up.

She wanted the right answer to appear before she had to do anything else.

Instead, Mara bent closer and held Lila’s hand with both of hers.

“God,” she whispered, so quietly only Lila could hear. “Please help her. Please help Lila. Please be here with us.”

Nothing outside changed.

The drones kept blinking. The crowd kept shifting. Lila’s ankle still hurt. The Guide kept flashing warnings in the corner of Mara’s vision.

But something changed inside Mara.

Not a voice. Not a bright answer. Not words she could repeat later and prove to anyone.

Just quiet.

A small, steady quiet that did not belong to the stage or the crowd or the Guide. It came underneath the fear, not pushing it away all at once, but making room around it. Mara could still hear everything, but it did not feel like everything was inside her anymore. The fear was still there. It just was not the only thing there.

Lila’s hand squeezed hers.

Mara took one breath.

Then another.

“I’m here,” Mara said, and this time her voice sounded more like her own. “God’s here too. Don’t try to stand. Just stay with me.”

Lila’s face crumpled like she was going to cry harder, but then she held onto Mara’s hand with both of hers and tried to breathe. The first breath caught in her throat. The second came out shaky and uneven. By the third, her shoulders had lowered a little from where they had been pulled tight near her ears. She was still scared. Mara could feel it in the way Lila’s fingers kept squeezing and releasing hers, like she needed to keep checking that Mara was really there. But the wild look in her eyes softened enough for her to focus on Mara’s face instead of the broken lights above them or the crowd beyond the stage.

“I’m trying,” Lila whispered.

“I know,” Mara said. “You’re doing it.”

Cam was still kneeling on the other side of her, pale and shaking, one hand pressed against the stage floor. Mara looked past him and saw the medical volunteer fighting through the side stairs with a red emergency pack bouncing against her hip.

The next thing was not everything.

It was just one thing.

“Mara,” Lila whispered.

“I see help,” Mara said. “They’re coming.”

She lifted one arm and waved hard. “Over here!”

Mom appeared at the edge of the stage stairs with Dad right behind her. Mom’s face looked the way Mara had never wanted to see it look: scared and relieved and angry and grateful all at the same time. She did not climb onto the stage because the medical volunteer had already lifted one hand to keep extra people back, but Mara could tell it cost her something to stay where she was.

“I’m okay,” Mara called.

Mom nodded, but her hand stayed pressed to her chest like she was holding herself in place. Dad stood beside her with one hand on her shoulder, looking from Mara to Lila to the crowd below. His face had gone serious in the way it did when he was trying to solve a problem without showing how scared he was.

The plaza below them was still a mess, but a different kind of mess now. The first panic had burned through and left people standing in clumps, breathing hard, looking around for instructions that were still not coming clearly. A few drones hung frozen above the river in half of a broken shape. Some still blinked red. The giant screens had stopped showing the celebration feed and now displayed one calm blue message.

TEMPORARY INSTABILITY.
PLEASE REMAIN IN PLACE.

People were listening to it too well.

The side aisle below the stage was blocked with people who had stopped moving halfway through moving. Some were trying to make room, some were trying to stay in their assigned spots, and some just looked stuck, staring from the message on the screen to the half-cleared path in front of them. The medical volunteer looked toward the aisle and then back at Lila, frustration flashing across her face before she smoothed it away.

“We need that aisle clear,” she said, mostly to the band director. “We can’t carry her through that.”

The band director shouted down to the security workers, but his voice got swallowed by the crowd. The blue message stayed calm and useless above them. PLEASE REMAIN IN PLACE. It was still telling everyone to do the thing that was keeping Lila trapped on the stage.

Mara looked at the aisle, then at Lila, then at the microphone lying on the floor near her knee.

She did not want to pick it up. That was the truth. Her hands were shaking, and her mouth was dry, and she was suddenly aware of how many people were out there. People from school. Parents. Teachers. Cameras. The entire city, maybe. She was thirteen years old and had no business telling anyone what to do.

But the adults who knew what they were doing could not move Lila until the aisle opened.

And the aisle was not opening.

Mara reached for the microphone.

The microphone was heavier than she expected. It hissed when she lifted it, and a red warning flashed at the edge of her vision.

UNAUTHORIZED BROADCAST.

Mara ignored it. She looked out at the crowd and immediately forgot every single thing she could have said. Thousands of faces looked back at her, scared and confused and waiting. Some people looked annoyed too, like she was one more thing going wrong in a day already full of things going wrong.

Mara looked down at Lila instead.

That helped.

“Lila needs the side aisle cleared,” Mara said.

Her voice echoed across the plaza, uneven and too loud at first. She swallowed and tried again, forcing herself not to sound like she was about to cry. “Please. The side aisle by the stage. Move back so they can carry her through.”

For a second, nothing happened.

Then Grandpa Frank’s voice cut through from below the stage, sharp and clear in a way the Guide had not been all afternoon. “You heard her. Left side back. Right side hold. Let the medical team through.”

Dad moved next, stepping into the open space and motioning people backward with both hands. Connor was suddenly there too, still holding part of a cable he had apparently decided was his responsibility now. The young security volunteer stopped staring at whatever alert was in his vision and started waving people aside. A woman near the front pulled her children back against her legs. A man lifted one of the portable barriers higher so people could pass under it. Someone shouted, “Make room,” and then other people repeated it, louder each time, until the words moved through the crowd faster than the Guide had.

Make room.

Move back.

Clear the aisle.

The aisle opened badly, not in a neat line and not without complaints. Someone tripped over a bag. Someone yelled that their family was still on the other side. One man kept asking if this was the official route until the woman beside him snapped, “It is now.” But the space opened wide enough.

The medical volunteer let out a breath. “Good. Okay. We can move her.”

Cam reached for a speaker cable and lifted it out of the way. His hands were shaking so badly the cable jerked once, but he did not drop it. When his face tightened and his eyes flicked away, Mara knew another prompt had hit him. He closed his eyes for half a second, breathed through his nose, and stayed where he was.

Mara saw it.

So did Mom.

So did Cam’s mother, standing near the bottom of the stairs with one hand over her mouth and tears on her face.

“Ready?” the medical volunteer asked Lila.

“yes,” Lila said immediately.

The volunteer gave her a small tired smile.

They carried Lila carefully down the side steps, moving slow because every bump made her grip the edge of the stretcher and suck in a breath. Mara walked beside her until they reached the bottom, and then Mom caught Mara and pulled her into a hug so tight it hurt.

“I’m okay,” Mara said into Mom’s shoulder.

“I know,” Mom said, but she did not let go. “I know.”

On the main screen, the calm blue message vanished.

For a second, the screen went black, and everyone in the plaza looked up because the whole crowd had learned to be nervous about blank screens. Then the Guide30 logo appeared again, but it was wrong. The gold circle only loaded halfway before breaking apart into scattered lines. A stream of system text flickered underneath it too quickly for Mara to read all of it, but a few words stayed long enough to make the back of her neck prickle.

CITYWIDE SYNCHRONIZATION INTERRUPTED.

PUBLIC ROUTING DELAYED.

PERFORMANCE CUE NETWORK OFFLINE.

GUIDE30 ADAPTIVE UPDATE INCOMPLETE.

The words disappeared almost as quickly as they had appeared, replaced by the same soft blue screen as before, but now the blue did not feel comforting. It felt like someone had covered a broken window with a curtain and expected everyone not to notice the glass on the floor.

Near the stage wing, adults in dark Guide30 jackets were talking over one another. One kept tapping the side of his head, trying to pull up a display that clearly was not loading. Another pointed toward the frozen drones over the river. The whole event had been designed to prove that the Guide could coordinate a city as one living system: every section of the crowd, every stage cue, every route home, every emergency response, every new support adjustment.

The update was supposed to roll out quietly during the final chorus, a seamless Guide30 upgrade for everyone present. No lines. No appointments. No waiting rooms. Just the next version of the Guide arriving with music and lights and applause.

Instead, the music had broken.

The routes had broken.

The drones had fallen.

And when Lila hit the ground, the Guide had told everyone to stay still.

The screen changed again, and Dr. Cole appeared.

He was not standing at the podium anymore. The camera had caught him from the side, too close and at the wrong angle, showing part of the stage wing and two people in headsets behind him. He looked less polished than he had during the speech. His collar was crooked. Sweat shone at his hairline. One hand was pressed flat against the table in front of him like he needed it to stay upright.

Ms. Cole rushed into the edge of the frame.

Mara recognized her immediately, the woman who had asked Mara careful questions and seemed to hear more than Mara had said. Now her calm was gone. Her hair had loosened near her face, and she grabbed Dr. Cole’s arm with both hands.

“Dad,” she said.

The microphone caught that much.

“No.” Ms. Cole shook her head, but she did not let go of his sleeve. She was looking past him toward the plaza, not at Lila exactly, but at the crowd, the frozen drones, the broken route displays, the families still standing where the Guide had told them to stay. Her face had gone tight in the same controlled way it had in the first time Mara had met her, except now there was too much happening for her to hide behind it.

“Dad,” she said, keeping her voice low, “the school systems were tied into this rollout.”

Dr. Cole looked at her.

“If the adaptive update only went through partway, I don’t know what state the students will be in on Monday,” she said. “Some profiles may have accepted the new layer. Some may not have. Some may be caught between versions.”

Behind them, someone off-screen said, “The adaptive layer did not complete.”

Another voice answered, low and urgent. “It crossed into emergency routing before the stabilization check finished. We do not know what else it touched.”

Dr. Cole’s head snapped toward them. “Do not say that on an open feed.”

The person off-screen went quiet.

For a moment, no one on stage seemed to breathe.

Mara did not understand every technical word, but she understood enough. The update had not just been lights and music. It had been meant to reach people. To adjust them. To smooth the city into the next version of itself before anyone could object to how it felt.

Cam’s review.

Mara’s review.

All the quiet little changes the Guide called support.

The same system that had just told everyone to remain in place while Lila lay hurt beside a speaker.

Ms. Cole lowered her voice, but the microphone still caught pieces of it. “You have to pause the reviews.”

Dr. Cole looked at her.

“No,” he said.

It was not loud, but it was sharp enough that Ms. Cole stepped back half an inch.

“Dad.”

“This was a synchronization failure,” he said. “A public systems failure. Not a failure of the Guide.”

People near Mara began whispering. Mom’s arm tightened around her shoulders.

Dr. Cole looked out across the plaza, and for a second Mara thought he might see them. Not as data points. Not as users. As people. Lila on the stretcher. Tobias still pressed against Nessa. Cam standing near the speaker cable, pale and shaking. Parents holding children too tightly. Strangers making an aisle because the Guide had not told them how.

Then his face changed.

Not all the way back into the polished Guide30 face.

Something harder.

“The future does not stop because one system overloaded,” Dr. Cole said. His voice steadied as he spoke, like the words themselves were pulling him back into the version of himself he trusted most. “We built the Guide because human beings need help becoming safer than their fear, stronger than confusion, better than impulse. Today proves we need more integration, not less.”

Ms. Cole stared at him. “People are scared.”

“People have always been scared before progress.”

“That is not the same thing.”

Dr. Cole’s jaw tightened. For one second he looked less like a father and more like the man from the giant banners, the man who had built the thing everyone else lived inside.

Someone off-screen said, carefully, “Dr. Cole, the review system is tied to the same adaptive support network. Until we know what crossed, continuing non-emergency recalibrations is a liability.”

He flinched at that word.

Not danger.

Not harm.

Liability.

That seemed to reach him faster.

Ms. Cole’s grip returned to his sleeve. This time her voice was quieter. “Pause them. Just pause them.”

Dr. Cole looked at her hand on his arm. Then he looked back toward the crowd, toward the broken drones over the river and the aisle opened by ordinary people shouting directions over the Guide’s calm instructions.

For a moment, he seemed trapped between two things: the girl who had called him Dad and the future he had promised everyone he could build.

When he spoke, his voice was lower.

“Pause all non-emergency reviews,” he said. “Temporary hold until the audit is complete.”

Ms. Cole closed her eyes.

But Dr. Cole was not finished.

“And lock the Guide30 update behind internal authorization. No public rollback unless I approve it.”

The headset operator glanced toward him. “Sir, on whose authority?”

Dr. Cole looked straight at him.

“Mine.”

The feed cut.

The plaza went silent in a way that was not like the silence after the drone fell. This one had weight to it. People had heard enough. Maybe not all of it. Maybe not every technical piece. But they had heard pause. They had heard update. They had heard authorization. Parents looked at one another. A few students near the front started whispering. Mom lifted her head from Mara’s shoulder, and Dad turned toward her with his mouth slightly open.

Pause them.

Not cancel.

Not admit everything.

Not fix Cam or Lila’s ankle or Tobias crying against Nessa’s shoulder. Not make the drones rise back into the sky or make the crowd forget how scared they had been.

But pause.

Across the aisle, Cam stood with one hand still resting on the speaker cable. His mother reached him and took both of his hands in hers.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

Cam looked down at their hands like he was not sure what to do with an apology in the middle of all of this. Then he looked over at Mara. His face was pale, his hair was stuck to his forehead, and he looked so tired that she wanted to tell him to sit down before he fell over.

But his smile was crooked.

Small, but his.

“Monday might be illegal,” he said.

Connor, who had somehow ended up with the cable looped over one arm, pointed at him. “There he is.”

Chapter 26

The Day After Guide30

The city was quieter on Sunday.

Not silent. Nothing in the city was ever silent. But quieter. The Guide30 music was gone. The countdown displays had stopped. The drones were docked somewhere out of sight, and most of the blue and gold banners hung limp in the morning rain. The plaza had already been cleaned before sunrise, at least on the official feeds. No overturned chairs. No spilled drinks. No broken drone pieces near the river wall. Just workers in gray jackets folding barriers and carrying away light stands like the whole thing had been an ordinary event that had ended a little badly.

The official feeds called it a “celebration interruption.”

Connor called it “the time Mara briefly became a public address system.”

Mom called it “not funny.”

Then she watched the clip again. The clip had already been shared everywhere. Not the whole thing. Just the part where the microphone caught Mara’s voice. Lila needs the side aisle cleared.

Then people moving.

That was the part everyone kept replaying. The aisle opening before the Guide updated. Adults helping. Students guiding younger kids back. Grandpa Frank pointing with the paper map in his hand like he had been waiting his whole life to direct traffic without permission. A medical volunteer moving once the path was clear.

Some feeds praised it. Some argued about it. Some said it proved the Guide needed stronger emergency control so crowds could not make panicked choices on their own. Others said it proved people had forgotten they were allowed to move without permission.

But by midmorning, the clip of Mara was not the only one being talked about.

Someone had recorded the open-feed moment from the stage wing.

The camera angle was bad. Half of Dr. Cole’s face was cut off. Ms. Cole stood beside him, one hand on his sleeve, looking out toward the plaza. People in headsets moved behind them, voices overlapping. Most of it was hard to hear, but enough had gotten through.

The adaptive layer did not complete.

It crossed into emergency routing before the stabilization check finished.

We do not know what else it touched.

Mom replayed that part once and then froze the screen.

No one said anything for a moment.

Mara sat at the kitchen table in one of Dad’s sweatshirts, eating toast that was not burned. Her whole body felt tired in strange places. Her legs ached from running. Her throat hurt from the microphone. Her head felt full of echoes, like part of her was still standing on the stage waiting for the next drone to fall.

Dad leaned closer to the wall display. “What does adaptive layer mean?”

Mom did not answer right away. Her face had changed. Focused. The kind of focused she got when something that had sounded official yesterday suddenly sounded dangerous today.

Grandpa Frank sat at the end of the table with the Guide30 paper map folded beside him like proof. “It means they were changing something.”

Mara looked up.

Dad turned toward him. “We don’t know that.”

Grandpa tapped one finger against the table. “You don’t call it an update if nothing is being updated.”

Mom opened the parent portal, then the city information feed, then three commentary panels before closing two of them because everyone was talking too fast and saying too little. One panel defended the rollout as a normal Guide30 improvement package, something all attendees had agreed to by entering a fully integrated event space. Another panel said the update was only meant to improve emergency response, performance synchronization, and crowd routing. A third asked why an “adaptive support layer” had been connected to a public celebration at all.

Mara read the headline once and then again, slower the second time, because the words seemed like they should rearrange into something less awful if she stared at them long enough.

DID GUIDE30 ATTENDEES RECEIVE PARTIAL SUPPORT UPDATES WITHOUT INDIVIDUAL CONSENT?

Her toast hovered halfway to her mouth. A minute ago she had been hungry in that tired, hollow way that came after too much crying and not enough sleep. Now the bread felt dry in her fingers, and the butter had gone shiny and cold on top.

“They were going to update everyone there?” she asked.

Dad did not answer right away. He leaned one hand on the back of the kitchen chair and rubbed his thumb along the edge of it, staring at the wall display like he was reading the headline and also trying to read three things underneath it. His mouth opened once, then closed again. Mara could tell he had an adult answer ready, something about terms and event agreements and how they needed more information before assuming anything, but he did not seem able to make himself say it.

Finally he let out a slow breath. “It looks like that may have been the plan.”

Mom’s head turned toward him. “Peter….”

“I’m not saying it was okay,” Dad said quickly. He looked at Mara then, and his face was careful in a way that made her stomach feel worse. “I’m saying that’s what we need to find out. What they pushed. Who approved it. And whether anyone had a real choice.”

Mom’s eyes moved over the screen. “It says the Guide30 upgrade was supposed to roll out during the final chorus to all attendees with active Guide implants.”

Mara stared at her.

The final chorus.

Lila singing.

The drones forming a perfect ring over the river.

Everyone clapping and looking up while something new entered their Guides quietly, beautifully, with music underneath it.

“But they didn’t ask,” Mara said.

Mom looked at Dad.

“They probably counted event attendance as agreement,” Dad said, but he sounded like he hated the words as he said them.

“I didn’t agree to anything.”

“You’re a minor,” Mom said, and her voice had gone flat.

That made it worse somehow.

Mara pushed the toast away. “So who agreed for me?”

No one answered.

The wall display kept talking. A man in a gray suit was saying the Guide30 update had been designed to “enhance public safety through improved predictive support.” A woman beside him argued that the public had known for months that Guide30 included a citywide synchronization demonstration. The man said demonstration did not mean experimentation. The woman said the word experiment was inflammatory. The man said undisclosed adaptive changes were worse than inflammatory.

Mom shut off the wall display.

The kitchen felt too quiet after.

Dad was on the phone with Bayline before noon.

Mom was on the parent portal.

Grandpa Frank unfolded the map again, even though everyone already knew where the plaza had been. He smoothed it with both hands and studied the printed lines like they might explain something the feeds would not.

“Say it again,” Grandpa said.

Mara looked at him. “What?”

“What Cam said.”

Mara stared at her cold toast. “You’ve already heard it.”

“I like that part.”

Mara tried not to smile. “He said Monday might be illegal.”

Grandpa nodded, satisfied. “Good boy.”

Mom gave him a look, but even she could not quite hide her face.

Dad ended his call and came back to the table. “Dr. Voss saw the footage.”

Mara sat up straighter.

“She said the public audit pause should include all pending non-emergency recalibration reviews, especially if the support network was connected to the Guide30 update.”

Mom looked up from the portal. “Already got it.”

She turned the tablet.

Mara leaned over to read.

PENDING WELLNESS RECALIBRATION RECOMMENDATION
STUDENT: MARA VALE
STATUS: TEMPORARILY PAUSED PENDING GUIDE30 SYSTEM AUDIT

Mara read it twice before she believed it.

Paused.

Not gone.

Not canceled.

But paused.

The Monday that had been standing behind Guide30 like a locked door was suddenly not locked anymore. It was still there somewhere, but farther away, and people were standing between her and it now.

Mom’s eyes were wet.

Dad put one hand on Mara’s shoulder.

Mara did not say anything because if she did, she might cry, and she was too tired to start.

The doorbell rang just after lunch.

Mom checked through the peephole and opened the door.

Lila stood in the hallway with a walking boot on one foot and her mother beside her. Her eyes were puffy, but her chin was lifted in the determined way Mara knew too well.

“I’m supposed to be resting,” Lila said.

Her mother sighed. “She insisted.”

Mom stepped back to let them in.

Lila moved slowly to the couch while Mara hovered nearby, not sure if she was supposed to help. Lila’s mother and Mom went to the kitchen to talk in low adult voices, and Mara heard the same words keep slipping out between them.

Update.

Consent.

Audit.

Monday.

For a minute, Mara and Lila sat in the living room with the space between them filled by everything they had not fixed.

Finally Lila said, “I watched the clip.”

Mara looked at the floor. “Everyone did.”

“You sounded bossy.”

Mara looked up.

Lila’s mouth curved slightly. “In a good way.”

“I was scared.”

“I know.” Lila looked down at her boot. “I was too.”

Mara sat on the other end of the couch. “Does it hurt?”

“Yeah. But it’s just a sprain. The doctor said I get to be dramatic for at least four days.”

“That sounds like your dream.”

Lila’s face softened. “Maybe before.”

The room got quiet again.

Then Lila said, “Did you know about the update?”

Mara looked at her.

“The Guide30 update,” Lila said. “The one they were going to push during the song.”

“No.”

“Me neither.”

Lila picked at the edge of the couch cushion. Her fingernails were still painted Guide30 blue, chipped at the edges from the fall. “They told us the final chorus would connect everyone. They said the crowd lights and route systems would sync with the performance and that it was going to be beautiful. They did not say it would change anything in us.”

Mara looked toward the dark wall display, where the last frozen headline still seemed to hang in the room even though Mom had shut it off. She kept picturing everyone in the plaza with their faces turned up toward the drones, clapping because they thought they were part of the show. She had been there too. So had Mom and Dad. So had Lila, singing while the update was supposed to slide quietly into every Guide in the crowd like it belonged there.

“Maybe they didn’t think of it like that,” Lila said, but she did not sound like she believed herself.

“That makes it worse,” Mara said.

Lila nodded slowly. “Yeah.”

From the kitchen, Lila’s mother said something in a sharp whisper. Mom answered in the voice she used when she was trying to stay polite and was not enjoying it.

Lila looked toward them, then back at Mara. “My mom is mad.”

“She should be.”

“She keeps saying if they could do it there, what else can they do at school?”

Mara did not answer.

Because that was the question.

Not just what had broken at Guide30.

What had almost worked.

Lila’s hands were folded in her lap, tight enough that her knuckles looked white. “I’m sorry.”

Mara looked at her.

“Not just for reporting you,” Lila said. “For thinking my fear meant I was right. I was scared something bad would happen to you, and I thought that meant I knew what to do.”

Mara did not answer right away. The old version of them would have filled the quiet faster. Lila would have made a face, Mara would have made one back, and the whole thing would have turned into a joke before either of them had to sit inside it for too long. But this quiet stayed, and Mara let it, even though it made her want to pick at the sleeve of Dad’s sweatshirt.

“When they sent me the peer forms this week, I kept thinking about the library,” Lila said. “About how I answered the questions about you and didn’t think about what happened after I told. I just felt better because I thought I had done something.”

Mara looked at Lila’s hands folded tight in her lap, part of her wanted to say it was fine because that would be easier. Part of her wanted to say it was not fine because that would be truer. Neither one felt completely right.

“I know you were trying to help,” Mara said finally.

Lila’s eyes filled, but she nodded like she knew that was not the same as everything being fixed.

“And I’m glad you came over,” Mara added.

Lila wiped under one eye with the side of her finger. “I wasn’t sure you’d want me here.”

“I wasn’t sure either,” Mara said.

Lila gave one tiny laugh and looked down at her boot. “Yeah. I probably wouldn’t have wanted me here either.”

Mara looked toward the kitchen, where their moms were still talking in low, serious voices. Then she looked back at Lila’s boot. “You kept singing.”

Lila breathed out shakily. “Because you said I knew the song.”

“You did.”

“Until I fell.”

She stayed for a little while after that, long enough for the conversation to get easier and for both of them to stop looking so carefully at each other before every sentence. They talked about Lila’s boot, and how June had already offered to decorate it, and how Connor would absolutely try to sign it with something stupid if no one stopped him. Then Lila’s mother came in from the kitchen and told Lila it was time to go.

“You need to go home and rest,” she said.

Lila sighed like rest was a personal attack. “I am literally sitting.”

“And now you can literally sit at home.”

Mara smiled as Lila reached for her crutches, slow and awkward but less shaky than when she had come in.

Later that afternoon, Mom got a call from Cam’s mother.

Mara was on the couch with one foot tucked under her, pretending to read the same paragraph in her history assignment for the fourth time, when Mom’s Guide chimed. She almost ignored it. Everyone had been getting calls and updates all day, and most of them were from people who wanted to talk about Guide30 like it was a news story and not something Mara could still feel in her legs. But then Mom looked at the caller name and sat a little straighter.

“It’s Cam’s mom,” she said.

Mara looked up.

Mom answered then put it on speaker after asking, “Is it okay if Mara hears?”

There was a pause on the other end. Then Cam’s mother said, “Yes. I think she should.”

Her voice sounded tired. Not polite tired. The kind of tired that came from crying, reading too much, and realizing something too late. “I owe you an apology,” she said. “All of you. I thought the review was helping him. And maybe parts of it were. But I didn’t understand what had been added. I didn’t understand how much it watched, or how hard it was making it for him to push back.”

Cam’s mother took a breath that crackled softly through the speaker. “Dr. Voss sent instructions for a guardian request to reduce prompt persistence until the review. I submitted it this morning. Because of the Guide30 audit pause, they approved a temporary adjustment.”

Temporary.

Another soft word.

Mara looked toward Mom, and Mom looked back at her like she hated soft words too, but this one might actually help.

Dad stepped closer to the table. “What did they approve?”

Cam’s mother read from the confirmation, her voice shaking just enough that Mara could hear it.

PROMPT PERSISTENCE REDUCED.
GUARDIAN TRANSPARENCY SET TO STANDARD.
DISMISSAL LIMITS TEMPORARILY SUSPENDED PENDING REVIEW.

For a moment, no one in Mara’s kitchen spoke.

Then Cam’s voice came faintly from somewhere on the other end. “Can I say hi, or is this still an adult guilt call?”

Mara’s mouth twitched before she could stop it.

Cam’s mother gave a tiny, watery laugh. “You can say hi.”

There was a rustle, like the Guide call had been shifted closer to him. Then Cam’s voice came through clearer.

“Hi.”

“Hi,” Mara said.

Another pause.

It was awkward, but not the smooth, empty awkwardness from after his review. This sounded like regular awkward. Real awkward. The kind where Cam was probably standing in his kitchen not knowing what to do with his hands.

Finally he said, “Say something annoying.”

Mara blinked. “What?”

“I want to see if I can be irritated normally.”

Mom closed her eyes like she was trying not to laugh. Dad looked down at the counter.

Connor was not there, which was a tragedy, because he would have loved this.

Mara thought for a second. “Your lunch has been weirdly neat.”

There was a short silence.

Then Cam made a sound of pure disgust. “I know.”

It came out so much like him that Mara burst out laughing.

Then Cam laughed.

That night, she opened Mom’s journal.

She wrote:

Monday is paused.

Lila came over.

Cam’s support layer got turned down.

He laughed like himself.

Not all the way maybe.

But enough to know he is still there.

The Guide30 update was supposed to go to everyone at the event.

They called it an upgrade.

They called it synchronization.

But no one asked me if I wanted it.

Maybe they thought the music and lights made it okay.

Maybe they thought if everyone got it at the same time, no one would notice.

She stopped, pen hovering over the page.

Then she added:

God, thank You for everything.

Chapter 27

On Monday morning, Mara woke up before her alarm.

At first she thought it was raining again, but it was only the building vents clicking on and the soft hum of traffic rising outside her window. Her room was still gray around the edges, not fully morning yet. The sweatshirt she had thrown over her chair the night before hung half off the back, one sleeve almost touching the floor. Her school bag sat open beside her desk because she had packed it, unpacked it, and packed it again before bed, as if putting the same books in a different order could make Monday less strange.

She stayed under the blanket and listened.

No music from the Guide30 feeds.

No countdown reminders.

No cheerful announcement about the city’s next chapter.

Just the ordinary sounds of the apartment waking up: water running somewhere, a cabinet closing downstairs, Dad’s low voice on a call already, Mom moving around the kitchen.

The city had glitched in front of everyone, drones had fallen into the river, and adults on a live feed had accidentally said enough to make half the city start asking questions. But Monday had still arrived with school and breakfast and Mara’s Guide opening her morning schedule in the corner of her vision.

REGULAR SCHOOL DAY.

NO WELLNESS REVIEW SCHEDULED.

She read the second line twice.

NO WELLNESS REVIEW SCHEDULED.

The words did not make everything okay. They were not even exciting words. They looked boring and official, like something stamped on a form by someone who had never been scared of it.

But Mara stared at them anyway.

Paused.

Not canceled. Not gone. Not safe forever.

But not today.

Today, no one was coming to pull her out of class before lunch and tell her she needed help becoming easier to manage.

Mara let herself breathe all the way out.

Then she got up.

Downstairs, Mom was already making eggs. Mara could smell butter and pepper before she reached the kitchen. Dad stood near the counter with his work bag open beside him, putting things in and taking them back out like he had forgotten how packing worked. The kitchen table was still covered in papers from yesterday, but now the piles looked more like piles and less like a paper storm had happened inside their apartment.

There were printed copies of the support record. Notes in Mom’s handwriting. A half-empty mug of coffee. Grandpa Frank’s folded map. A list of questions Dad had written for the district and crossed out and rewritten three times.

Mom looked up when Mara came in.

“No review today,” she said.

Mara nodded and slid into her chair.

Mom set a plate in front of her. “I know paused is not the same as canceled.”

“I know.”

“But paused means time.” Mom pointed the spatula at the stack of papers. “And time means we keep asking questions.”

Dad zipped his work bag with more force than necessary. “I’m calling the district again at nine.”

Mom slid eggs onto Mara’s plate. “Didn’t you already call them twice yesterday?”

“Three times.”

“That makes this feel less like a new plan.”

“It’s a follow-up.”

“It’s been twelve hours.”

Dad picked up his coffee, took one sip, and made a face because it was probably cold. “Then it’s a very timely follow-up.”

Mara looked down at her eggs so he would not see her smile.

Mom set the pan in the sink. “Just eat first.”

Dad glanced at the wall clock, then at his bag, then at the stack of printed notes on the counter, “ok, I will.”

Mara picked up her fork. The eggs were too salty, probably because Mom had been thinking about something else while making them, but Mara ate them anyway. Salty eggs felt better than no breakfast. Salty eggs meant Monday was still happening,

The Guide pulsed softly.

DEPARTURE RECOMMENDED IN EIGHT MINUTES.

Mara almost laughed.

Of course it was still there. It had not disappeared. It had not been destroyed or switched off forever because one event had gone wrong. It still opened schedules. It still sent reminders. It still watched for delays and suggested breathing cycles and told people when to leave for school.

That was almost worse, somehow.

The Guide was still there, acting like Monday was Monday.

But Mara was not sure Monday was the same anymore.

At school, the Guide30 displays were still up, but they looked different now. Not ruined exactly. Just awkward. Like decorations left up after a party where everyone had cried.

The big screen near the entrance still flashed GUIDE30 THANKS YOU in blue and gold, but one corner flickered every few seconds. A few of the light strips along the ceiling were out. The floating celebration graphics had been replaced by plain school notices.

AUDIT IN PROGRESS.

GUIDE BASIC SUPPORT REMAINS ACTIVE.

ROUTE OVERLAYS TEMPORARILY LIMITED.

USE POSTED ROOM LISTS.

Mara stood under the message for a second, reading it twice.

So the Guide was not gone.

It could still send messages. It could still open schedules. It could still remind people to drink water and answer peer messages and leave for class. But for now, at least inside the school, it was not drawing glowing paths through every hallway. It was not automatically rerouting students around each other. It was not telling everyone where to put their feet.

Beside the office door, someone had taped up actual paper room lists.

They were crooked. One corner had already started peeling. The tape was cloudy and wrinkled, and the list for eighth year had a coffee ring near the bottom.

Connor stood in front of it with his hands on his hips, staring like he had discovered ancient writing.

“I never thought I’d say this,” he said, “but I love paper now.”

Mara stopped beside him. “That seems fast.”

“I have been through a lot.”

“It’s been two days.”

“Exactly. I am older now.”

“You said that last week.”

“I age often.”

A sixth-year boy squeezed between them to check the list, then looked embarrassed because he had to lean close and read it with his actual eyes. Mara understood the feeling. Everyone knew how to read, obviously, but reading a wall list felt different than having your room appear automatically in front of you. It required standing there. Looking. Finding your own name. Not knowing for three whole seconds.

A girl nearby lifted her hand halfway, like she wanted to ask the Guide to highlight her room, then seemed to remember it would not. She dropped her hand and looked around to see if anyone noticed.

Mara noticed.

She also pretended she had not.

Lila arrived a few minutes later on crutches with June carrying her bag and Nessa hovering so close she almost tripped all three of them. Lila had a black medical boot on one foot and the expression of someone who had already been asked “does it hurt?” too many times that morning.

Lila arrived a few minutes later on crutches with June carrying her bag and Nessa walking beside them. Her hair was pulled back messily, and one strand kept sticking to her cheek no matter how many times she tried to blow it away. The medical boot made every step slower than she wanted, and Mara could tell from Lila’s face that she hated needing everyone to wait for her.

Mara started toward her before she had time to think too hard about it.

“Nice boot,” she said.

Lila looked down at it. “Thanks. It makes me look very athletic.”

“You did fall off a stage.”

“True. Very advanced sport.”

June adjusted Lila’s bag on her shoulder. “The nurse said no stairs unless absolutely necessary.”

Lila made a face. “The nurse also said I should rest, which is basically impossible in this building.”

Nessa pointed down the hall. “History is upstairs.”

“Of course it is,” Lila said. “Because the building is personally against me.”

Mara laughed, and this time it did not feel careful. It came out the way laughs used to come out before everything had gotten strange.

Lila shifted on her crutches. “I saved you a seat in history.”

Mara looked at her. “You saved me a seat while on crutches?”

“I’m injured, not useless.”

“Good point.”

“June did most of the actual saving.”

June nodded. “I placed the bag with authority.”

“That sounds official,” Mara said.

“It was,” June said.

Nessa looked toward the stairs. “We should go before the hallway gets worse.”

Connor finally turned from the room list. “I can carry something.”

Lila looked at him. “Are you actually being helpful?”

“I’m trying something new.”

Mara took Lila’s water bottle before it slipped out of the side pocket of her bag, and June shifted the heavier strap onto her other shoulder. Nessa walked on Lila’s other side, close enough to help if she needed it.

They started toward history together, slower than usual because of the crutches and because half the school was still stopping under the paper lists to check room numbers. Someone near the stairs asked if room 214 was upstairs, and Lila muttered, “I really hope so, because I am not emotionally ready for extra walking.”

Mara smiled and walked beside her, careful not to bump the crutch on Lila’s left side.

It was not exactly normal.

But it was close.

Cam arrived late, which was the first encouraging sign.

His hair was a mess. His backpack was half open. One shoe was untied. He looked tired, but not smoothed over. Not polished. Not brochure-Cam. Just regular Cam, with dark circles under his eyes and a pencil somehow stuck sideways in the front pocket of his bag.

Connor put one hand dramatically over his heart. “Look at this disaster. Nature is healing.”

Cam gave him a look. “I hate that I missed you saying bizarre things.”

“I do not say bizarre things.”

Mara watched Cam closely.

He noticed immediately. “Stop studying me like I’m a bug.”

“You’re late,” Mara said.

“My mom almost made me leave on time, but then my Guide suggested an optimized morning routine and I dismissed it.”

Mara stared at him.

“You dismissed it?”

Cam nodded, trying not to look pleased and completely failing. “It came back once. Then it stayed gone.”

Mara felt something warm and painful open in her chest. “Are you okay?”

Cam’s smile faded, but not all the way.

He did not answer fast. He did not look away and let the Guide answer for him either. His face did that thing where it looked like he was searching through a messy drawer inside his head.

Finally he said, “Not totally.”

“Me neither,” Mara said.

Connor nodded. “Nobody here is okay. Very inclusive.”

Cam looked at him. “That was almost helpful.”

The first bell rang, and for once Cam did not immediately say they should go. Nobody moved right away, actually. Around them, students kept checking the paper lists and then checking them again, as if the room numbers might change if they stared hard enough.

A teacher stood by the office answering the same question over and over.

“Yes, room 214 is still upstairs.”

“No, the Guide is not drawing hallway routes today.”

“Yes, your schedule is still correct.”

“Yes, you may walk there without a route line.”

That last one made three kids laugh nervously.

Mara looked at the list.

History. Room 214.

“This way,” she said.

She started down the hall.

The others followed.

It was such a small thing. Walking to class from a paper list. No glowing path. No blue line. No soft voice telling them they were correct. Just lockers, scuffed floors, students moving too slowly because everyone had to remember where stairs were.

Mara would not have noticed it a month ago.

Now she did.

In history, Mr. Bennett did not pretend nothing had happened.

That was new.

Usually adults loved pretending. They used words like restore and support and adjustment, and somehow those words were supposed to make everyone forget the part where people had screamed and drones had fallen and the whole city had frozen for half a second because the thing that always told them what to do had gone quiet.

Mr. Bennett stood at the front of the room. The wall display was on, but it was not running the usual Guide lesson feed. Instead of glowing slides and automatic class prompts, it showed one plain message in black letters.

TEMPORARY INSTRUCTION MODE.

MANUAL LESSON DELIVERY IN EFFECT.

On his desk sat a stack of printed lesson pages.

Connor leaned toward Mara. “This day is extremely papery.”

Lila, sitting one seat over, whispered, “Shh.”

Connor whispered back, “I’m processing.”

Mr. Bennett picked up a marker and turned to the board.

“I had a different lesson planned,” he said. “The Guide suggested we continue with our scheduled unit on civic coordination.”

Mr. Bennett wrote three words on the board.

Memory.

Judgment.

Care.

Mara stared at them.

They were not impressive words. They did not glow. They did not come with a progress bar or a district-approved definition. The marker squeaked slightly on the last letter of care.

Mr. Bennett capped the marker and faced the class.

“When systems fail,” he said, “communities do not survive because everyone has perfect instructions. They survive because people remember things, make judgments, and care for whoever is near them.”

A boy near the back raised his hand. “Are we allowed to say the Guide failed?”

Mr. Bennett took a breath.

Mara could tell every student in the room was watching him decide whether to answer like a teacher or like a person.

“Yes,” he said finally. “If something fails, we are allowed to say it failed.”

Lila looked down at her desk.

Nessa’s face tightened.

Connor’s eyebrows went up like he wanted to applaud but knew that would be weird.

Mr. Bennett continued. “We are also allowed to say the Guide has helped people. Both things can be true. That is why we need more than slogans when we talk about it.”

Mara thought about Grandma remembering faces because of the Guide. She thought about Tobias. She thought about Cam going quiet after his review. She thought about Lila’s boot and the microphone in her own hand.

Both things can be true.

She hated that less than she used to.

The rest of class was not exactly a lesson. It was messier than that. Mr. Bennett asked what people remembered from Guide30, and at first no one wanted to talk. Then someone said their little brother got separated for three minutes and still had not stopped talking about it. Someone else said her dad tried to follow three different Guide routes and ended up walking in a circle. Nessa said Tobias could not process the crowd noise after the system cut out, and that without the Guide he felt like the floor had disappeared.

She said it with her chin lifted, like she was daring anyone to argue with her.

No one did.

Mara looked at her.

For the first time, she understood Nessa a little better.

After history, the school day kept going in that strange way days do, even when everyone inside them has changed. The cafeteria still smelled like warmed bread, cleaner spray, and something pretending to be soup. People still complained about homework and took bites of food while talking.

But underneath it all, something had shifted.

Not everyone. Not everything.

Some kids were already joking like Guide30 had been a wild disaster they had survived and now could turn into stories. Some were angry because their parents were angry. Some said the Guide needed better backup systems, not less control. Some said people were overreacting because at least no one had died. Some said that like it solved everything.

A girl at lunch kept opening and closing her messages even though no new messages came in. A boy beside the drink station asked his Guide three times what he should eat, then looked embarrassed when he remembered nutrition recommendations were temporarily limited. Two sixth-years sat across from each other not talking, both staring at the table like conversation had disappeared along with the prompts.

Mara understood that too.

Quiet could feel like being left alone in a room you did not know how to leave.

After school, Mara did not go straight home.

Mom and Dad knew. The Guide knew too, because it opened her usual dismissal reminder twice before she dismissed it and turned toward Merrick Repair & Restoration instead. It did not draw the route for her. Since the audit started, public route overlays had been limited to emergencies and essential transit updates, which meant the streets looked strangely unfinished without the thin blue line hovering at the edge of her vision.

Mara walked anyway.

She knew the way to Eli’s shop.

Mostly.

The bell over Eli’s door gave its uneven little ring when Mara stepped inside.

For a moment, nothing seemed to have changed. The clocks still disagreed with each other. The workbench still had three lamps, two open tool trays, and a cup of cold tea balanced dangerously close to a pile of tiny screws. The air smelled like metal polish, old paper, and soup from somewhere in the back. After the plaza, after the screens, after school hallways full of people pretending they were not listening for updates, the shop felt almost impossible. Too quiet. Too ordinary. Too allowed to stay itself.

Eli looked up from the counter. “You found it.”

Mara smiled a little and came farther inside.

Cam was sitting on the floor near the back shelves with an open box of parts in front of him. He looked up when she came in, and for one second Mara expected the smoother version of him: the careful posture, the too-even expression, the voice that sounded like it had been checked before he used it. But this Cam had a smudge on one wrist, his hair was falling into his eyes, and he was holding two nearly identical screws between his fingers with obvious irritation.

“I hate sorting these,” he said.

Mara felt something in her chest loosen. “Good.”

“That is a mean response.”

“It’s a healthy response.”

Cam looked at Eli. “Is that true?”

Eli did not look up from the tiny gear he was cleaning. “I am not entering that dispute.”

On the front counter, beside the old register, lay a folded newspaper.

Mara noticed the front page picture.

Guide30 filled the front page. Not the official picture with the bright lights and the perfect crowd. This one had been taken from above, probably from one of the emergency drones that had not fallen. Mara was near the stage with the microphone lowered at her side, hair half out of place, shoulders stiff, face pale enough that she wanted to turn the page immediately.

“Oh no,” she said.

Eli followed her gaze. “Ah.”

“Why do you have that?”

“It is a newspaper.”

“I know what it is.”

Mara reached for the paper, already hating it, but Eli placed one hand gently on the corner before she could fold it shut.

“Look at the whole picture,” he said.

That made her pause.

At first, all she saw was herself, which was terrible. Then she saw Dad near the side aisle, one arm out, pointing people away from the blocked stairs. Mom stood at the bottom with Lila, her face turned up toward the stage. Connor was holding a cable out of the way with both hands, his mouth open like he was probably yelling something unnecessary but useful. Nessa had both arms around Tobias near the front row, her head bent close to his. Cam stood beside a speaker, one hand pressed against it for balance, face pale and serious.

And all around them, people were moving.

Not perfectly. Not in one beautiful heroic wave. A woman was pulling her child back from the crowded steps. A man had lifted one of the light barriers and was holding it up while strangers ducked underneath. A teenage girl was pointing toward an open side path. Two older people were helping each other stand. Someone had dropped a bag, and someone else had picked it up.

The bell over the shop door rang behind her.

Mom stepped inside, brushing rain from the sleeves of her coat. She paused when she saw Mara at the counter with the newspaper open in front of her, and for a second she did not say anything. Her eyes moved over the photo the same way Mara’s had, first finding Mara on the stage, then Dad near the aisle, then Lila, then the crowd.

“Dr. Voss moved our call to tonight,” Mom said finally. “Not a full review. Just a first meeting.”

Mara nodded, but she kept one hand on the edge of the newspaper.

Eli folded the paper carefully, lining up the corners like the picture deserved not to be wrinkled. “First meetings are useful,” he said. “As long as no one mistakes them for endings.”

Outside, the streetlights had started to come on, pale against the sidewalk. Mara thanked Eli, then looked toward the back shelves where Cam had been sorting parts earlier. He had already left with his mother, but one of the little trays was still on the floor, half-finished and crooked, which somehow made Mara feel better than if it had been perfectly done.

The district had confirmed receipt of their request for full support records, review delay, and independent oversight. There were still too many soft words. Too many pending timelines. Too many places where the answer was not an answer yet.

That night, after the call with Dr. Voss, Mara opened Mom’s journal again.

The call had not fixed everything. Dr. Voss had kind eyes and a serious voice, but Mara had learned that kind eyes did not always mean simple answers. She had asked a lot of questions. Mom had asked more. Dad had asked the same question three different ways until Dr. Voss finally admitted that “temporary pause” did not mean “permanent removal.”

Still, Dr. Voss had said something Mara wrote down because Mom told her to.

No child should be required to accept additional support layers without understanding what they do.

Mom had written that in her own notes so hard the pen almost tore the paper.

Mara smiled a little thinking about it.

Then she wrote:

Monday after Guide30.

My review is paused during the audit.

Paused is a weird word because it sounds calm, but really it just means everyone is waiting to see what happens next.

The Guide still works.

Mostly.

It still reminds me to leave for school and drink water and answer messages and go to dinner.

But school route overlays are limited right now, so today we had to read paper room lists like people in old movies.

Connor says he loves paper now. I do not believe him.

Dr. Voss said support can help some people.

She also said people should understand what kind of help they are getting.

Mom liked that part a lot.

Cam is not all the way back.

But today he was late and messy and dismissed his morning routine, so that seems like a very Cam kind of miracle.

Lila saved me a seat.

Nessa talked about Tobias, and I think I understand her more now.

Not completely.

But more.

Mara stopped and looked at the page.

The house was not silent. Mom was downstairs opening cabinets. Dad was talking on the phone in the low, careful voice he used when he was trying not to sound angry. Somewhere outside, a shuttle hummed past the building. The city was still moving. Still glowing. Still full of people probably reaching for answers before they knew what question they were asking.

Mara touched her pen to the page again.

I used to think prayer would feel like getting answers.

Like the right words would show up if I did it correctly.

But maybe prayer is not like that.

Maybe sometimes it feels like enough light for one step and not the whole map.

She hesitated.

That sounded like something Eli might say, or Grandpa Frank, or Mom in her journal when she was being dramatic in her twenties. Maybe it was too much.

Maybe it was true anyway.

Mara added one more line.

God, help me stay quiet enough to hear You.

She stared at it for a while.

Then underneath, smaller, she wrote:

And thank You for not leaving us alone in the quiet.

Downstairs, Mom called her name for dinner.

Mara closed the journal carefully and set it on her desk. The repaired page held. The newer pages were filling. Her handwriting was messier than Mom’s had been, and there was a tiny drawing of Connor holding a piece of paper like a sacred object in the corner of the page.

The Guide pulsed softly.

DINNER IN FIVE MINUTES.

SUGGESTED ROUTE: STAIRS.

Mara looked at the notification.

Then she looked at the bedroom door, the hallway, and the stairs she had walked down every day for years.

For a second, she almost laughed.

Not because it was funny.

Because she had once needed the Guide to tell her things she already knew.

Maybe she still would sometimes.

Maybe everyone would.

But not this time.

Mara dismissed the route.

Then she opened the door and went anyway.
